For older travelers booking a Branson / Table Rock cabin, the protective playbook: (1) book ONLY via Airbnb, VRBO, or Booking.com platform payment — NEVER Zelle, Venmo, Cash App, or wire transfer; (2) for direct-operator bookings, verify physical address and BBB rating: legitimate major operators include Branson Cabin Rentals (bransoncabinrentals.com), Table Rock Lake Vacation Rentals (tablerocklakevacation.com), and Branson Shores Resort (bransonshores.com); (3) for peak seasons (Memorial Day, July 4, Labor Day, Silver Dollar City's An Old Time Christmas in November-December), book 4–6 months ahead; (4) REFUSE 'last-minute deal' Facebook ads with Zelle-only payment — fraud 95%+ of the time; (5) confirm reservation number with the operator by phone 48 hours before arrival — verify property address; (6) 'cleaning fees' above $150 on 2-night stays are overcharges — dispute via Airbnb/VRBO or credit card. How to avoid: Book ONLY via Airbnb, VRBO, or Booking.com platform payment Verified operators: Branson Cabin Rentals, Table Rock Lake Vacation Rentals, Branson Shores Resort Book 4–6 months ahead for Memorial Day, July 4, Labor Day, Old Time Christmas Refuse last-minute Facebook cabin ads with Zelle-only payment Confirm reservation + property address 48h before arrival

Scam alert in Brasília, Brazil — Brasília (BSB) Airport Taxi & Late-Night Transfer Overcharge (transport, severity: moderate). Brasília International Airport (Aeroporto Juscelino Kubitschek, IATA BSB) sits 12 km SW of the Plano Piloto (the Lúcio Costa planned-city core) and 10 km from the Eixo Monumental + Esplanada dos Ministérios (the federal government monument corridor). Despite being a capital-city airport, 2025 late-night arrivals show a recurring taxi + rideshare overcharge pattern. Legitimate 2026 cost: Uber / 99 / Cabify from BSB to Asa Sul hotels (Carlton, Kubitschek Plaza, Grand Mercure) R$40–R$65 (20 min); to Asa Norte R$50–R$75 (25 min); to the Setor Hoteleiro Sul (SHS) R$35–R$55 (15 min); to Lago Sul (upmarket residential + embassies) R$70–R$110 (30 min); to Plano Piloto's Eixo Monumental (Congresso Nacional, Palácio do Planalto) R$45–R$65 (20 min). Budget public: the Ônibus 'Executivo Aeroporto-Rodoviária' links BSB to the Rodoviária do Plano Piloto at R$5.00 per person (40 min), runs 5 AM–11 PM. The 2025 scam patterns: (a) 'Taxi Comum' rank outside BSB quotes 'flat R$180 to Asa Sul' (real Uber R$40–R$65); (b) 'Special Taxi' / 'Taxi Executivo' kiosks quoting R$200–R$350 to Plano Piloto; (c) late-night arrivals (after midnight) — BSB has many congressional / business flights arriving 11 PM–2 AM; Uber wait times spike to 15–30 min and unlicensed drivers fill the gap; (d) Uber driver refusing in-app price after pickup, demanding cash top-up R$50 'because airport surcharge' — Uber Brazil has no airport surcharge; (e) hotel-arranged transfer at 30–50% markup vs Uber (hotel R$140, Uber R$50); (f) fake 'official Brasília tourism airport tour-desk' selling combined 'airport transfer + city-tour R$400' — real DIY: Uber + DIY walking of Eixo Monumental = R$60; (g) for late-night arrivals, some BSB taxis demand a 'night surcharge R$80' — legitimate night-surcharge is limited to 20% over daytime meter; (h) mototaxi street offers at the arrivals curbside — do NOT use with luggage or as a tourist. For travelers: (1) book Uber / 99 / Cabify on airport Wi-Fi AFTER luggage — confirm driver name + plate + photo match app BEFORE getting in; (2) meet driver at the designated 'Aplicativos' pickup zone — at BSB this is on the Upper Level Pick-Up / Desembarque Nível Superior (follow 'Aplicativos' signs from the arrivals hall, NOT 'Taxi' ranks); (3) for late-night arrivals (after 11 PM), pre-book a transfer via your hotel or Brasília Transfers at R$80–R$150 fixed — worth avoiding Uber-wait frustration in an unfamiliar city; (4) IGNORE every 'Taxi Comum' / 'Special Taxi' quote inside the terminal above R$100 — those are the overcharge operation; (5) NEVER hand a credit card to any taxi driver; (6) if your Uber driver demands cash top-up for 'airport surcharge', refuse + cancel in-app + use in-app safety button (there is no Uber Brazil airport surcharge); (7) for return to BSB, pre-book Uber the night before from your hotel — saves 20 min of pickup friction; (8) DEATUR Brasília +55 61 3362 5522 (Polícia Militar Turística, some English); Polícia Militar 190, SAMU 192. How to avoid: Uber / 99 / Cabify from BSB to Asa Sul R$40–R$65; to Asa Norte R$50–R$75 Meet driver at 'Aplicativos' zone on Upper Level Pick-Up (signposted) Late-night (after 11 PM): pre-book Brasília Transfers R$80–R$150 fixed IGNORE every 'Taxi' rank quote above R$100; NEVER hand card to driver DEATUR Brasília +55 61 3362 5522; Polícia Militar 190; SAMU 192

Scam alert in Brasília, Brazil — Esplanada dos Ministérios & Congresso Nacional Pickpocket & 'Tourist Guide' Scam (pickpocket, severity: moderate). The Esplanada dos Ministérios (a 2-km ceremonial boulevard anchoring the Palácio do Planalto, Congresso Nacional, STF supreme court, and Catedral Metropolitana) is Brasília's mandatory tourist circuit — and 2025 'tourist guide' scams + phone-snatch incidents cluster around the Three Powers Plaza. The 2025 scam patterns: (a) 'official tourist guide R$80–R$150' offered on the Esplanada by someone claiming Cadastur license — MOST are unlicensed; legitimate guides carry a visible Cadastur ID card, are listed in Brasília's tourism office database, and cost R$200–R$350 for a 2-hour tour (book via the official SETURC tourism office at www.turismobrasilia.com.br); (b) phone-snatch on the Esplanada walk — tourists take photos of the twin ministry buildings or Oscar Niemeyer's Congresso 'bowl' roof, a pedestrian or cyclist snatches the phone; (c) 'cadeira de roda acessível' (accessible chair) tourist-desk scam at the Catedral Metropolitana — offers to 'rent' a wheelchair R$100 for a 10-min cathedral visit (the Catedral has free accessibility assistance — request at reception); (d) 'mandatory Congresso Nacional tour R$60' offered in the parking area — the actual Palácio do Congresso guided tour is FREE (weekdays 10 AM, 11 AM, 3 PM; book at tours.congresso.leg.br 1–5 days ahead, bring passport); (e) 'exclusive Palácio da Alvorada tour R$200' — the Presidential residence Alvorada is currently closed to public tours per 2025 SFP security policy; 'exclusive' offers are fraudulent; (f) 'Brasília by night tour R$350 per person' with kickback commission stops at souvenir shops + overpriced Lago Paranoá restaurants (real DIY: Uber to Pontão Lago Sul sunset + Juscelino Kubitschek bridge photo R$40 round-trip); (g) Praça dos Três Poderes 'model photo' scam — 'take your picture with this historical flag R$50' using a regular Brazilian flag; (h) at the Catedral Metropolitana, 'mandatory donation R$30' demanded at the entrance — the cathedral is free; a voluntary donation box is inside the nave. For travelers: (1) for guided Esplanada tours, book via official SETURC tourism office (www.turismobrasilia.com.br) at R$200–R$350 for 2 hours — REFUSE every street-approach 'guide' offer; (2) the Congresso Nacional guided tour is FREE — book at tours.congresso.leg.br 1–5 days ahead (English tours available on request), bring passport for security check; (3) for the Palácio do Planalto, FREE guided tours on Sundays 9:30 AM–1:30 PM only — book at www.planalto.gov.br/presidencia/visita; (4) carry decoy phone + R$100 cash for the Esplanada walk; leave passport + cards in hotel safe; take photos QUICKLY then stow phone; (5) at the Catedral Metropolitana, entry is FREE (voluntary donation box inside nave) — REFUSE every 'mandatory donation' at entrance; (6) for the Lago Paranoá sunset + Juscelino Kubitschek bridge (a genuinely beautiful Brasília experience), Uber R$40–R$60 round-trip from Asa Sul — skip every 'private night tour R$350' offer; (7) for travelers, the gold-standard 1-day Brasília circuit: morning Catedral (9 AM) + Itamaraty Palace (guided tour Wed/Thu/Fri 2:30 PM, free with booking) + Esplanada walk + Congresso tour + lunch at Setor de Clubes Sul (Veleiros, Asa Delta, Pontão waterfront) + afternoon Memorial JK (tomb of Kubitschek, R$10) + sunset at Pontão; (8) DEATUR Brasília +55 61 3362 5522; Polícia Militar 190; SAMU 192. How to avoid: Book guide via official SETURC www.turismobrasilia.com.br R$200–R$350 for 2 hours Congresso tour FREE via tours.congresso.leg.br; Planalto FREE Sun 9:30 AM–1:30 PM Catedral entry FREE (voluntary donation inside only); Itamaraty guided Wed/Thu/Fri 2:30 PM Decoy phone + R$100 cash on Esplanada; passport + cards in hotel safe DEATUR Brasília +55 61 3362 5522; Polícia Militar 190

Scam alert in Brasília, Brazil — Brasília Restaurant Couvert + Serviço Padding & 'Comida por Kg' Weighing Trap (tourist-trap, severity: minor). Brasília's dining culture is dominated by weekday 'comida por kg' (pay-by-weight) lunch buffets + upscale Asa Sul / Asa Norte dinner restaurants — the pay-by-weight format is a 2025 tourist-overcharge vector alongside the standard couvert + serviço patterns. A person with a clipboard approaches and asks you to sign a petition for a good cause — disability rights, children's charities, environmental protection. You sign, feeling virtuous. Then they insist on a cash donation to accompany the signature, becoming pushy and sometimes following you. Your personal information is now on a clipboard with an unknown party. How to avoid: Never sign anything or hand over personal details to strangers on the street Ignore or walk past clipboard petitioners without engaging If you want to donate to a cause, do it through a verified charity website

Scam alert in Budapest, Hungary — Honey Trap Bar Scam (nightlife, severity: high). You're walking near the ruin bars when an attractive woman strikes up a friendly conversation and suggests you grab a drink together at a nearby bar she knows. The evening seems great — until the bill arrives for €500 to €5,000 for a few drinks. The bar is in on it, bouncers block the exit, and victims have reported being forced to make ATM withdrawals. This is one of Budapest's most serious and well-documented scams. How to avoid: Never follow strangers to bars they choose — pick your own or go to established ruin bars Check prices before ordering anything and see a written menu If you're handed a massive bill, know that many victims have successfully refused to pay and left — call the police if needed

Scam alert in Budapest, Hungary — Taxi Price Gouging (transport, severity: high). You hail a taxi outside a popular area and the driver mentions a 'special tourist rate' or the meter runs at triple speed. Some drivers take elaborate routes while the meter ticks up. Victims have been charged €50-100 for trips that should cost €10-15. Unofficial 'fake taxi' drivers also operate near the airport and party district. How to avoid: Only use Bolt (most popular app in Budapest) or licensed taxi companies like City Taxi Never get into an unmarked taxi Fares from airport to city center should be around 7,000-9,000 HUF

Scam alert in Budapest, Hungary — ATM Currency Conversion Trap (DCC) (money, severity: moderate). You use an ATM and it asks whether you want to complete the transaction in your home currency (e.g., USD/EUR) or in Hungarian Forints. The screen makes it seem like choosing your home currency is the helpful option. In reality, choosing your home currency activates Dynamic Currency Conversion — a terrible exchange rate that costs 5-15% more than letting your bank convert it. How to avoid: Always choose to pay/withdraw in local currency (Hungarian Forints) Use ATMs attached to actual banks rather than standalone machines Decline DCC at every ATM and card terminal in Hungary

Scam alert in Budapest, Hungary — Restaurant Bill Inflation (overcharging, severity: moderate). You sit down at a traditional Hungarian restaurant and order goulash and palinka. When the bill comes, it includes items you didn't order — bread, amuse-bouche, service charges — that weren't mentioned or priced on the menu. Some restaurants also charge extra for table service, bring unsolicited items, or pad the receipt with mysterious line items. How to avoid: Ask to see a full menu with prices before sitting down Send back any food you didn't order before touching it Ask for itemized receipt and compare to menu prices before paying

Scam alert in Budapest, Hungary — Fake Transport Pass Online (transport, severity: moderate). Before your trip, you find what appears to be BKK's (Budapest public transport) official Facebook page advertising discounted travel passes. The deal looks great — a 7-day pass for half price. You pay, receive a confirmation, but the pass either never arrives or is counterfeit and gets rejected at barriers. The Facebook page is a fake impersonating the real BKK. How to avoid: Only buy BKK passes from official BKK apps, official website, or station ticket offices Check the URL carefully — official site is bkk.hu If the deal seems too cheap to be real, it almost certainly is

Scam alert in Budapest, Hungary — Friendly Stranger Chess Game Hustle (distraction, severity: low). A friendly older man challenges you to a game of chess in the park, claiming it's a local tradition. He seems casual and friendly, and the stakes start small. But he's a skilled hustler who loses early on purpose, raises the stakes, and before you know it you're down €20-50 and he suddenly becomes much better at chess. It's a long-con version of street gambling. How to avoid: Only play games with strangers in formal public settings Never bet money in informal street games Enjoy watching chess in the park but decline to play for money

Scam alert in Buenos Aires, Argentina — Florida Avenue 'Cambio!' Touts & Counterfeit Peso Exchange (nightlife, severity: high). Calle Florida is Buenos Aires's main pedestrian shopping street and ground zero for Argentina's informal exchange (cambio) touts — men (arbolitos, 'little trees') who shout '¡Cambio, cambio! Dollar, euro!' at every passing tourist. Community reports document the 2025 pattern after Argentina's Milei-era peso reforms: the historic arbitrage between 'blue dollar' (informal) and official rate has largely collapsed in 2025 — as of late 2025 the blue dollar sometimes trades below the official rate. This means the classic 'get blue dollar from Florida Ave' advice is now often a net loss before fraud even enters the picture. Community reports document the economic inversion. The scam variants: (1) counterfeit peso bills passed as change; (2) bait-and-switch exchange rate (quoted rate drops once you commit); (3) distraction pickpocketing during the transaction; (4) fake 'cueva' (informal exchange office) upstairs that turns out to be a robbery setup. For older travelers in Buenos Aires, the 2025 defensive playbook: (1) refuse all Florida Ave '¡cambio!' approaches — 'No gracias' and keep walking; (2) for USD-to-peso conversion in 2025, Western Union (Plaza San Martín, Retiro branch, and 40+ other city locations) still offers the best rate for cash USD pickups — typically matches or beats blue rate with no counterfeit risk; (3) alternative: download Lemon Cash, Belo, or Ripio apps to receive USDT (stablecoin) and convert to pesos at in-app rates — Legal and competitive; (4) for card payments, most foreign credit cards now automatically apply the MEP/blue-equivalent rate via Argentina's tourist-card scheme (no IVA reimbursement needed) — verify with your card issuer; (5) if you must use an informal cueva, use an established one on the upper floors of Galería Güemes (Florida 165) or similar — never street-level with a stranger; (6) always count bills in daylight and check watermarks + security thread on every note (especially the 1000, 2000, and 10000-peso notes which have the highest counterfeit rate). How to avoid: Refuse all '¡cambio!' street approaches — 'No gracias' + walk Use Western Union for USD-to-peso cash pickup (best 2025 rate) Alternative: Lemon Cash / Belo / Ripio USDT apps for legal crypto conversion Foreign card payments in 2025 auto-apply MEP-equivalent rate — verify with issuer Always count bills in daylight; check watermark + security thread

Scam alert in Buenos Aires, Argentina — Buenos Aires Taxi 'Tacheros Estafadores' — Cloned Meter, Long Route, Short-Change (transport, severity: high). Community reports document Buenos Aires's persistent taxi-driver scam ecosystem through 2025, with travelers describing the pattern in trip-planning posts asking about areas to avoid. Three main variants operate in 2025: (1) Cloned Meter — the meter runs 2–3x legitimate rate; a San Telmo-to-Retiro ride that should cost ~ARS3,500 shows $10,000+ on the meter; drivers target obvious tourists with luggage; (2) Long Route — driver takes a 4–6 km detour ('traffic' excuse) on what should be a direct 2–3 km trip; (3) Counterfeit Return — you hand over a clean 10,000-peso note; driver quickly swaps it for a pre-prepared counterfeit, shows it back to you, claims it was counterfeit, and demands a clean replacement. Variant (4): floating tariff — driver has 'just changed tariff' mid-ride without authorization; refuses printed receipt. Variant (5): credit-card 'broken' — POS terminal 'fails' so you must pay cash, at which point counterfeit-return or rounded-up-cash scam runs. For older travelers in Buenos Aires, the 2025 defensive playbook: (1) use Uber, Cabify, or DiDi exclusively — all three operate legally in BA and bypass every taxi scam variant; fares are transparent and app-paid (no cash handling); Uber/Cabify from San Telmo to Recoleta runs ~$2,500–$4,000 ARS in 2025; (2) if you must take a street taxi, use only clearly-marked 'Radio Taxi' cars (yellow-and-black with roof light) — never unmarked or 'remis' flagged down on the street; (3) insist the meter starts at the base tariff (ARS260 in 2025, check sign on dashboard); watch it count up; (4) pay with small bills matched closely to the fare ($100 / $500 / $1,000 denominations) — never hand over a 10,000 or 20,000 peso note; (5) demand the printed receipt (recibo) and the driver's name/número; legitimate drivers always provide both; (6) for airport runs, use Manuel Tienda León shared-shuttle bus (ARS15,000), Tienda León private taxi ($35,000), or Uber — avoid Terminal-A 'Remis' touts. How to avoid: Use Uber / Cabify / DiDi exclusively — all legal, transparent fares in BA If street taxi: Radio Taxi only (yellow-and-black + roof light) Pay in small bills ($500/$1,000) matched to the fare — never $10,000+ Demand printed recibo + driver's name/número Airport: Manuel Tienda León shuttle ($15k) or Tienda León taxi ($35k)

Scam alert in Buenos Aires, Argentina — Bird Poop / Mustard Distraction Pickpocket (pickpocket, severity: high). Community reports document Buenos Aires's most effective distraction-pickpocket operation, with one 2025 solo traveler writing about falling for the scam; the canonical Southern-Cone variant has been documented since at least 2016 in Santiago. The setup runs in 3 phases: (1) a confederate squirts a liquid (mustard, ketchup, chocolate syrup, or actual bird-droppings simulant) onto the victim's back or shoulder from above or behind; (2) a second team member appears with napkins, offering to 'help clean' — they pat the victim down enthusiastically; (3) during the patting, a third team member lifts wallet, phone, or passport from an unzipped bag or back pocket. Peak-activity zones in Buenos Aires: Plaza de Mayo during weekday business hours, Caminito's narrow cobblestone streets, Recoleta Cemetery entrance queue, San Telmo Feria de Pedro crowded aisles, and Puerto Madero dinner-hour foot traffic. The scam often targets 55+ travelers because of slower reaction time and higher-value items (watches, camera gear). For older travelers in Buenos Aires, the defensive playbook: (1) if you feel anything hit your back/shoulder unexpectedly, do not stop — walk briskly to a shop entrance, cafe, or hotel lobby and check yourself in their bathroom mirror; (2) refuse all 'cleaning help' from strangers, no matter how apologetic or insistent they seem; the 'good Samaritan' is part of the team; (3) keep wallet in a front pocket or money belt under clothing — never in a back pocket or bag top; (4) keep phone + passport in separate locations (e.g., passport in hotel safe + phone in zipped bag + wallet in money belt) so one loss doesn't cascade; (5) in Caminito, Recoleta, and San Telmo peak hours, wear a small crossbody bag in front of your body with one hand on the strap; (6) if you're hit while alone with no nearby business, call '911' (BA emergency) or walk to the nearest cafe and use their bathroom; (7) report theft to the Comisaría Turística (Tourist Police, Av. Corrientes 436, +54 11 4346 5748, 24/7 English service) within 24h — Required for travel insurance claims. How to avoid: If something hits your back: walk briskly to a cafe/shop — Do NOT stop on the street Refuse all 'cleaning help' from strangers — the 'helper' is part of the team Wallet in front pocket or money belt; never back pocket or bag top Passport + cash in separate locations (hotel safe vs money belt) Report theft: Comisaría Turística Av. Corrientes 436, +54 11 4346 5748

Scam alert in Buenos Aires, Argentina — EZE / AEP Airport 'Remis' Overcharge & Meet-Greet Service Scam (transport, severity: moderate). Community reports document Buenos Aires airport-transfer scams and overlapping taxi-driver estafador patterns throughout 2025. EZE (Ezeiza) is 35 km from central Buenos Aires (45–60 min drive); AEP (Aeroparque) is 3 km from central BA (15–20 min). Legitimate 2025 options: (1) Manuel Tienda León shared bus from EZE to Retiro (downtown BA) — ARS15,000 one-way, departs every 30 min, scam-proof; (2) Manuel Tienda León private taxi at the official counter — $35,000–$45,000 ARS flat to most central addresses; (3) Uber/Cabify via app from EZE designated rideshare zone — typically $25,000–$40,000 ARS depending on surge; (4) from AEP, Uber/Cabify $6,000–$12,000 ARS to central BA. Scam variants: (1) 'Remis' touts in Terminal-A arrivals hall quoting $80,000–$150,000 ARS ('flat rate' 3–4x legitimate); (2) 'Private Meet & Greet Service' websites demanding USD prepayment at $80–$150 USD for what costs ARS35,000 ($35 USD) via Tienda León; (3) driver claims 'meter broken' then demands cash in USD; (4) driver takes indirect route via Autopista Ricchieri (adds 30% distance); (5) 'shared shuttle' tout charging per-person at ARS20,000 × 4 passengers when Tienda León bus is $15,000 one-way total. For older travelers arriving at EZE or AEP in 2025, the clean playbook: (1) walk past all 'Remis' and 'Meet & Greet' touts in the arrivals hall — they're unlicensed and overcharge; (2) proceed to the official Manuel Tienda León counter (clearly marked 'Tienda León' signage inside the terminal) for bus or taxi tickets — $15k/$35k respectively; (3) for Uber/Cabify/DiDi, walk to the designated rideshare pickup zone (EZE: 'Parking de Ride Sharing' signs outside Terminal A) and request via app — use WiFi in the arrivals hall to confirm fare screenshot before walking out; (4) if you prefer pre-booked, use Viator, GetYourGuide, or your hotel concierge (verified operators) — expect to pay $45–$60 USD for EZE-to-central-BA private; (5) refuse pre-booking via unfamiliar 'Meet & Greet' websites demanding USD prepayment; (6) always confirm the driver's license plate matches the app screenshot; photograph the plate before entering the car; (7) pay via app (Uber/Cabify/DiDi) or card at Tienda León — avoid cash payment at the end of the ride. How to avoid: Walk past all arrivals-hall 'Remis' / 'Meet & Greet' touts Manuel Tienda León bus $15k ARS to Retiro — buy at official counter inside terminal Tienda León private taxi $35k–$45k ARS at same counter Uber/Cabify/DiDi from designated rideshare zone with app fare screenshot Pay via app or card at Tienda León — avoid cash at end of ride

Scam alert in Buenos Aires, Argentina — Counterfeit Peso Bills Returned as Change (nightlife, severity: high). Community reports frame the counterfeit-peso pattern, which remains active in Argentina throughout 2025. Argentina's high-denomination bills (1000, 2000, 10000 pesos; 20000 note introduced 2024) have elevated counterfeit rates — particularly the 1000 and 2000 notes. The primary scam vectors: (1) unofficial 'cambio' / 'cueva' exchange returns a stack with 1–3 counterfeit bills mixed in; (2) taxi driver performs bill-switch — you hand over a clean note, driver shows you a counterfeit and demands a real replacement; (3) small-shop clerk gives change with counterfeits after you pay with a large denomination; (4) street-vendor 'Mercado Pago' QR scam where the scan shows a payment that was reversed; (5) ATMs at small independent operators (not Banco Nación, Santander, BBVA, HSBC, or Galicia main branches) occasionally dispense counterfeit. For older travelers in Buenos Aires in 2025, the defensive playbook: (1) know the security features: genuine 1000-peso note (General Juan Manuel de Rosas) has a 3D-effect security thread, watermark of Rosas's face, and color-shifting '1000' in lower right corner; genuine 2000-peso note (Ramón Carrillo + Cecilia Grierson) has a color-shifting '2000' and tactile relief; (2) always count exchange and change in daylight or strong artificial light — Hold each high-denomination bill up to the light to check watermark; (3) if a bill feels 'flat' or 'papery' rather than having the tactile relief of genuine pesos, it's counterfeit — Real pesos have raised ink you can feel; (4) use cards (Visa/Mastercard) for any transaction over ARS50,000 — Virtually eliminates counterfeit-return risk; (5) use ATMs only at Banco Nación, Santander Río, BBVA, HSBC, Galicia, or Macro main branches — Not at street-level small ATMs in pharmacies or mini-markets; (6) for taxi payment, match bills as close as possible to the fare — ARS3,500 ride should be paid with $3,500 or $4,000 in small bills, not a $10,000 bill; (7) if you receive suspected counterfeit, report to the Banco Central (BCRA) hotline at 0800-999-6663 and the Comisaría Turística. How to avoid: Count all exchange + change in daylight — Hold up to light for watermark Feel for tactile relief on genuine pesos (raised ink on portrait + numerals) Use Visa/Mastercard for transactions over ARS50,000 ATMs: Banco Nación / Santander / BBVA / HSBC / Galicia / Macro main branches only Pay taxis with small bills ($500/$1,000) matched to fare — never $10,000+

Scam alert in Buenos Aires, Argentina — Buenos Aires Airbnb / Temporary Rental Off-Platform & 'Illegal Cash' Fraud (nightlife, severity: high). Community reports document the 2025 Buenos Aires-specific Airbnb fraud pattern, including a traveler who booked a month-long Buenos Aires Airbnb and couldn't check in, alongside broader platform-level reports on Buenos Aires 'cash-only' TOS-violation fraud. Argentina's long-term rental market (mes por mes, 'month by month') traditionally priced in USD cash due to peso instability, and Milei-era reforms haven't fully changed the informal-cash culture by 2025. Common scam patterns: (1) Airbnb host requests the stay be 'paid partly via Airbnb, partly in USD cash on arrival' to 'avoid Argentina taxes' — this violates Airbnb TOS and leaves the guest with zero protection on the cash portion; if anything goes wrong, Airbnb support treats the reservation as fraudulent; (2) off-platform WhatsApp 'Buenos Aires long-term rental' listings demanding USD cash on arrival + 'deposit' — property is often fake, host disappears; (3) Facebook Marketplace 'Palermo apartment' at 30% below market rate with Zelle/PayPal/crypto demand; (4) legitimate-seeming 'host' photos stolen from real Airbnb listings; (5) in-person viewing where 'landlord' shows the apartment then disappears after cash hand-off. For older travelers booking Buenos Aires accommodation, the protective playbook: (1) book short-term stays only through Airbnb, VRBO, or Booking.com platform payment in full — never accept 'partly cash on arrival' requests, regardless of what the host says about Argentina taxes (it's a TOS violation and invalidates your protection); (2) for long-term stays (1+ month), use ZonaProp, ArgenProp, or Remax Argentina (the three legitimate local real-estate portals) — never WhatsApp or Facebook Marketplace listings; (3) for USD-cash-required legitimate rentals, require a signed Spanish-language contract (contrato de alquiler temporario) with the landlord's DNI (national ID) + property escritura (title) information; (4) pay any USD cash via Western Union transfer (generates a paper trail) rather than hand-to-hand; (5) legitimate Buenos Aires hotels and serviced apartments: Alvear Palace Hotel (Recoleta), Palacio Duhau - Park Hyatt, Faena Hotel (Puerto Madero), NH Collection Buenos Aires Jousten, Hotel Madero; (6) avoid Palermo / Recoleta 'luxury apartment' ads at <50% of comparable verified listings — Too-good-to-be-true is the tell; (7) report fraud to the Defensa del Consumidor (consumer protection, 0800-666-1518) and to the Comisaría Turística. How to avoid: Book STRs only through Airbnb / VRBO / Booking.com platform payment in full Long-term rentals: ZonaProp / ArgenProp / Remax Argentina only — never WhatsApp If USD cash is legally required: signed Spanish contract + landlord DNI + property escritura Pay USD cash via Western Union (paper trail) — never hand-to-hand Report fraud: Defensa del Consumidor 0800-666-1518 + Comisaría Turística

Scam alert in Búzios, Brazil — Rio-to-Búzios Private Transfer Overcharge & 1001 Bus Alternative (transport, severity: moderate). Búzios is Rio state's premier weekend beach getaway — 175 km east, 2.5–3 hr drive — and the transfer ecosystem hosts a 2025 overcharge pattern targeting foreigners unfamiliar with the budget alternatives. Legitimate fares (2025): 1001 Auto Viação direct bus from Rio Rodoviária Novo Rio terminal to Búzios is R$95–R$130 (2.5–3 hr, 4–6 daily departures). Private transfer via reputable operators (BR Transfers, Carioca Transfers, Rio Transfer Service): R$350–R$500 per car (1–4 passengers). Uber Rio-to-Búzios is theoretically possible but often R$600–R$900 due to the long inter-city ride. The 2025 scams: (a) GIG airport tour-desk 'private transfer to Búzios R$1,200–R$2,000' (3–4× real reputable rate); (b) Rio Zona Sul hotel concierge 'recommended driver R$1,500' kickback markup; (c) 'shared shuttle van R$250 per person' that's identical to 1001 bus at 2× the price; (d) WhatsApp 'private apartment + transfer combo US$400 per person' bundled with kickback markup; (e) Búzios Rodoviária arrival 'taxi to your pousada R$150' for trips under 2 km (real R$30–R$50 via local taxis or 5-min walk); (f) return-Rio quote inflated as urgency at end-of-trip ('only R$1,800 available today, last bus sold out'); (g) 'door-to-door' driver claiming insurance includes Costa do Sol toll fees — toll is R$26 each way and should be in quoted price. For travelers: (1) take 1001 Auto Viação bus from Novo Rio terminal R$95–R$130 — comfortable air-conditioned coach with reclining seats, restroom, WiFi; book at 1001.com.br 1–2 weeks ahead in high season; (2) for door-to-door private, book BR Transfers or Carioca Transfers via direct website at R$350–R$500 per car; (3) IGNORE every GIG / hotel-concierge 'recommended transfer' above R$800; (4) at Búzios Rodoviária, walk to Rua das Pedras (center) in 5–10 min, or local taxi R$30–R$50 to most pousadas (Búzios is small, 9 km long); (5) for return to Rio, book 1001 ticket at the Búzios Rodoviária box office on arrival OR online; refuse 'last bus' urgency upsells; (6) Costa do Sol highway tolls (R$26 each way) should be included in private-transfer quotes — NOT a surprise add-on; (7) for a budget-conscious Rio-Búzios round-trip, total bus cost is R$190–R$260 vs private R$700–R$1,000. How to avoid: 1001 Auto Viação bus Novo Rio-Búzios R$95–R$130 (book 1001.com.br) Private door-to-door: BR Transfers or Carioca Transfers R$350–R$500 per car IGNORE 'recommended transfer' offers above R$800 At Búzios Rodoviária, walk 5–10 min to center OR local taxi R$30–R$50 Costa do Sol toll R$26 each way should be included in private quote

Scam alert in Búzios, Brazil — Búzios Beach-Hopping Schooner Tour Overcharge & Unlicensed Operators (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). The Búzios beach-hopping schooner tour (Passeio de Escuna) — a 5–6 hour boat trip stopping at 8–12 of the peninsula's beaches with snorkelling and a buffet — is the destination's flagship excursion and hosts a 2025 overcharge + unlicensed-operator ecosystem. Legitimate cost: a reputable group schooner tour (Buzios Trolley, Tour Shop, Maravilhas do Mar) is R$80–R$130 per person for 5–6 hours including buffet lunch + snorkel gear + soft drinks; with cocktails / open bar add R$50. Private speedboat or yacht charter is R$800–R$2,500 per group (4–8 people). The 2025 scam patterns: (a) Rua das Pedras pier-front touts selling 'private schooner R$600 per person' (real group tour R$80–R$130); (b) 'VIP exclusive route to Praia das Caravelas R$1,200' — Caravelas is a public beach included in the standard route; (c) unlicensed boats without life jackets, VHF radio, insurance, or Marinha (Brazilian Navy) registration — documented serious safety issues during summer storms; (d) 'all-inclusive open bar premium R$350 per person' that's the standard tour with 2 extra beers; (e) 'glass-bottom boat upgrade R$200' — glass-bottom boats exist but the regular schooner stops at all the same snorkel sites; (f) 'private chef on-board R$800' — included buffet is a generic Brazilian beach lunch served on every reputable tour; (g) 'photo + drone video package R$400' upsells that rarely deliver. For travelers: (1) book schooner tour ONLY through Google 4.5+ operators with at least 50 reviews: Buzios Trolley (Pier Marina), Tour Shop (Rua das Pedras), Maravilhas do Mar (Praia da Armação) — R$80–R$130 per person 5–6 hours; (2) VERIFY life jackets for every passenger BEFORE boarding; check operator's Marinha registration sticker on the boat (mandatory for licensed Brazilian boats); (3) REFUSE every 'private schooner' / 'VIP exclusive' / 'all-inclusive premium' upsell; the group tour is the same experience; (4) pre-book online at the operator website 2–3 days ahead in high season (Dec–Feb, July) — the popular boats sell out; (5) bring biodegradable sunscreen ONLY — Búzios beaches have coral; (6) for travelers with motion-sickness, take Dramamine 30 min before departure; sit in the center of the boat (less rocking); (7) the standard 12-beach stops include João Fernandes, Azeda, Azedinha, Tartaruga, Ferradura, Forno, Brava — verify your operator covers these; (8) skip the 'cocktail open bar add-on' — overpriced; bring your own can drinks for the boat ride. How to avoid: Book Google 4.5+: Buzios Trolley, Tour Shop, Maravilhas do Mar R$80–R$130 Verify life jackets + Marinha registration sticker BEFORE boarding REFUSE every 'private' / 'VIP' / 'premium' upsell Pre-book 2–3 days ahead in high season (Dec–Feb, July) Standard route: João Fernandes, Azeda, Azedinha, Tartaruga, Ferradura

Scam alert in Búzios, Brazil — Búzios Rua das Pedras Restaurant Tourist-Menu & 'Couvert Artístico' Bill-Padding (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Búzios Rua das Pedras (the cobblestone main street with most tourist restaurants) hosts a 2025 bill-padding ecosystem common to Brazilian beach destinations, plus a unique 'couvert artístico' (artistic cover charge for live music) inflation pattern. The 2025 scam patterns: (a) Rua das Pedras waterfront restaurants with USD-only menus at 2–3× local prices (Brazilian moqueca dish US$35+ vs R$80–R$120 at non-tourist spots); (b) 'couvert artístico' (artistic cover) added at R$80–R$200 per person for 'live music' that's a single guitarist playing 30 min; legitimate couvert artístico is R$15–R$40 per person and disclosed before seating; (c) 'serviço 10%' (service charge) added — Brazilian law requires this be OPTIONAL but waiters often present as mandatory; you can refuse; (d) 'agua mineral R$25' (real R$6–R$12) — bottled water padding; (e) 'lagosta peso variável' (lobster, market price) verbal quotes at R$800–R$1,500 per kg without weight disclosed; (f) credit-card surcharge 5–10% added unannounced; (g) bill-switcheroo where R$ amount on receipt differs from what's charged to card by R$100–R$500. For travelers: (1) eat 1–2 blocks OFF Rua das Pedras at authentic Búzios spots: Cigalon (Orla Bardot waterfront, Google 4.7+, French-Brazilian), Sawasdee (Thai, Manguinhos), Bar do David (working-class spot Centro), Fishbone (Praia da Armação seafood) — transparent pricing R$70–R$180 per meal; (2) BEFORE sitting, ask for the menu and CONFIRM (a) couvert artístico amount per person, (b) 'serviço 10%' policy (you can refuse), (c) credit-card surcharge — photograph the menu; (3) for water, order 'água sem gás copo' (tap water glass, free) at most spots OR bring your own bottled water (can-drinks usually allowed at sit-down tables); (4) for seafood, agree weight in writing BEFORE cooking — fair lobster R$400–R$700 per kg (1 kg feeds 2); fair red snapper R$80–R$150 per kg; (5) 'serviço' is OPTIONAL by Brazilian law (Lei 13.419/2017 makes it explicit) — tip 10% if happy with service, refuse if not; (6) USD-priced menus pad 10–15% exchange — request real R$ amount; (7) for sunset cocktails, the Orla Bardot promenade boardwalk (free public space) with view of bay is more atmospheric than overpriced 'sunset bar' tables. How to avoid: Eat off Rua das Pedras: Cigalon, Sawasdee, Bar do David, Fishbone BEFORE sitting confirm couvert / serviço / card surcharge in writing 'Serviço 10%' is OPTIONAL (Lei 13.419/2017); refuse if poor service Lobster: agree weight × R$400–R$700/kg in writing BEFORE cooking Sunset: free Orla Bardot boardwalk beats overpriced sunset-bar tables

How to avoid: Buy tickets only at the official booth — there is no secondary 'registration' required Real tourist police in Egypt wear light blue uniforms with official insignia — not casual khaki If approached by someone claiming authority, walk to the main ticket desk and verify with staff there Don't hand over your passport to anyone at the pyramids unless it's the official ticket window The Giza tourist police hotline is 02-3376-7888 — save it before visiting

At the Citadel, a different man tells you there's a separate photography permit needed for your DSLR — also 50 pounds. Both are unofficial extractions that work on tourists who don't know the rules.
