A third variant uses Google Ads targeting 'best fado in Lisbon' and 'Lisbon fado tickets,' routing to third-party reseller domains marking up authentic-venue tickets 50–100% (authentic Mesa de Frades at €60/person becomes €110 via reseller). Book direct at community-vetted fado houses. Mesa de Frades, in a former 18th-century chapel on Rua dos Remédios in Alfama, runs €50–€70 for dinner + show. A Baiuca, a traditional family-run venue on Rua de São Miguel, is €30–€45. Clube de Fado (Rua de São João da Praça) is the established classic at €50–€75. And Tasca do Chico, on Rua do Diário de Notícias in Bairro Alto, hosts amateur-led nightly 'fado vadio' starting 8 PM with no cover charge — just pay for drinks. For older travelers prioritizing a single high-quality experience, Mesa de Frades is the community benchmark. Avoid: Baixa street touts; hotel concierge 'fado dinner' upsells (book direct instead); Google Ads reseller domains; any venue without visible RNEAL licensing. For the most affordable authentic experience, Tasca do Chico's 'fado vadio' (amateur/student) nights are €0 cover — just order drinks and dinner normally, and the fado is a free community tradition. How to avoid: Book direct at community-vetted fado houses: Mesa de Frades, A Baiuca, Clube de Fado (Alfama); Tasca do Chico (Bairro Alto, free 'fado vadio') For free authentic experience, Tasca do Chico's nightly amateur 'fado vadio' (8 PM start) has zero cover charge — just pay for drinks/dinner Avoid: Baixa street touts, hotel-concierge 'fado dinner' upsells, Google Ads reseller domains Verify RNEAL licensing before paying; check venue's own website (not a reseller); look for established reputation and local reviews in Portuguese For older travelers, choose early show (8 PM–9 PM) over late (11 PM+) — quieter crowd, easier walk back to hotel, Alfama cobbles are steep

Scam alert in Lisbon, Portugal — Lisbon Metro Ticket Machine 'Helper' Distraction Scam (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Lisbon Metro stations concentrate a specific 'helper' distraction scam targeting older tourists struggling with the Viva Viagem card system, which has a famously unfriendly interface — a recurring community complaint is that the public transport ticketing system is actively hostile to tourists. The pattern: tourist approaches ticket machine, fumbles with €1.65 single-ride purchase, a friendly English-speaking 'local' offers to 'help.' In the simplest form, the helper enters the transaction, receives cash from tourist, pockets €5–€10 of the 'change.' A second version uses a card-skimming sleeve installed over the machine card slot to capture card details during 'help.' A third twist has the 'helper' distract tourist at the machine while accomplice lifts wallet or phone from open bag. Community reports document both the hostile UX and the helper-scam overlay in detail. The Metro Red Line airport station, Baixa-Chiado interchange, and Rossio exits are the highest-density helper-scam spots because they concentrate first-time visitors. A fourth angle is the 'buy my ticket' approach where a stranger says 'I have an extra ticket, only €2' and sells you a used or counterfeit Viva Viagem — a country-wide pattern. The fifth pattern targets the Santa Justa elevator queue: offers to 'validate' a Viva Viagem card that doesn't need validation, pocketing the 'validation fee' of €2–€5. The Paris Metro has the same 'helper' pattern, which applies identically to Lisbon. Buy the rechargeable Viva Viagem card (€0.50 one-time card fee, loaded with €1.65 single ride or €6.80 day pass) at the Metro ticket office (bilheteira) inside each station where a real uniformed Metro Lisboa employee runs the counter — not at the self-service machines if you're a first-time visitor. Carry exact coins for any machine use; refuse all helpers at machines regardless of claimed goodwill ('obrigado, não preciso de ajuda'). Never buy a Viva Viagem card from a stranger offering 'extra tickets.' never hand your card or cash to anyone at a Metro machine. If you're confused about the machine interface, walk to the bilheteira or ask a uniformed Metro employee identified by the Metropolitano de Lisboa badge. Save PSP Turismo (+351 21 342 1634) in phone to report any helper-scam attempt. How to avoid: Buy Viva Viagem card at the Metro ticket office (bilheteira) from a uniformed Metropolitano de Lisboa employee — NOT self-service machines for first-time visitors Refuse all helpers at Metro machines with 'obrigado, não preciso de ajuda' and keep walking Never buy a Viva Viagem card from a stranger offering 'extra rides' — always fresh-purchase at the bilheteira Carry exact coins for machine use; shield the card slot with your hand when tapping to prevent skimmer-device observation Save PSP Turismo (+351 21 342 1634) in phone; report any helper-scam attempt immediately

Scam alert in Lisbon, Portugal — Lisbon Street Drug-Tout Counterfeit 'Hashish' Scam (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Rossio and surrounding Baixa squares concentrate a specific Lisbon street-drug scam that targets male tourists (solo and in couples). The pattern: a 'dealer' approaches offering 'hashish,' 'cocaine,' 'weed,' or 'Xanax' at aggressive low prices (€10–€20 for 'a gram'). The products are always fake — soap, oregano, aspirin, baking soda, or wood shavings — sold as drugs because actual drug-possession prosecution is complex and victims rarely report. Community reports document the demographic targeting (primarily male tourists) and the fake-substance consistency, and list it among the top Lisbon scams. The scam has three escalation patterns beyond simple fake-drug sales. Pattern 1 — 'quality upsell' where initial €10 becomes 'better quality for €30' with intensifying pressure. Pattern 2 — 'police trick' where a second 'dealer' approaches claiming to be plainclothes police, demanding €100–€300 'fine' or 'bribe' to avoid arrest — this is 100% fake, Portuguese police do not operate this way and Portugal decriminalized small-quantity drug possession in 2001. Pattern 3 — tout leads tourist to a 'quieter alley' for the transaction and robs them directly. This last variant is rare but documented. A fourth pattern works after hours: touts on Bairro Alto street corners offer drugs to tourists returning tipsy from bars, and escalate to bag-snatch or wallet-lift if the buyer refuses. The right response to all drug-tout approaches is firm refusal and steady forward walk without engagement. Say 'não, obrigado' or just 'no' and keep walking. Never engage in price discussion or demonstrate interest — this is what the scam targets. If approached by 'plainclothes police' claiming to be investigating drugs, the authentic Lisbon pattern is NO plainclothes drug stops on the street of random tourists — demand to see a PSP/GNR badge and request to walk to the nearest police station (they'll vanish). For older travelers, avoid Rossio and Restauradores after 10 PM and Bairro Alto alleys after 11 PM; stick to well-lit main arteries (Rua Augusta, Rua da Prata). Save PSP Turismo (+351 21 342 1634, English-speaking 24/7) in phone. If harassed or threatened, walk into the nearest café or hotel lobby and ask them to call the police. Portuguese drug decriminalization does NOT legalize sales — dealers are operating illegally regardless of substance authenticity. How to avoid: Say firm 'não, obrigado' or 'no' to all drug-tout approaches and keep walking — never engage in price discussion If approached by 'plainclothes police' claiming drug investigation, demand PSP/GNR badge and request walk to nearest police station (they'll vanish) Avoid Rossio and Restauradores after 10 PM and Bairro Alto alleys after 11 PM; stick to well-lit main arteries (Rua Augusta, Rua da Prata) Save PSP Turismo (+351 21 342 1634, English-speaking 24/7); emergency 112 for threats or harassment If harassed, walk into nearest café/hotel lobby and ask them to call police; Portuguese drug decriminalization does NOT legalize sales

Scam alert in Liverpool, United Kingdom — Football Match Day Taxi Cherry-Picking (transport, severity: moderate). You're leaving Anfield after a Liverpool match and flag a black cab to take you to Lime Street station. The driver doesn't switch on the meter and quotes £20 for the trip. If the meter had been running, the fare would have been £7-9. You're one of thousands of fans streaming out of the ground, it's raining, and the next train is in 40 minutes — so you pay.

Liverpool City Council's licensing enforcement officers specifically target this behavior through Operation Topaz, which runs during football season. The Liverpool Express reported that 'licensing officers take part in Operation Topaz, which targets rogue cab and private hire drivers who prey on fans.' Last season, 17 hackney carriage drivers were reported for 'demanding higher fares than they would have received from a metered trip,' a practice known locally as 'cherry-picking.' A further 18 private hire drivers were caught 'plying for hire' — picking up street fares without pre-booking, which is illegal for private hire vehicles.

The council issues specific taxi scam warnings at the start of each football season. The advice: always insist the meter is on in a black cab, and only use pre-booked private hire vehicles (Delta Taxis, Alpha Taxis, or Uber). If a driver refuses the meter, report them to Liverpool Licensing. How to avoid: Always insist the meter is running in a black cab — this is legally required in Liverpool Use Uber or pre-book with Delta Taxis or Alpha Taxis for transparent pricing Know the approximate fare: Anfield to Lime Street should be £7-9 on the meter If a driver refuses to use the meter, note their cab number and report to Liverpool Licensing Consider the Anfield-to-Sandhills train service as a scam-proof alternative to taxis on match days

Scam alert in Liverpool, United Kingdom — Matthew Street and Cavern Quarter Nightlife Overcharge (nightlife, severity: moderate). You head to the famous Matthew Street area, home of the Cavern Club, for a night out. The first bar seems reasonable. By the third venue, prices have crept up. You order rounds without checking prices and wake up to a credit card bill of £180 for what you thought was a £50 night. Some bars on Matthew Street charge £8-10 for drinks that would be £4-5 a block away. The tourist tax on Matthew Street is well-known locally, but first-time visitors drawn by the Beatles heritage rarely check prices before ordering.

TravelSafe's Liverpool guide notes that visitors are 'way more likely to get mugged off by both a minute number of scummy drunk and scufflin' scousers AND the bar prices in cavern quarter (matthew st, home of the cavern club).' The Cavern Club itself is a legitimate venue with fair pricing, but the surrounding bars exploit the area's fame with tourist-oriented pricing. Reolink's Liverpool safety analysis confirms that nightlife areas have higher rates of alcohol-fueled incidents and tourist-targeted overcharging.

The defense: check prices before ordering (they should be displayed), explore bars outside the Matthew Street tourist bubble (Bold Street and the Baltic Triangle have better prices and atmospheres), and pay per round rather than running a tab. How to avoid: Check drink prices before ordering at every new venue — prices should be displayed behind the bar Pay per round rather than running a tab, keeping track of your spending Explore Bold Street, the Baltic Triangle, and Smithdown Road for better-priced bars favored by locals Visit the Cavern Club for the heritage experience but drink at non-tourist bars nearby for value Set a cash budget for the night and leave cards at the hotel to avoid overspending

Scam alert in Liverpool, United Kingdom — Fake Charity Collector Fraud (nightlife, severity: moderate). A man approaches you on Church Street wearing a lanyard and carrying a clipboard with a Marie Curie logo. He tells you an emotionally compelling story about a sick relative and asks for a cash donation. His pitch is polished and persuasive. You give £20. The money never reaches any charity — the man is running a fraud, using fake identification and fabricated stories to collect cash from sympathetic passersby.

A real case: William Redmond, 33, from Walton Breck Road, Liverpool, was sentenced to four-and-a-half years in prison at Liverpool Crown Court for two counts of fraud by false representation. Merseyside Police reported that he 'originally told the victim that he was working for the charity Marie Curie and then fabricated other reasons why he needed more money.' The Crown Prosecution Service documented a broader fraud gang 'jailed after stealing charity donations in organized scam' operating across UK cities including Liverpool.

Legitimate charity collectors in the UK carry verifiable ID from the Fundraising Regulator and will never ask for cash — they set up direct debit payments. If someone asks for cash, they are not a legitimate charity collector. How to avoid: Never give cash to street collectors — legitimate charity fundraisers set up direct debits and carry verifiable ID If you want to donate, give directly through the charity's website rather than to a street collector Ask to see their Fundraising Regulator badge and note the charity's official phone number to verify Politely say 'no thank you' and keep walking — do not stop to hear the pitch Report suspicious collectors to the Fundraising Regulator (0300 999 3407) or Merseyside Police

Scam alert in Liverpool, United Kingdom — QR Code Parking Meter Scam (Quishing) (nightlife, severity: high). You park near the Albert Dock and walk to the pay-and-display machine. There's a QR code on the machine with a sticker saying 'Pay Here — Quick and Easy.' You scan it with your phone. The website looks exactly like the PayByPhone parking app. You enter your car registration, parking duration, and bank card details. Except the website is a sophisticated fake — a phishing site that captures your card details. You don't get a valid parking ticket (risking a real fine), and within days your card is used for fraudulent purchases. Some victims have also been unknowingly signed up for recurring subscription charges.

This 'quishing' (QR code phishing) scam has swept UK car parks. Liverpool City Council itself posted a warning on Facebook: 'If you see a QR code like this on a parking meter — DO NOT scan it. This is a scam.' The Bureau of Investigative Journalism reported that 'quishing' had hit 123 out of 373 UK local authorities surveyed, with Action Fraud receiving nearly 800 reports totaling £3.5 million in losses in the 12 months to April 2025. One victim who parked in Cirencester had £406 stolen from her account after a fake QR code mimicked the PayByPhone website. Carwow's guide confirms that fake QR codes are 'plastered on ticket machines or street signs' and lead to sites that mimic legitimate parking apps.

The defense: never scan QR codes on parking machines. Instead, download the official parking app (PayByPhone, RingGo, or JustPark) directly from the App Store or Google Play, or pay with coins at the machine. How to avoid: Never scan QR codes on parking machines — download the official app (PayByPhone, RingGo, JustPark) directly from the App Store or Google Play Pay with coins or contactless at the machine if the app isn't available If you must scan, check the URL carefully before entering any payment details Report suspicious QR codes to Liverpool City Council and the parking operator If you've entered details on a suspicious site, freeze your card immediately and contact your bank

Scam alert in Liverpool, United Kingdom — Petition Distraction Pickpocketing (pickpocket, severity: moderate). You're walking through the Church Street pedestrian zone when a person with a clipboard approaches ... You're walking through the Church Street pedestrian zone when a person with a clipboard approaches asking you to sign a petition for an environmental cause. While you stop to read the petition and hold the pen, your focus is entirely on the clipboard. An accomplice behind you slips a hand into your jacket pocket or unzips your backpack. The petition is meaningless — it's a prop designed to keep your hands busy and your eyes forward for 30 seconds.

Rick Steves' Europe-wide tourist scam guide documents the petition scam as one of the most common distraction techniques across European tourist cities. GoDigit's UK tourist scam guide confirms that 'a petitioner demanding a cash donation' is a known UK variant, 'and at worst, people can be pickpocketed while distracted by the petitioner.' The Guard Mark security analysis of UK pickpocketing ranks Liverpool among cities where the distraction technique is used at transport hubs and pedestrian shopping areas.

The defense: never stop for clipboard petitioners on busy streets. If you want to support a cause, look it up online later. Keep your valuables in zipped front pockets. How to avoid: Politely decline and keep walking — say 'no thank you' without stopping Keep valuables in zipped front pockets, especially in crowded pedestrian areas If you do stop, maintain awareness of who's around you and keep your bag in front of you Support causes online through official websites rather than through street signature campaigns Be especially alert around Lime Street station, Church Street, and Albert Dock

Scam alert in Liverpool, United Kingdom — Drink Spiking in Nightclubs (nightlife, severity: high). You're out with friends at a club on Seel Street. You set your drink on a table to check your phone and pick it up again a minute later. Within 30 minutes, you feel dramatically more intoxicated than you should after two drinks. Your legs are weak, your vision blurs, and you can barely stand. You've been spiked. In the worst reported cases, victims were robbed of phones, wallets, and jewelry after being incapacitated. During the UK's 2021-2022 spiking crisis, some victims reported being spiked by needle injection — feeling a sharp prick in their arm or leg on a crowded dance floor before losing consciousness.

Liverpool was one of the UK cities at the center of the 2021-2022 spiking wave. Liverpool World reported a Liverpool student who was 'traumatised after becoming victim of needle spiking in nightclub.' The National Police Chiefs' Council documented 1,382 needle spiking reports across the UK by January 2022, with the peak coinciding with university term start. The wave led to a national 'Girls Night In' boycott of nightclubs. Euronews covered the phenomenon spreading from the UK to France, calling it an alarming new trend.

While the needle spiking wave subsided, drink spiking remains a persistent risk. Never leave your drink unattended, use drink covers (StopTopps or silicone cup covers), and if you feel unusually intoxicated, tell your friends immediately and leave together. How to avoid: Never leave your drink unattended — take it with you even to the bathroom Use drink covers (StopTopps lids or silicone covers) to prevent anything being dropped in Go out with a group and agree to watch each other throughout the night If you feel unexpectedly ill or intoxicated, tell your friends immediately and leave together If you suspect spiking, go to A&E immediately and report to both the police and the venue

Scam alert in Liverpool, United Kingdom — Unlicensed Private Hire Vehicle Plying for Hire (nightlife, severity: moderate). It's 2 AM outside a club on Concert Square. The taxi rank queue is 45 minutes long and it's raining. A car pulls up and the driver offers you a ride. It looks like a private hire vehicle, but it hasn't been pre-booked through a licensed operator. This is 'plying for hire' — illegal for private hire vehicles in England — and the driver may not be licensed, insured, or vetted. You get in and the driver charges £25 for a £10 trip. Without a booking through a licensed operator, you have no recourse and no record of the journey.

Liverpool City Council's Operation Topaz specifically targets this behavior. Last season, 18 private hire drivers were reported for plying for hire around the city center and football grounds. The council's official guidance warns that unlicensed vehicles pose safety risks beyond just overcharging — passengers have no insurance coverage, no driver vetting verification, and no GPS-tracked journey record. Zoom Taxi's guide on spotting unlicensed cabs notes that a real licensed private hire vehicle will always have a plate on the rear bumper and a disk on the windscreen.

Always pre-book through a licensed operator (Uber, Delta Taxis, Alpha Taxis) or take a black cab from an official rank. Check for the rear bumper plate and windscreen disk before getting into any vehicle. How to avoid: Always pre-book through Uber, Delta Taxis, or Alpha Taxis rather than accepting rides from vehicles that approach you Check for the rear bumper plate and windscreen disk that all licensed private hire vehicles must display Use official black cab ranks rather than flagging random vehicles on the street after midnight If using a cab rank, confirm the meter is on before the journey starts Plan your transport home before going out — pre-book a return ride for a specific time

Scam alert in Lombok, Indonesia — Lombok Praya Airport (LOP/BIL) Taxi Mafia & Kuta-Lombok Transfer Overcharge (transport, severity: high). Lombok Praya Airport (LOP) has an entrenched 2025 taxi-mafia pattern that mirrors Bali's DPS problem but worse — the airport is 40km from Kuta-Lombok (the main tourist base) and tourists are targeted by price-gouging at the arrivals kerb. Community reports document the transfer-overcharge pattern in detail. The scam: airport 'Bluebird' or 'Koperasi Taxi' kiosks quote Rp 500K–1M (US$30–$65) for the Kuta-Lombok transfer vs the real Grab rate of Rp 200K–300K (US$13–$20), 45–60 min drive. At arrivals a separate layer of sign-holders offers 'fixed price to Kuta 400K, 500K, 700K' and insists Grab 'doesn't work at the airport' — both untrue. Broader Lombok tourist-targeting and sharky-transport patterns are also well documented. The Senggigi transfer variant: some drivers offer 'Kuta AND Senggigi tour included' at Rp 900K — there's no real 'tour'; they'll dump you at a commission-kickback restaurant or silver shop. For older travelers, the practical defense: (1) book Grab or Gojek yourself on airport Wi-Fi AFTER luggage — typical fare LOP to Kuta-Lombok is Rp 200K–300K, to Senggigi Rp 250K–350K, to Mataram Rp 180K–250K; (2) if Grab has no cars (Lombok supply thinner than Bali), the airport Koperasi Taxi counter IS legitimate but negotiate hard — posted rate sheet starts at Rp 350K to Kuta (still 1.5x Grab but fair fallback); (3) IGNORE every arrivals-kerb sign-holder or kiosk quoting Rp 500K+; (4) pre-book your hotel's airport pickup (many Kuta-Lombok hotels include free transfers); (5) for ferry-bound travelers heading to Bangsal or Teluk Nare (Gili Islands boats), book a driver-plus-ferry combo via Klook (Rp 350K–450K all-in) rather than risk double-tout pricing at each node. How to avoid: Book Grab/Gojek on airport Wi-Fi after luggage — Rp 200K–300K LOP to Kuta-Lombok Koperasi Taxi counter IS legitimate; negotiate from posted rate sheet IGNORE every 'Rp 500K+' arrivals kiosk and kerb sign-holder Pre-book hotel airport pickup (many Kuta-Lombok hotels free) For ferry-bound trips, book driver+ferry combo via Klook at Rp 350K–450K

Scam alert in Lombok, Indonesia — Bali-Lombok Fast Boat Overcharge & Padang Bai Taxi Mafia Blockade (transport, severity: high). The Bali-Lombok fast-boat corridor is one of Indonesia's most-scammed tourist transits. Community reports document the Manta Express overcharge and delay pattern, and the safety-compliance issues of low-cost operators that go further than financial scams — overcrowded boats, no life jackets, crew pressure. Travelers also document the combined ferry-plus-taxi-mafia blockade pattern at Padang Bai. The specific scams: (a) fake-ticket resellers at Padang Bai entrance selling 'Gili fast boat' at Rp 450K–700K one-way for seats that don't exist or for already-cancelled boats; the real rate is Rp 250K–400K via 12go Asia, Klook, or the operator's direct website; (b) 'express upgrade' at the pier claiming the regular boat is cancelled and 'only VIP available' at 2x price; (c) Padang Bai taxi mafia — when tourists arrive at Padang Bai via Grab, local taxi drivers physically block the Grab from entering the port and force transfer to local taxis at 3x fare. This Grab-blockade pattern at Padang Bai is a well-documented 2025 community anchor. For older travelers, the practical defense: (1) book fast-boat tickets ONLY through 12go Asia, Klook, or the operator's direct website (Eka Jaya, Blue Water Express, Gili Getaway, Idola Express); confirmation email is your ticket; (2) NEVER buy from pier-front kiosks or walk-up 'fast boat' touts; (3) for the Padang Bai Grab blockade, have your Grab drop you 300–500m BEFORE the port entrance (at the Mandala parking lot) and walk in — local taxi drivers can't physically block foot traffic; (4) avoid the cheapest operators (Semaya One, Eka Jaya complaints) — pay Rp 50–100K extra for reputable Gili Getaway or Blue Water Express with real safety records; (5) the DIRECT boat from Serangan/Sanur (Bali) to Gili Trawangan is faster (2 hours) and skips the Padang Bai mafia entirely — worth the Rp 400K–550K; (6) bring seasickness meds — the crossing can be rough. How to avoid: Book via 12go Asia, Klook, or operator direct (Eka Jaya, Blue Water, Gili Getaway) NEVER buy tickets from pier kiosks or walk-up touts At Padang Bai, exit Grab 300–500m before the port entrance and walk in Avoid Semaya One and aggressive cheap operators; pay extra for safety Consider the direct Serangan/Sanur-Gili Trawangan route (skips Padang Bai)

Scam alert in Lombok, Indonesia — Mount Rinjani Trek Unlicensed Operator & Porter Overload Scam (tourist-trap, severity: high). Mount Rinjani (3,726m) is Lombok's iconic multi-day trek destination and hosts a 2025 unlicensed-operator and porter-overload ecosystem. Community reports describe the trek-operator landscape and cost gotchas. Legitimate 2-day-1-night Rinjani trek (Sembalun to crater rim summit, basic): Rp 2.5M–3.5M (US$160–$225) per person including National Park fee (Rp 200K), guide, porter, meals, camping gear. 3-day-2-night summit + Segara Anak lake descent: Rp 3.5M–5M (US$225–$320). The 2025 scams: (a) unlicensed operators in Mataram / Senggigi booking offices offering 'Rinjani special' at Rp 1.8M — the savings come from skipping the National Park permit (illegal, you'll be fined), using unlicensed guides without insurance, or overloading porters with 50–80 kg each (legal limit 25 kg per porter); community reports document the porter-welfare issue; (b) 'all-inclusive' packages that secretly exclude the descent, leaving climbers stranded or charging Rp 800K extra at Segara Anak lake; (c) on-trail equipment upsells: 'you need the premium sleeping bag for Rp 300K' (already included in reputable package); (d) gift-shop-stop trek extensions that eat 2 hours of climbing time. Broader Lombok tourist-targeting patterns are also well documented. For older travelers (Rinjani is strenuous — NOT recommended above 65 with mobility issues): (1) book ONLY licensed operators with Mount Rinjani National Park partnership — Rudy Trekker, John's Adventures, Rinjani Trekking Club are the best-reviewed; verify their permit number; (2) confirm porter load is ≤25 kg per porter (ethical Rinjani operators post this publicly); (3) get EVERYTHING in writing: start time, route, meals, descent, summit-night plan, permit-included confirmation; (4) for older fit travelers, take the 3-day-2-night route (NOT the exhausting 2D1N summit-descent in one push); (5) purchase trip insurance with evacuation coverage (helicopter rescue Rp 15M+ if uninsured); (6) acclimatise in Senggigi or Sembalun for 1–2 nights at altitude before the climb; (7) if you have heart, breathing, or joint conditions, skip Rinjani and do Mount Batur in Bali instead (gentler, one-day sunrise trek). How to avoid: Book ONLY licensed operators: Rudy Trekker, John's Adventures, Rinjani Trekking Club Confirm porter load ≤25 kg per porter (ethical Rinjani standard) Get route, meals, permit, descent plan IN WRITING before deposit Take 3D2N route (not exhausting 2D1N) — and skip above age 65 if mobility issues Purchase trip insurance with helicopter evacuation coverage

Scam alert in Lombok, Indonesia — Kuta Lombok Scooter Rental Pre-Damage & 'Road Police' Bribe Shakedown (transport, severity: high). Kuta Lombok's scooter-rental ecosystem mirrors Bali's worst scooter scams but with thinner enforcement. Community reports document the scooter-rental risks and the cross-region pre-damage pattern. The scams: (a) 'pre-damage' fraud where rental shacks hand over a scooter with unphotographed scratches and claim Rp 1.5M–3.5M (US$95–$225) for damage at return; (b) 'spare key theft' variant — operator has a spare key, takes scooter back overnight, claims Rp 5–10M replacement cost next morning; (c) 'road police' checkpoint bribe shakedowns on Kuta-to-Tanjung-Aan road and Selong Belanak approach, where plain-clothes 'officers' demand Rp 200K–500K for 'no international license' violation. The Indonesian Traffic Police (Polisi Lalu Lintas) DO conduct legitimate document checks, and foreigners riding on an Indonesian scooter DO need an IDP (International Driving Permit) with motorcycle endorsement PLUS their home-country motorcycle license — NO EXCEPTIONS. Community itinerary and safety reports reinforce these rules. Legitimate fines are written tickets paid at the police station (Polres Lombok Tengah) — NEVER cash on the spot. 'Road police' demanding cash-only bribes are either uniformed officers running a shakedown or plain-clothes impersonators. For older travelers — or any traveler without strong scooter experience — SKIP scooter rental in Kuta Lombok and hire a driver instead (Rp 500K–700K per day, 8 hours) via your hotel or Klook. If you do rent: (1) book ONLY via your hotel or a top-reviewed Google shop (Kuta Scooter Rental, Lombok Scooter Rental with 4.7+ stars); (2) take photo/video of EVERY scratch, dent, and scuff with a timestamp BEFORE signing anything; (3) KEEP THE KEY AND PUT YOUR OWN PADLOCK on it — do not let the shop keep a spare; (4) bring IDP with motorcycle endorsement + home-country motorcycle license; (5) if stopped by 'police', ask for credentials, for the ticket to be written, and for payment at Polres Lombok Tengah — NEVER pay cash on the spot; (6) photograph any 'officer' demanding cash; (7) wear a helmet and closed-toe shoes ALWAYS — enforcement is lax but accidents are common and hospital bills real. How to avoid: SKIP scooter entirely; hire a driver via hotel/Klook (Rp 500K–700K/day) If renting, use only Google 4.7+ shops; document every scratch on video KEEP THE KEY — put your own padlock; never leave spare with operator Bring IDP with motorcycle endorsement + home-country motorcycle license NEVER pay cash to 'police' on the spot — request written ticket at Polres

Scam alert in Lombok, Indonesia — Senggigi Beach Tout & Restaurant Menu-Swap Bill Padding (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Senggigi is Lombok's original resort strip (pre-Kuta-Lombok boom) and hosts an entrenched 2025 tout and restaurant-bill-padding problem. Community reports document how Senggigi has declined in quality as Kuta-Lombok grew, and mention the commercial-scam density shifting to Senggigi's dwindling tourist pool. The patterns: (a) beach touts selling 'sarong, massage, henna tattoo, bracelet' with aggressive approach and walk-away-tax (where they pocket the cash and claim the tourist 'agreed'); (b) seafront seafood restaurant bait-and-switch — menu shows 'fish of the day Rp 120K' but at serving the bill shows 'lobster Rp 450K + fish extra 180K' — common at unnamed beach warungs near the Art Market. Broader Lombok tourist-scam patterns are also well documented. The sunset-bar scam: some Senggigi beach bars charge Rp 80K for a beer on the menu but Rp 300K for 'premium beer' delivered without asking. Travelers also note the cross-island trend where tourists are consolidated into Kuta-Lombok/Gili and Senggigi has become commercial and hustle-heavy. For older travelers, the practical defense: (1) firm 'tidak, terima kasih' (no, thank you) and walk AWAY from every beach-tout approach; (2) eat at reputable Senggigi restaurants with verified Google 4.5+ ratings and printed menus (Asmara Restaurant, Square Restaurant, Quali Bali) rather than anonymous beach warungs; (3) ALWAYS ask for a written bill before paying; review each line-item against the menu; (4) for seafood, agree weight (gram) and price/kg BEFORE the cook starts — 1 kg snapper at Rp 180K–240K/kg is fair; 'lobster' is Rp 1.2M–1.8M/kg; (5) avoid 'premium beer' orders at sunset bars — insist on brands shown on menu (Bintang, Bintang Radler, Storm Beer); (6) pay with credit card when possible for chargeback leverage; (7) the Gili Islands and Kuta-Lombok are cleaner tourist experiences; Senggigi is best for 1–2 nights en route, not a multi-day stay. How to avoid: Firm 'tidak, terima kasih' to every tout; walk away without engaging Eat at Google 4.5+ restaurants with printed menus (Asmara, Square, Quali Bali) ALWAYS review written bill line-item by line-item before paying For seafood, agree weight (gram) and price/kg BEFORE cook starts Insist on named beer brands (Bintang, Bintang Radler) at sunset bars

Scam alert in Lombok, Indonesia — Lombok ATM Skimming, Money Changer Shortchange & Currency Fraud (tourist-trap, severity: high). Lombok shares the Bali ATM-skimming and money-changer-shortchange problem but with thinner banking infrastructure and fewer legitimate money-changer options. Community reports document the 2025 ATM-skimming pattern and warn about money-changer crews that operate in both Bali and Lombok. The specific Lombok patterns: (a) freestanding ATMs at Kuta-Lombok convenience stores (Indomaret, Alfamart) and hotel lobbies are the highest-risk skimmer targets — card-reader overlays and pinhole cameras; (b) Senggigi street-front 'no-commission' money changers with tampered calculators displaying wrong conversion and sleight-of-hand short-counting (a Rp 2M handover becomes Rp 1.5M by the time the tourist counts again); (c) 'premium Australian dollar rate' kiosks at Mataram that use lookalike calculators or bills with added-rupiah-looking-IDR notes. Lombok community threads describe the defensive protocol in detail. For older travelers: (1) use ONLY bank-branch ATMs during business hours — Bank BNI, BRI, Mandiri, BCA, CIMB Niaga all have branches in Kuta-Lombok, Senggigi, and Mataram; (2) for money exchange, use ONLY PT Central Kuta Money Changer (Kuta-Lombok and Senggigi locations) or BMC Central (Mataram) — both with verified Google 4.6+ reviews and published daily rates; (3) count bills yourself IN FRONT of the teller three times before leaving — the sleight-of-hand happens at hand-over; (4) compare rate to the day's Bank Indonesia mid-rate (bi.go.id) and refuse any rate more than 2% below; (5) use RFID-blocking wallet for contactless cards; (6) set daily withdrawal limit Rp 2M and transaction alerts; (7) for large currency exchange (US$500+), go to a bank-branch teller during business hours — slightly worse rate but zero-risk; (8) keep one dedicated travel debit card separate from your main account; if skimmed, contact your bank's emergency line and file a complaint at Polres Lombok Tengah within 24 hours for chargeback documentation. How to avoid: Use ONLY bank-branch ATMs during business hours (BNI, BRI, Mandiri, BCA, CIMB) Exchange ONLY at PT Central Kuta Money Changer or BMC Central (verified 4.6+) Count bills yourself IN FRONT of teller three times before leaving Refuse rates more than 2% below Bank Indonesia daily mid-rate (bi.go.id) Set low daily withdrawal limits and transaction alerts on bank app

Scam alert in London, United Kingdom — The Westminster Bridge Shell Game (pickpocket, severity: moderate). You're crossing Westminster Bridge when you spot a crowd watching a guy shuffle three cups over a ball on a folding table. A few bystanders seem to be winning big — one just pocketed £50! You put down £20, guess correctly, but somehow the ball has mysteriously vanished. The 'winners' around you are planted accomplices, and you never stood a chance. The game has been running on this bridge for literally centuries, and tourists still fall for it every single day. How to avoid: Never bet money on street games — the house always wins The spectators cheering you on are accomplices Walk past, don't make eye contact with touts

Scam alert in London, United Kingdom — The Moped Phone Snatch (pickpocket, severity: high). You step out of the tube and pull up Google Maps to find your hotel. Before you can process the screen, a moped zips past and the pillion rider rips the phone right out of your hand — they're gone before you even realize what happened. Tube theft in London has soared 83% in recent years, and moped-based phone theft is the #1 crime tourists face. The thieves park nearby watching for people who check their phones the moment they exit. How to avoid: Put your phone away before exiting the tube Step inside a shop to check directions Use a phone wrist strap or grip case Download offline maps before arriving

Scam alert in London, United Kingdom — The Fake Holiday Let / Airbnb Scam (pickpocket, severity: high). You book what looks like a gorgeous Mayfair flat on Booking.com for £2,000 for 4 nights. The day before check-in you get a message: to receive the actual address, you need to send a £1,500 PayPal 'security deposit' directly to the host. That's when you realize the listing photos were stolen from a real property across town — the flat doesn't exist. A Wired UK investigation found entire operations running fake listings of real occupied London properties, catching hundreds of tourists. How to avoid: Never pay outside the official booking platform Verify listing address on Google Street View before booking Book through platforms with guest protection policies Contact platform support immediately if asked to pay off-platform

Scam alert in London, United Kingdom — The Unlicensed Minicab Trap (nightlife, severity: high). It's 2am, the tube has stopped, and a friendly bloke outside the club offers you a ride home for 'just £20 cash.' You get in without checking if it's a licensed vehicle. The driver takes a long route and when you arrive, the price has magically become £60 — and he's not moving until you pay. Unlicensed minicab touts are specifically common at night around tourist entertainment areas, targeting tired and tipsy visitors who don't know the laws. How to avoid: Use Uber, Bolt, or a licensed app to pre-book Black cabs can be hailed legally on the street and have meters Never get into a car that approaches you proactively

Scam alert in London, United Kingdom — The Charity Clipboard Pickpocket (pickpocket, severity: moderate). You're walking down Oxford Street when someone in a charity vest and clipboard approaches you — they're collecting signatures for a good cause. While you're reading the clipboard, their partner brushes past you or lingers very close. By the time you hand the clipboard back, your wallet has quietly changed pockets. These gangs work in teams of three or four and are extremely practiced at the distraction-and-lift. How to avoid: Keep your bag in front and hand on wallet whenever approached Simply say 'no thanks' and keep walking without stopping Be especially alert on Oxford Street, Covent Garden, and Leicester Square

Scam alert in London, United Kingdom — The Overpriced Tourist Restaurant Trick (overcharging, severity: low). You duck into a busy-looking restaurant near Covent Garden — the outside menu looked reasonably priced. But when the bill arrives, it has a 12.5% 'optional' service charge already added, plus a cover charge, plus 'still or sparkling?' water that's not optional. What should have been a £20 lunch became £45. These aren't really scams in the legal sense but are extremely common traps for tourists who don't know to ask about charges upfront. How to avoid: Ask if service charge is included before ordering Specify 'tap water please' to avoid bottled water charges Check menu prices carefully — no-frills pubs near attractions often serve the same food for half the price

Scam alert in Lyon, France — Pickpocketing (pickpocket, severity: high). Pickpockets in Lyon work the tourist-heavy areas and crowded public transport, usually in teams: one person asks for directions, bumps into you, or stages a scene while the others lift your wallet or phone. At the Confluence tram stop, groups of women carrying oversized bags have been observed surrounding tourists to get at backpacks. On Métro Line D and the T2 tram, thefts cluster around rush-hour boarding and exiting when movement is chaotic enough to mask the lift. How to avoid: Wear bags across your body with zippers facing inward. Keep only minimal cash and one card on you. Use money belts or hidden pouches. Stay alert during metro boarding and exiting.

Scam alert in Lyon, France — Fake Metro Ticket Scam (fraud, severity: moderate). Ticket touts approach tourists who appear lost or confused at major Lyon train stations. They offer to sell metro tickets at seemingly reasonable prices, but the tickets are either fake, expired, or already used. The scammer may claim they have ‘extra’ tickets or offer a ‘discount’ compared to the official ticket machines. When you try to use the ticket, it won’t work at the turnstile. How to avoid: Only buy tickets from official TCL machines or counters. Use the TCL mobile app for digital tickets. Ignore anyone offering to sell tickets outside official channels.

Scam alert in Lyon, France — Fake Charity/Petition Scam (pickpocket, severity: moderate). Someone approaches along Rue de la République with a clipboard and opens with ‘Do you speak English?’ They want you to sign a petition for a deaf-mute charity. Once you’ve signed, they flip to a donation column and pressure you for cash — while your attention is on the clipboard, an accomplice is often working your bag from behind. The charity is fake. How to avoid: Simply say ‘Non, merci’ and keep walking. Never sign anything handed to you on the street. Legitimate charities in France only ask for email addresses, not cash.

Scam alert in Lyon, France — Restaurant Overcharging (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Tourist-centric restaurants near Lyon’s historic areas may present inflated bills. Tactics include: adding items you didn’t order, charging for bread and water that appeared ‘free,’ using ‘tourist menus’ with elevated prices. Some establishments trade on Lyon’s reputation as France’s gastronomic capital to justify excessive prices for mediocre food. How to avoid: Check prices before sitting down. Ask for itemized bills and review carefully. Eat where locals eat, away from main tourist streets.

Scam alert in Lyon, France — Shell Game / Three-Card Monte (gambling-scam, severity: high). A scammer sets up a makeshift table with three cups or cards. They invite you to bet on guessing the ball’s location. ‘Winners’ in the crowd are accomplices who pretend to win to draw you in. The game is completely rigged through sleight of hand — you cannot win. How to avoid: Never play street gambling games — they are always rigged. Do not stop to watch. Remember that bystanders are likely accomplices.

Scam alert in Lyon, France — Gold Ring Scam (street-scam, severity: low). A person ‘finds’ a gold ring on the ground near you and asks if you dropped it. When you say no, they show you a marking claiming it’s real gold and offer to sell it for a ‘good price.’ The ring is worthless brass. They may also ask for money ‘for food’ or ‘for their children.’ How to avoid: Don’t engage — say ‘Non’ and keep walking. Never accept items ‘found’ on the street.

Scam alert in Lyon, France — Friendship Bracelet Scam (aggressive-selling, severity: moderate). A vendor grabs your hand in Vieux Lyon and weaves a colorful string bracelet around your wrist, finishing with a knot you can’t untie. Then they demand €10–€20. If you refuse, they become aggressive — and in the confrontation, an accomplice often works your pockets. How to avoid: Keep your hands in your pockets when approached. Say ‘Non’ firmly and keep walking. Don’t let anyone touch you or attach anything.

Scam alert in Lyon, France — Rose/Flower Scam (aggressive-selling, severity: low). A seller approaches couples dining outdoors, offering a rose with ‘Flower for the pretty lady!’ The moment you touch or accept the flower, they demand 5-10 euros. If you try to return it, they refuse and become aggressive until you pay out of embarrassment. How to avoid: Don’t touch or accept any flowers offered. A simple ‘Non, merci’ and wave sends them away. Ask restaurant staff to intervene if needed.

Scam alert in Lyon, France — Fake Police Scam (impersonation, severity: high). Criminals pose as plainclothes police, flash fake badges, and say they need to check your wallet for counterfeit bills or ‘drug money.’ While examining the cash, they palm bills. Sometimes a ‘lost tourist’ accomplice has just asked you to break a large note, and the fake officer arrives moments later claiming street currency exchange is illegal. How to avoid: Real officers only ask to see ID, never the wallet. Ask to see their *carte de police* and offer to walk to the nearest *commissariat* together — genuine police will comply; scammers won’t. Dial 17 if something feels off.

Scam alert in Lyon, France — Taxi Overcharging (transport, severity: moderate). Some taxi drivers take advantage of tourists unfamiliar with Lyon’s layout. They take long routes to inflate the fare, ‘forget’ to start the meter, or select the higher night or weekend tariff during regular hours. Airport runs are particularly vulnerable — the legitimate fare from Lyon-Saint Exupéry to the city center is around €50–€70. How to avoid: Only use taxis from official ranks. Ensure the meter is zeroed before departure. Use GPS on your phone to follow the route. Consider using Uber or Bolt.

Scam alert in Lyon, France — ATM Skimming / Private ATM Scam (financial-fraud, severity: high). Criminals attach skimming devices to ATMs that steal your card data and PIN. Private ATM companies like Euronet place machines that charge excessive fees and poor exchange rates — up to 4x more than bank ATMs. They may offer Dynamic Currency Conversion at terrible rates. How to avoid: Use ATMs inside bank branches only. Look for major French banks: BNP Paribas, Société Générale, LCL. Always cover keypad when entering PIN. Decline dynamic currency conversion.

Scam alert in Lyon, France — Broken Camera Scam (fraud, severity: low). Someone asks you to take their photo using their camera. After you return the camera, they claim you broke it and demand money for repairs. The ‘camera’ was already broken — they use it repeatedly for this scam. How to avoid: Politely decline to take photos with others’ cameras. If accused of damage, suggest filing a police report together — scammers will refuse.

Scam alert in Macau, China — Macau Taxi Overcharge & 'Black Taxi' at Ferry Terminals (transport, severity: high). Macau's ferry terminals (Outer Harbour from Hong Kong, Taipa Ferry for Hong Kong / Shenzhen) and the airport (MFM) are scam-density hotspots for unlicensed 'black taxi' drivers. The legitimate metered taxi fare from Outer Harbour Ferry Terminal to Cotai Strip casinos is MOP$80–$120 (20 min); Outer Harbour to Senado Square is MOP$50–$80 (10 min); MFM airport to Cotai is MOP$60–$100. Unofficial drivers at terminal exits quote HKD$200–$400 or MOP$200–$400. The scam is aggressive because Macau's tourism economy depends on cross-border flow from Hong Kong and mainland China — black taxi operators rotate terminal exits daily. Community reports frame the southern-China taxi-scam ecosystem including Macau. Macau has legitimate alternatives: free casino shuttle buses (all major Cotai and Peninsula casinos — Venetian, Galaxy, Wynn, MGM, City of Dreams — run free shuttles between their properties and all three ferry terminals plus MFM airport). The hotel-branded shuttles are genuine and scam-free. Additionally, the Macau Light Rapid Transit (LRT) opened 2019 — extends from Taipa Ferry Terminal via casino district to Cotai East for MOP$6 (15 min). For older travelers, the practical playbook: (1) check which casino shuttle serves your arrival terminal — free transfers even if you're not staying at that casino; from Outer Harbour, the Venetian, Galaxy, and MGM shuttles run every 15–30 min; (2) use the LRT (MOP$6) to connect between Taipa Ferry and Cotai; (3) if taking a licensed taxi, walk to the official outdoor rank (black and yellow cabs are legitimate), say 'da biao' for metered fare; (4) pay in MOP where possible — black-taxi operators sometimes quote HKD at 1:1 exchange when the actual rate is 1.03:1, adding 3% opacity to the overcharge; (5) the Grand Lisboa and Wynn offer 'free pickup' shuttle services for verified hotel guests — confirm via your hotel's concierge before arrival. How to avoid: Use free casino shuttle buses from ferry terminals and MFM airport (Venetian, Galaxy, MGM, Wynn all run shuttles) Macau LRT from Taipa Ferry Terminal to Cotai East: MOP$6, 15 min If licensed taxi, walk to official rank; say 'da biao'; expect MOP$50–$120 for short trips Pay in MOP, not HKD; confirm 1 HKD = 1.03 MOP, not 1:1 Photograph the taxi plate number from rear windscreen

Scam alert in Macau, China — Casino VIP Room 'Junket' & Rigged Private-Game Scams (tourist-trap, severity: high). Macau is the world's largest gambling center by revenue, and its 'junket' system (pre-Covid, 95% of VIP table play flowed through junket intermediaries) has a dark reputation for rigged private games. Major operators (Venetian, Wynn, MGM, Galaxy) run the licensed regulated floors; but VIP rooms operated by third-party junket promoters have been documented for loaded dice, marked cards, and 'credit extension' scams that trap tourists into unpayable debts enforced through extra-legal channels. Community reports reference Macau gambling scams in the broader China-wide tourist scam framework. The specific scam pattern for foreign tourists: (1) hotel staff or casino host offers 'introduction' to a 'private gaming room' with 'better odds' or 'higher limits'; (2) the room is operated by a junket promoter (sometimes unregistered), not the licensed casino; (3) games are conducted with non-casino-standard equipment; (4) tourist is offered credit (¥50,000+ markers) that spiral rapidly; (5) repayment is enforced by the junket operator's unofficial collection network. The Macau Gaming Inspection and Coordination Bureau (DICJ) has cracked down significantly 2022–2025 and most major junket operators are now licensed, but unlicensed operators still exist on the Cotai periphery. For older travelers who visit Macau casinos: (1) play ONLY on the main gaming floors operated directly by the casino (Venetian Piazza, Galaxy, Wynn, MGM, City of Dreams, Parisian) — all are DICJ-licensed with published house rules; (2) NEVER accept a 'private room' or 'VIP' introduction from a hotel host, casino staffer, or 'helpful local' — the VIP system exists for high rollers bringing millions, not tourists; (3) decline ALL credit-marker offers — pay only in cash or certified chips; (4) set a hard gambling budget before entering and stop at the limit; (5) if threatened or intimidated over gambling debts, contact Macau Judiciary Police (PJ) at +853 2855 7111 or your consulate immediately. How to avoid: Play only on licensed main gaming floors: Venetian Piazza, Galaxy, Wynn, MGM, City of Dreams, Parisian Decline all 'private room' or 'VIP' introductions from staff or intermediaries Pay only in cash or certified casino chips — refuse credit markers Set hard gambling budget before entering; stop at the limit If threatened over gambling debts, contact Macau Judiciary Police (PJ): +853 2855 7111

Scam alert in Macau, China — Senado Square Tourist-Menu Restaurant Overcharge (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Macau's Portuguese colonial core — Senado Square, Rua da Felicidade, and the approach to the Ruins of St. Paul's — is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a dense tourist-food strip. Many restaurants here run laminated-English-photo menus at 2–3x residential rates. Common overcharges: Portuguese egg tart (Macau's iconic snack) at MOP$40–$60 each versus MOP$10–$15 at Lord Stow's in Coloane or a Taipa Village bakery; Macanese pork-chop bun at MOP$80–$120 at Senado-area venues vs MOP$40–$50 at Tai Lei Loi Kei in Taipa Village; African chicken at MOP$280 at tourist-strip Portuguese restaurants vs MOP$150–$200 at Fernando's in Hac Sa. Community reports document the general tourist-menu pattern across China and extend the context to Macau. For Portuguese-Macanese cuisine (the city's signature food culture), the community-vetted residential alternatives are: (1) Lord Stow's Bakery (Coloane Village) — the original egg tart at MOP$10; (2) Tai Lei Loi Kei (Taipa Village) — famous pork-chop bun at MOP$45; (3) Fernando's (Hac Sa Beach, Coloane) — landmark Portuguese-Macanese at MOP$150–$300 per person; (4) Restaurante Litoral (Taipa) — mid-range authentic Macanese. For older travelers, the practical playbook: (1) skip Senado Square food stalls except for window-shopping; walk to Taipa Village or Coloane Village for authentic Macanese at fair prices; (2) Macau's public buses (MOP$6 per ride) connect Senado to Taipa Village (Bus 22, 26A, 28A) and Coloane (Bus 15, 21A, 25) — scam-free transit; (3) avoid any restaurant on Rua da Felicidade with an English-only menu and photos of every dish; (4) for egg tarts specifically, the MOP$40+ tourist-strip versions are ALWAYS commercial-kitchen products, not freshly made — Lord Stow's and Margaret's Café e Nata at Grand Lisboa are the two hand-baked legitimate options. How to avoid: Go to Taipa Village or Coloane Village for authentic Macanese Lord Stow's Bakery (Coloane) for egg tarts (MOP$10) Tai Lei Loi Kei (Taipa) for pork-chop bun (MOP$45) Fernando's (Hac Sa) for Portuguese-Macanese dining (MOP$150–$300) Macau public buses (MOP$6) connect Senado to all authentic food villages

Scam alert in Macau, China — Currency Exchange & Counterfeit Note Scams at Border Areas (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Macau uses MOP (pataca) as its local currency, but HKD (Hong Kong Dollar) circulates at roughly 1:1 (actual rate 1 HKD = 1.03 MOP). Casinos operate in HKD. Tourists crossing from Zhuhai (mainland China) bring CNY and need to exchange to MOP or HKD. The scam variants: (1) unlicensed exchange booths in Senado and near Outer Harbour offer 'better rate than bank' — actually 3–8% worse with opaque receipts; (2) counterfeit ¥100 CNY notes or counterfeit HKD$500 notes swapped into returned currency; (3) casino VIP cages (not the main floor cage) sometimes give unfavourable exchange rates on chips cashed out. Community reports document the counterfeit-bill variant: vendors receiving an RMB 50 or RMB 100 bill from you, telling you it's a fake and asking you to exchange. For older travelers, the protective playbook: (1) use licensed banks for currency exchange: Bank of China (Macau branch), HSBC, ICBC, Hang Seng Bank — all have visible branded signs and posted rates; (2) alternatively, use a multi-currency card (Wise, Revolut) at a Bank of China ATM for ~1% forex margin; (3) at casinos, use ONLY the main-floor cage (posted rates, regulated by DICJ); avoid VIP-room cages operated by junket promoters; (4) at Portas do Cerco border crossing, the Bank of China Macau has a dedicated counter for CNY↔MOP; (5) AVOID Senado-area unlicensed exchange booths — 3–8% markup plus counterfeit-bill risk. How to avoid: Use licensed banks: Bank of China Macau, HSBC, ICBC, Hang Seng Multi-currency card (Wise, Revolut) at Bank of China ATM for ~1% margin At casinos, use ONLY the main-floor cage — avoid junket VIP-room cages Portas do Cerco border crossing has Bank of China counter for CNY↔MOP AVOID Senado-area unlicensed exchange booths

Scam alert in Macau, China — Fake Hotel Booking & Airbnb in Macau (nightlife, severity: moderate). Macau has a licensing system for tourist accommodation operated by the Macau Government Tourism Office (MGTO). All legal hotels, guesthouses, and short-term rentals require an MGTO license (a number visible on the establishment's signage and booking listings). Unlicensed rentals — common on Airbnb, Facebook, and WeChat from individual hosts — are technically illegal, and when authorities inspect, guests are required to leave. The scam variants: (1) 'Airbnb' listing at 30–50% below comparable hotel rates turns out to be unlicensed; guest arrives to find police notice or no key; (2) 'host' demands full payment via bank transfer before arrival; disappears; (3) listing photos are reverse-image-search matches to hotels in Hong Kong or Shenzhen. Community reports apply the universal anti-fraud rule to booking-scam ecosystems across China. For older travelers booking Macau accommodation, the defensive playbook: (1) book only licensed hotels through Booking.com, Agoda, or Trip.com — verify the hotel appears on the MGTO Registered Hotels list (macaotourism.gov.mo); (2) refuse off-platform payment requests (Bizum, bank transfer, WeChat Pay without platform escrow); (3) for Airbnb listings, verify the MGTO license number on the listing; legal short-term rentals must display this; (4) major licensed hotels in Macau include the Venetian, Galaxy, Wynn, MGM, City of Dreams, Grand Lisboa Palace, Sheraton Grand, Banyan Tree, St. Regis — any of these booked via platform are guaranteed legitimate; (5) if defrauded on arrival, contact Macau Tourism Crisis Management Office: +853 2833 3000. How to avoid: Book only licensed hotels via Booking.com, Agoda, or Trip.com Verify hotel on MGTO Registered Hotels list (macaotourism.gov.mo) Refuse off-platform payment requests — use platform card transactions only For Airbnb, verify MGTO license number on listing Major licensed hotels: Venetian, Galaxy, Wynn, MGM, City of Dreams, Grand Lisboa Palace, Sheraton, Banyan Tree, St. Regis

Scam alert in Macau, China — Tourist-Area Pickpockets at St. Paul's Ruins & A-Ma Temple (pickpocket, severity: moderate). Macau is one of Asia's safest cities overall — violent crime against tourists is extremely rare, and the casino-heavy economy produces above-average policing. However, pickpocket activity exists in the UNESCO World Heritage compact — particularly at the Ruins of St. Paul's stairway (the city's #1 photo site), Senado Square weekends, and A-Ma Temple during incense-festival days. The crews are smaller and less organized than Beijing/Shanghai but operate the same opportunist patterns. The general Chinese pickpocket-tourist pattern applies in Macau's tourist core. For older travelers visiting St. Paul's Ruins, Senado Square, and A-Ma Temple, the standard posture: (1) zipped crossbody bag in front during all stairway climbs and crowded plaza moments; (2) phone in zipped inner pocket, never back pocket; (3) split valuables — ¥200 / HKD$200 / MOP$200 in front pocket, passport + backup in hotel safe; (4) at A-Ma Temple during busy incense-festival periods, keep small valuables especially secure — the crowds press intensely; (5) Macau's Judiciary Police are responsive — call +853 2855 7111 or 999 (emergency) within 24 hours for denuncia documentation if theft occurs. How to avoid: Zipped crossbody bag in front at all heritage-site crowds Never place phone or wallet in back pocket or outer backpack compartment Keep valuables split: pocket cash + card, passport + backup in hotel safe At A-Ma Temple during festivals, extra vigilance in incense-buying crush Call Macau Judiciary Police (+853 2855 7111) or 999 within 24 hours if theft occurs

Scam alert in Madrid, Spain — Madrid Barajas (MAD) Airport Taxi Overcharge (transport, severity: high). You land at Madrid Barajas after a long flight and take the taxi queue outside Terminal 4. The legal Madrid airport flat fare to anywhere inside the M-30 ring road (including the city center, Retiro, Salamanca, Chueca neighborhoods) is €33. Drivers who claim the meter is broken or add 'luggage fees,' 'terminal transfer fees,' or 'night surcharges' are running one of Europe's most-documented airport scams. Community reports document specific cases where drivers charged €60–€110 for €33 rides. The 'legal' variant is especially insidious — drivers obey the meter but take an indirect route via the M-40 ring road instead of the M-11/M-30, adding 20 minutes and €20 to the fare. One traveler wrote: the driver added a flat 'airport fee' charge before the meter even started. Terminal-to-terminal taxis at Barajas run a separate shakedown — quoting €30–€50 for what should be €5 or a free shuttle bus. Your protection: the Madrid airport flat rate to anywhere inside the M-30 is €33 — posted on signs at every Barajas taxi queue. Anything quoted above that is overcharging. For terminal transfers, take the free Airport Shuttle bus (yellow, 'Bus Express 12') rather than a taxi. Alternatives to taxi: Metro Line 8 runs directly from all Barajas terminals to Nuevos Ministerios for €5 (includes the €3 Barajas supplement; 30 minutes); the Renfe Cercanías C-1 commuter train from Terminal 4 to Atocha or Chamartín is €2.60 (25 minutes). Use Uber, Bolt, FreeNow, or Cabify for app-regulated fares; all four work in Madrid with digital receipts. How to avoid: Demand the €33 flat rate for anywhere inside the M-30 — posted on signs at the queue Take Metro Line 8 from Barajas to Nuevos Ministerios (€5, 30 min, scam-free) Or Renfe Cercanías C-1 from T4 to Atocha or Chamartín (€2.60, 25 min) Between terminals, use the free Bus Express 12 yellow shuttle — not a taxi For app taxis, use Uber, Bolt, FreeNow, or Cabify — all show fixed prices

Scam alert in Madrid, Spain — Metro Sol + Atocha Pickpocket Teams (transport, severity: high). Madrid Metro is otherwise clean and safe, but two corridors see concentrated pickpocket activity: Line 1 (Atocha–Sol–Chamartín, the airport-to-center axis) and the Sol station transfer concourse where Lines 1, 2, and 3 meet. Teams operate in three- or four-person groups — one distracts, one lifts, one receives, one keeps lookout. Community reports document tourists hit at Atocha while transferring trains, and the airport-Metro run: 'I had no issues with pickpockets but I was attacked while walking to the Atocha train station to head to Barcelona.' The most common 2025 patterns: fake crowd crush at carriage doors where someone pushes from behind while another reaches into your outer pocket; 'map distraction' where someone asks for directions with a large open map blocking your view of your bag; escalator bump where a passenger 'falls' into you. Travelers offer the comparative context: 'Madrid is much safer than Barcelona. Do not put your valuables in a backpack on your back. Keep your wallet/passport front pocket.' The same threads note pickpocket teams rotate between Barcelona and Madrid's Gran Vía/Sol stretch seasonally. The damage is typically a phone (€600–€1,200 replacement for a current iPhone) or a wallet (€50–€300 cash plus card cancellation overhead). For insurance, you need a Policía Nacional report filed at a police station within 24 hours — Comisaría de Centro at Calle Leganitos 19 handles tourist reports. Your protection: wear a zipped crossbody bag in front of you in any crowded environment; never use a backpack's outer pocket; keep phone in a zipped inner pocket, not a back pocket; do not pull out your phone on crowded escalators or at carriage doors. At Atocha train station specifically, keep bags between your knees when seated waiting for trains. How to avoid: Wear a zipped anti-theft crossbody bag in front of you in any crowded environment Keep phone in a zipped inner pocket or jacket pocket; never in a back pocket Split cash across pockets — €20 front pocket, rest in a money belt or hotel safe Do not pull out phone on crowded escalators, at carriage doors, or on Line 1 at rush hour Report thefts at Comisaría de Centro (Calle Leganitos 19) within 24 hours for insurance

Scam alert in Madrid, Spain — Bird Poop Distraction Pickpocket (pickpocket, severity: high). You are walking across Puerta del Sol when you feel something wet hit your shoulder — 'bird poop,' but suspiciously mustard-yellow or cream-colored. A friendly bystander appears immediately with tissues and helps you wipe it off while expressing sympathy. You thank them and walk on; ten minutes later you realize your wallet is gone. One traveler wrote: 'That happened to me in Madrid years ago. Mustard on my jacket.' Community reports describe the mechanic precisely: 'They pick pocket you while they help wipe off the fake bird poop.' The scam teams operate at Puerta del Sol (the Kilometre Zero plaza in central Madrid), Plaza Mayor, along Gran Vía, and near tourist photo spots like the Bear and Strawberry Tree statue. The pattern is flagged across Barcelona, Madrid, and Lisbon. The 'poop' is typically mustard, ketchup, shaving cream, or paint — sprayed from a pocket-sized bottle as you pass. The 'helpful stranger' appears within seconds, carrying tissues already in hand — the giveaway that they were expecting this 'accident.' Your protection: if you feel something wet hit you unexpectedly, do NOT stop to examine or clean it. Walk immediately to a nearby café, shop, or hotel lobby — a secure indoor space — before dealing with the stain. Do not accept help from any stranger who appears immediately. The stain will wash out later; your wallet and phone are the priority. Keep valuables in a zipped front pocket or crossbody bag worn in front. If you were pickpocketed, file at Comisaría de Centro (Calle Leganitos 19) within 24 hours for insurance documentation. Madrid Policía Nacional takes these reports seriously — Spain's Ministry of Interior has published warnings about the bird-poop variant specifically. How to avoid: If hit by something wet unexpectedly, walk IMMEDIATELY to an indoor space (café, shop, hotel) Do not accept help from any stranger who appears within seconds of the 'accident' Keep valuables in a zipped front pocket or crossbody bag worn in front Photograph the 'helpers' from a distance if you have time — useful for police report File at Comisaría de Centro within 24 hours if pickpocketed for insurance claim

Scam alert in Madrid, Spain — Puerta del Sol Bracelet & Clipboard Petition Scam (pickpocket, severity: moderate). A young woman approaches at Puerta del Sol with a clipboard — 'signing a petition for deaf children.' You stop to listen. She gestures for you to sign. While you hold the pen, a partner opens your day-bag from behind, and a third accomplice tries to tie a colorful 'friendship bracelet' to your wrist. One traveler wrote: 'Tourist from the US here. Got approached by 2 girls with clipboards asking for some petition for disabled children.' The team operates at Puerta del Sol, Plaza Mayor, the entrance to the Royal Palace (Palacio Real), and the Temple of Debod — all high tourist-foot-traffic zones. The bracelet component is the same Syntagma/Athens mechanic. Another traveler witnessed it: 'I did witness the bracelet scam where a guy hands someone a bracelet and then won't take it back.' The charity petition adds a social-obligation hook specifically targeting older travelers — the 'deaf children' or 'disabled orphans' framing is designed to make you feel guilty about walking away. No legitimate Spanish charity collects signatures from tourists in Puerta del Sol; the Spanish Federation of Deaf People and ONCE (the National Organisation of the Spanish Blind) use verifiable volunteer kiosks with uniforms, not clipboard teams. Your protection: if anyone approaches with a clipboard or bracelet, cross your arms and step back immediately. Do not stop to read the clipboard, do not make eye contact, and do not slow your walking pace. Say 'no, gracias' firmly and keep moving. If a bracelet is already on your wrist, walk to a café and cut it off with scissors — do not pay anything. Keep your wallet in a front zipped pocket and your phone in an inner jacket pocket when walking through Puerta del Sol, Plaza Mayor, or near the Royal Palace. These scams peak in April–October; Policía Nacional's Unit for Tourism Assistance (SATE) patrols Puerta del Sol during summer evenings. How to avoid: Cross your arms and step back if approached with a clipboard or bracelet Say 'no, gracias' firmly and keep walking — do not engage Legitimate Spanish charities (ONCE, Federación de Personas Sordas) use uniformed kiosks, not clipboard teams Keep wallet in front zipped pocket or crossbody bag worn in front at Puerta del Sol Report persistent crews to SATE (Tourism Assistance police) — active summer patrols at Puerta del Sol

Scam alert in Madrid, Spain — Fake Prado Museum & Royal Palace 'Skip-the-Line' Ticket Websites (tourist-trap, severity: high). You plan ahead. Weeks before your trip you search 'Prado Museum tickets' and click the first result — a professional-looking site named something like myprado-tickets.com or prado-skiptheline.es. You pay €35 per person for 'skip-the-line' tickets. At the Prado entrance on arrival, the QR codes scan as invalid. One traveler wrote: 'I've tried to buy tickets from Prado's official website but it's glitchy. It keeps asking for a confirmation email address even though I had entered one' — fraud sites exploit the real site's technical issues to funnel tourists. The only official Prado ticket website is museodelprado.es. The Royal Palace (Palacio Real) official tickets are at patrimonionacional.es. Tickets outside these two domains from any 'skip-the-line' or 'official Spain ticket' reseller should be treated with suspicion. Legitimate third-party resellers with customs guarantees include GetYourGuide, Viator, and Tiqets. Community reports reference Prado and Royal Palace tour quality — tours with licensed Spanish guides are legitimate; 'official skip-the-line' tickets at 2x the posted price are resale scams. The Prado posted admission is €15 (or free for the final two hours daily, 6–8 PM, currently as of 2025). The Royal Palace admission is €14. If a reseller charges €35 per person for 'skip-the-line' access that should cost €15–€14, they are marking up the ticket 100–130% — and in the worst case producing fake QR codes entirely. At the site, buy tickets at the official booth or use the free-entry window if budget is the issue. Licensed Spanish tour guides wear a Ministry of Tourism-issued credential (a yellow card with Ministerio de Industria seal); ask to see it before hiring a guide on-site. Pay by credit card for any online ticket purchase; chargeback window is 60–120 days in most jurisdictions. How to avoid: Book Prado tickets only at museodelprado.es; Royal Palace only at patrimonionacional.es Verified third-party resellers: GetYourGuide, Viator, Tiqets (credit card with chargeback) Search the domain name plus 'scam' before paying any online Madrid ticket seller At the Prado, visit in the free 6–8 PM window if budget is the issue Licensed Spanish tour guides wear a Ministerio de Industria yellow credential card — ask to see it

Scam alert in Madrid, Spain — Puerta del Sol & Plaza Mayor Tourist-Menu Restaurant Overcharge (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). You sit at a Plaza Mayor arcade restaurant for lunch. You order paella, a Spanish salad, and two glasses of wine. Bread and olives arrive — unrequested. The bill totals €85. The menu outside showed paella at €18; at the table it was €32. 'Welcome' bread, olives, and a small plate of Manchego added €12. Community reports consistently flag Plaza Mayor arcade restaurants as overpriced tourist traps. One traveler captured the community view: 'It's difficult to go wrong with food. In any case, avoid places very close to tourist attractions and the classic tourist traps.' The mechanic is opaque pricing plus 'optional' extras that arrive unordered. Restaurants on Puerta del Sol's perimeter, around Plaza Mayor's arcades, and along Gran Vía's tourist spine often serve bread, olives, and small tapas 'as a welcome' — each appearing on the bill at €3–€10. The menu at the entrance may show lower prices than the one at the table, or the 'tourist menu del día' may have fine print adding 'bebidas' (drinks) and 'postre' (dessert) at premium prices. Spanish consumer law (Ley General para la Defensa de los Consumidores) requires prices to be clearly disclosed; restaurants violating this can be fined, but enforcement on Plaza Mayor is weak. Your protection: read the menu at the entrance before sitting, and confirm prices at the table match when the menu arrives. Decline any 'welcome' items explicitly when they arrive — 'no, gracias' is enough. Count the bill line by line against the menu you ordered from. For genuine Spanish food at local prices, walk one block away from the main tourist spine: La Latina, Chueca, and Malasaña all have well-reviewed, honestly-priced tapas bars (Casa Lucio, Casa Labra, Bodega de la Ardosa are community-respected for transparent pricing). The 'menu del día' tradition is a Spanish lunch institution — €12–€18 for starter, main, bread, drink, and dessert — but only at restaurants outside the tourist triangle. On Plaza Mayor the same 'menu del día' is often €25–€30 with worse food. How to avoid: Read the menu at the entrance before sitting; confirm prices at the table match Decline 'welcome' items explicitly — 'no, gracias' politely waves them off Eat one block away from Plaza Mayor — La Latina, Chueca, Malasaña have fair-priced local tapas bars Community-respected posted-price Madrid options: Casa Lucio, Casa Labra, Bodega de la Ardosa Proper 'menu del día' is €12–€18 at local restaurants — anything above €22 on Plaza Mayor is tourist pricing

Scam alert in Madrid, Spain — Hotel & Booking Off-Platform Payment Fraud (accommodation, severity: high). Three days before your Madrid arrival, an email appears in your inbox that looks exactly like Booking.com — same logo, same color scheme, same footer. The message says your payment needs to be finalised through a 'secure link.' The URL is close but not identical: booking-com.net, bookingcom-pay.org, or similar. You pay €450; on arrival, the real hotel has no record of the payment, and your original Booking.com reservation appears to have been cancelled. Community reports document that the Booking.com impersonation scam hits Madrid hotels as frequently as Athens or Barcelona, and confirm the mechanic: scammers infiltrate the Booking.com chat system itself, impersonating hotel staff. A Madrid-specific variant targets the Airbnb and short-term rental market in Chueca, Malasaña, and Lavapiés — neighborhoods with high tourist demand and dense apartment conversion. Operators create lookalike listings using photos stolen from legitimate properties, accept deposits, and cancel 48 hours before arrival citing 'water damage' with an offer to relocate you to an 'alternative' that requires off-platform cash payment. Community reports flag booking verification as a genuine concern. In 2025, Ekathimerini-style Spanish media has reported organized Airbnb fraud rings operating in Madrid, with Policía Nacional making arrests during a May 2025 operation. Your protection: book only through Booking.com, Hotels.com, Expedia, or Airbnb with credit card payment and screenshot all confirmations. Never click payment links in emails, even ones that appear to come from the booking platform — log into the platform directly through a fresh browser tab and check your reservation status. Call the hotel through the Google Maps phone number (not the one in any recent email) to verify any payment request. Read the most recent 30 days of hotel reviews looking for 'payment link,' 'water damage,' or 'moved to sister property' complaints. Pay only by credit card for chargeback protection (60–120 days). For Madrid peak season (April–October and Christmas markets), book six or more weeks ahead through official channels to reduce exposure to last-minute 'deal' messages. How to avoid: Book only through Booking.com, Hotels.com, Expedia, Airbnb with credit card — screenshot confirmations Never click payment links in emails; log into booking account directly in a fresh browser tab Call the hotel through the Google Maps number (not the email's) to verify any request Pay only by credit card — chargeback is your strongest protection (60–120 days) Book six or more weeks ahead for peak season (April–October, Christmas)

Scam alert in Málaga, Spain — Málaga Airport (AGP) & Late-Night Taxi Overcharge (transport, severity: moderate). Málaga–Costa del Sol Airport (AGP) is one of Spain's busiest, serving the entire Costa del Sol package-tourism belt from Torremolinos to Marbella. The legitimate licensed taxi fare from AGP to central Malaga is €20–€28 on the meter; to Torremolinos €20–€30; to Marbella €60–€90.
