Brazilian restaurant law (Lei 13.419/2017) makes the 10% serviço charge OPTIONAL — you can refuse it, particularly for poor service. The 2025 scam patterns: (a) Ponta Negra orla 'couvert artístico R$80–R$150 per person' (legitimate R$15–R$35 for a genuine Amazonian musician — boi-bumbá, carimbó, forró); (b) 'peixe do dia preço de mercado' (daily fish market price) with no R$ per kg quoted — bill arrives R$280 for a 500g tambaqui fillet (real R$100–R$180 for same quantity); (c) 'pirarucu fresco R$350 mandatory weight' arrives as 900g serving billed R$850 (fair pirarucu is R$120–R$220 per kg, portion 400–500g is R$60–R$110); (d) 'tucunaré grelhado' at Ponta Negra barracas billed as 1kg when served 600g (weigh in front of you before cooking); (e) 'serviço 10%' added silently with the menu showing 'serviço opcional' fine print; (f) credit-card surcharge 5–10% only at bill-time ('we prefer PIX'); (g) Mercado Adolpho Lisboa food-stall 'tacacá gringo price' R$35 (local R$12) + 'tucupi shot R$15' (local R$4); (h) 'caldeirada de tambaqui para dois' at Ponta Negra restaurants served as portion for one, billed R$280 (fair R$120–R$180 for a genuine 2-person portion). For travelers: (1) BEFORE sitting, ask for the menu (carta) in Portuguese AND confirm in writing: (a) the couvert artístico R$ amount per person, (b) serviço 10% policy — photograph the menu page showing 'serviço opcional' (OPTIONAL under Lei 13.419/2017), (c) credit-card surcharge percentage; (2) for Amazonian fish, AGREE weight in R$ per kg IN WRITING BEFORE cooking — fair 2026 prices: tambaqui R$100–R$180 per kg, pirarucu R$120–R$220 per kg (pricier as it's a managed fishery), tucunaré R$80–R$150 per kg, matrinxã R$70–R$140 per kg; (3) reputable Ponta Negra restaurants: Banzeiro (Google 4.6+, Amazonian fine dining, R$120–R$280), Caxiri (riverside, R$80–R$180), Tambaqui de Banda (Ponta Negra barraca tradition, R$60–R$120); reputable Centro: Peixaria do Moraes (Centro Histórico, R$70–R$160), Mercado Adolpho Lisboa's upper-floor stalls (tacaça R$12–R$18 LOCAL PRICE); (4) AVOID English-only menus posted outside — walk 1–2 blocks inland for authentic local prices; (5) if serviço is added against your wishes for poor service, politely REFUSE and cite Lei 13.419/2017 — the manager knows this; (6) for Mercado Adolpho Lisboa food stalls, pay in Portuguese ('quanto é?') + small bills (R$10, R$20 notes); if a stall quotes you R$35 for tacacá, walk to the next stall — the next will be R$12; (7) for tucupi + tambaqui cooking demos at your hotel's partnered restaurant, confirm the R$ per kg BEFORE the demo starts; (8) PROCON Amazonas 151 for billing disputes; DEATUR Manaus +55 92 3584 1373. How to avoid: BEFORE sitting, confirm couvert + serviço + card surcharge IN WRITING; photograph menu Fish: agree R$ per kg BEFORE cooking (tambaqui R$100–R$180/kg; pirarucu R$120–R$220/kg) Reputable: Banzeiro / Caxiri / Tambaqui de Banda (Ponta Negra); Peixaria do Moraes (Centro) REFUSE serviço if poor service (Lei 13.419/2017 — OPTIONAL); PROCON Amazonas 151 Mercado Adolpho Lisboa: pay in small bills + Portuguese; walk to next stall if gringo-priced

Scam alert in Manaus, Brazil — Amazonas Regional Uber & Mototaxi Coordinated-Scam Pattern (Santarém / Alto do Chão Template) (transport, severity: high). The broader Amazonas state (including side-trip destinations like Santarém, Alto do Chão, and Parintins) has a documented 2025 coordinated Uber / rideshare scam pattern that Manaus-based travelers encounter when venturing beyond the capital. Community reports document a team of drivers + passengers working together to defraud tourists via fake route detours, 'broken-meter' cash demands, and passport-card skimming. Manaus-parallel safety discussions, Amazon-context operator-verification threads, a regional Fortaleza app-scam pattern, and 2025 solo-traveler threads all reinforce the same defensive rules. The 2025 Santarém / Alto do Chão pattern (translatable to Manaus regional Uber and side-trips): (a) coordinated driver-passenger team — you book Uber, the app shows a driver 5 min away; en route to pickup, a passenger (planted accomplice) is already in the car; at pickup the driver claims 'another ride ahead of you' and asks you to wait or share — accomplice-passenger engages you in conversation while driver takes a 'shortcut' detour padding the fare; (b) 'meter / app failed — R$100 cash' demand mid-trip; (c) driver asking to 'see your card to confirm the Uber payment' — card skimming via hidden reader; (d) driver taking a deliberately long route to pad the in-app fare (Uber Brazil allows surge + long-route charges); (e) destination 'changed' — driver claims 'your hotel is closed' or 'that area is dangerous, I'll take you to a better hotel' — steering you to a commissioned 'safe' hotel that charges 3x normal rate; (f) in Parintins during Boi-Bumbá festival (June), rideshare supply collapses — unlicensed mototaxis + private-car drivers emerge charging 5–10x normal with robbery risk; (g) Alto do Chão river-beach day-trip: 'driver package R$600 round-trip + waiting' offered by airport tout — real Uber R$150–R$250 round-trip + hold on driver with hourly wait rate via in-app. For travelers: (1) ALWAYS verify driver name + car plate + photo MATCH the in-app profile BEFORE entering the vehicle — if mismatched, cancel + rebook; (2) NEVER share an Uber with an already-present 'other passenger' unless YOU explicitly booked UberPool — if a stranger is in the car on pickup, cancel in-app + report via safety button; (3) NEVER hand your credit or debit card to any driver for any reason — payment is ONLY via the in-app card or cash at the end of trip; refuse 'let me scan your card to confirm payment' demands; (4) FOLLOW the route on your phone's GPS (Google Maps in split-screen with Uber) — if the driver deviates significantly, ask 'está certo o caminho?' and if suspicious, ask to stop at the next public place (metro, mall, hotel) and cancel / rebook; (5) REFUSE every mid-trip 'meter broke, R$100 cash' demand — Uber Brazil uses GPS not a meter, the in-app price is final; if threatened, rule 911 / Polícia Militar 190; (6) if driver claims 'your hotel is closed / dangerous', tell them to take you to the original address or STOP immediately at the nearest public place — never let a stranger redirect your destination; (7) for Parintins Festival de Boi-Bumbá (late June), book transfers 3–6 months ahead via reputable operators; rideshare supply collapses during festival — do NOT plan last-minute mototaxi; (8) for Alto do Chão day-trip, book Uber round-trip with driver wait (via in-app 'Hora por hora' feature at R$40–R$60 per hour) — typical R$150–R$250 round-trip + R$200–R$300 wait for 6 hours = R$400–R$550; REFUSE every 'R$600 package' airport tout; (9) DEATUR Manaus +55 92 3584 1373; Polícia Militar 190; Uber in-app 24/7 safety line. How to avoid: VERIFY driver name + plate + photo MATCH app BEFORE entering; cancel if mismatched NEVER share Uber with 'other passenger'; NEVER hand card to driver for any reason Follow GPS route on your phone; if deviation, demand stop at public place + cancel REFUSE every 'meter broke R$100 cash' mid-trip demand (Uber uses in-app GPS pricing) Book Parintins / Alto do Chão transfers via reputable operators 3–6 mo ahead; DEATUR +55 92 3584 1373

Scam alert in Manchester, United Kingdom — The Fake Concert Ticket Seller (tourist-trap, severity: high). You've been trying to get tickets to a sold-out show at the AO Arena. Scrolling Facebook Marketplace, you find someone selling two tickets at face value. They seem legitimate, sharing screenshots of the confirmation email and insisting on PayPal Friends and Family to 'avoid fees.' You send the money and receive what looks like a valid PDF. On the night of the show, the QR code is rejected at the gate -- it's already been used, or it's completely fabricated. As reported by Greater Manchester Police and flagged repeatedly in local traveler forums, fake ticket scams exploded during the 2025 Oasis Heaton Park residency. Action Fraud logged over 10,500 ticket scam complaints since early 2024, with losses exceeding 10 million pounds nationwide. How to avoid: Buy tickets only from official sources like Ticketmaster, AXS, or the venue's own website If buying resale, use platforms with buyer guarantees like Twickets or the venue's official resale partner Never pay via Friends and Family or bank transfer -- use payment methods with fraud protection Verify the ticket by asking the seller to transfer it through the official ticketing app rather than sending a PDF Check the seller's profile history and reviews -- legitimate sellers have established accounts

Scam alert in Manchester, United Kingdom — The Piccadilly Gardens Pickpocket (pickpocket, severity: moderate). You're sitting on a bench in Piccadilly Gardens, checking your phone for directions, when a group ... You're sitting on a bench in Piccadilly Gardens, checking your phone for directions, when a group of teenagers starts an argument nearby. It's loud and chaotic, and everyone turns to watch. One of them bumps into you while gesturing wildly, apologizes, and moves on. Five minutes later, you reach for your phone and it's gone from your jacket pocket. Piccadilly Gardens has long been flagged by locals as a hotspot for opportunistic theft, and Greater Manchester Police regularly issue warnings about the area. The staged argument or commotion is a classic distraction technique, and the narrow benches and tram platforms make it easy for a quick hand to find an unguarded pocket or open bag. How to avoid: Keep your phone in a zipped inner pocket and avoid using it while seated in the open Stay aware of your surroundings -- if a commotion starts nearby, protect your belongings first Use the Metrolink tram shelters rather than exposed benches when waiting in Piccadilly Gardens Carry a cross-body bag with the clasp facing your body rather than a backpack or shoulder bag Avoid lingering in Piccadilly Gardens after dark when opportunistic crime increases

Scam alert in Manchester, United Kingdom — The Sob Story Beggar (nightlife, severity: minor). You're walking toward Manchester Piccadilly Station when a well-spoken man approaches you looking distressed. He explains he's an ex-soldier who just got out of hospital, his wallet was stolen, and he needs 15 pounds for a train ticket home to Liverpool. He shows a cardboard sign that adds to the story. Feeling sympathetic, you hand over the cash. An hour later, you spot the same man on Market Street giving the exact same pitch to another tourist. As local residents explain, these targeted sob stories rotate between several operators who pass the same props and signs between shifts. A genuine person in crisis would be directed to the station staff or local services, not approaching strangers individually with a polished story. How to avoid: Offer to buy a train ticket at the counter rather than handing over cash -- a genuine person will accept Direct them to Manchester's Street Support service or Booth Centre for real assistance Politely decline and keep walking -- 'Sorry, I can't help' is sufficient If you want to help the homeless, donate to local charities like the Mustard Tree or Barnabus Report persistent aggressive begging to British Transport Police at the station

Scam alert in Manchester, United Kingdom — The Unlicensed Late-Night Cab (transport, severity: high). It's 3 AM on a Saturday and the clubs on Deansgate are emptying out. The taxi queue stretches down the block and the Uber surge price is eye-watering. A car with no markings pulls alongside and the driver calls out, 'Taxi? No queue, no wait.' Relief wins over caution and you climb in. There's no meter, no partition, and no license plate visible. The driver asks where you're going, then names a price double the normal fare. Some passengers have reported being driven to isolated areas and pressured for larger payments, or having their bank details compromised after paying by card in these vehicles. Greater Manchester Police describe these as 'pirate taxis' and warn they are entirely unregulated. How to avoid: Pre-book a licensed private hire vehicle through Uber, Bolt, or a local firm like Street Cars before you leave the club Use the official taxi ranks on Deansgate and Peter Street where licensed Hackney cabs queue Check that any Hackney cab has a valid plate on the rear and a driver badge on the dashboard Travel in groups and share official taxis to reduce wait times and costs Consider the night bus service or walk to a well-lit main road where licensed cabs are easier to find

Scam alert in Manchester, United Kingdom — The Clipboard Charity Collector (nightlife, severity: minor). You're walking down Market Street toward the Arndale Centre when someone steps in front of you with ... You're walking down Market Street toward the Arndale Centre when someone steps in front of you with a clipboard and a laminated badge. They gesture as if they're deaf and push a sponsorship form at you showing a charity logo and a list of names with donation amounts of 10 to 20 pounds. You feel pressured to match what others have given and write your name and a 10-pound note. As warned by Greater Manchester Police, these collectors are not affiliated with any registered charity. The form is designed to create peer pressure with pre-filled donation amounts, and the money goes directly to the operators. Genuine charity street collectors in the UK must have a council license and will carry official identification. How to avoid: Ask for the charity registration number and verify it on the Charity Commission website before donating Legitimate UK street collectors carry a council-issued license and official charity ID Say 'no thank you' firmly and keep walking -- you have no obligation to stop or sign anything Never write your name, address, or bank details on a street clipboard If you want to support a charity, donate directly online through their verified website

Scam alert in Manila, Philippines — NAIA Airport Taxi Overcharge (nightlife, severity: high). You land at NAIA and head to a taxi outside. The driver either refuses to use the meter or 'the meter is broken,' quoting you a flat rate of ₱4,000 to your hotel in Makati — a trip that should cost ₱200-300 by meter. Some drivers charge by terminal: the shuttle bus between T1 and T3 is free, but touts have been known to charge ₱4,000 for the five-minute ride. How to avoid: Use Grab (rideshare app) from the designated Grab pickup zones at each terminal Or use the official airport taxi counters inside arrivals where rates are metered Never get in a taxi that won't run the meter — walk away

Scam alert in Manila, Philippines — New Friend Card Game (distraction, severity: high). You're approached by a very friendly Filipino who says he studied in your country and is now visiting his family in Manila. He invites you to his aunt's house nearby for some food. The 'aunt' sets up a card game where you're shown a rigged winning streak, bet increasing amounts, and then lose everything in one final hand. The entire family is part of the operation. How to avoid: Never follow a stranger you just met to a private residence The 'friendly local with a connection to your home country' opener is the most common Manila scam intro If invited anywhere private within minutes of meeting someone, politely decline and leave

Scam alert in Manila, Philippines — Kalesa Carriage Overcharge at Intramuros (transport, severity: moderate). You visit Intramuros and decide to take a traditional kalesa (horse-drawn carriage) for a romantic ride through the historic streets. The driver quotes ₱200 for a short loop. Afterward, the bill is ₱1,500 — you're told that's the 'full tour rate' and the ₱200 was just the starting fee. The driver becomes aggressive and bystanders seem to side with him. How to avoid: Ask specifically: 'What is the TOTAL price for the full ride back to this point?' Official kalesa rates in Intramuros are posted — look for the tourism board rate card Pay only the pre-agreed amount — have exact change ready

Scam alert in Manila, Philippines — Money Changer Short Change (overcharging, severity: moderate). You exchange $100 at a money changer in Ermita and the teller counts out a stack of pesos quickly, placing them on the counter. When you get to your hotel and count the bills, you're short by several hundred pesos — the teller palmed some bills during the fast count. This is so common that locals call it the 'quick hand' scam. How to avoid: Count every bill yourself, in front of the teller, before leaving the counter Use ATMs or hotel exchange desks instead of street money changers Say clearly 'I need to count this' and do not be rushed

Scam alert in Manila, Philippines — Fake Police Drug Setup (counterfeit, severity: high). You're approached by someone who sells you something you believe to be a harmless product. Shortly after, men identifying themselves as police officers stop you and claim you've just purchased illegal drugs. They threaten arrest unless you pay a 'fine' on the spot — often hundreds of US dollars. The 'police' and the seller are working together. How to avoid: Never buy anything from street sellers in Manila's entertainment districts Real Philippine police do not collect cash fines on the street If approached, insist on going to the actual police station — scammers will back down

Scam alert in Manila, Philippines — Overpriced Jeepney 'Tourist' Fare (transport, severity: low). You take a jeepney — the iconic Filipino transport — and hand over a large bill for what should be a ₱15 ride. The conductor gives you change, but you're short by ₱50 or more. When you question it, the conductor speaks rapidly in Tagalog and waves away your concern. First-time visitors who don't know the exact fare are regular targets. How to avoid: Carry exact change for jeepney fares — ask fellow passengers what the fare is before boarding The standard minimum fare is ₱13-15 for the first 4km Use Grab or the new EDSA Carousel BRT for hassle-free fixed-price travel

Scam alert in Manuel Antonio, Costa Rica — Fake 'Park Ranger' Road Blockers on Route 618 — 'Park Full / Park Closed' Parking Extortion (impersonation, severity: high). This is the single most documented tourist scam in Costa Rica, and the US Embassy San José explicitly flagged it in its November 25, 2025 Security Alert, citing 'impostors impersonating police officers and asking for money.' Community reports describe the canonical account: three men 500 m short of the real entrance, one in khaki with a fake ID badge and a fake ticket scanner; when the traveler refused their $12 parking lot, the scammer leaned into the driver window, pretended to phone the park, and shouted 'you know what? I just cancelled your tickets, no entry for you today.' Travelers describe identical operators dressed 'kinda like Indiana Jones — hats, khaki clothes, radios' blocking every tourist car about 5–10 minutes before the real gate; one group had a scammer slap the side of the car and flip them off. Community reports confirm the racket still runs in 2026. Travelers report being asked for '6 million colones' (~$11,000, an absurd number meant to confuse), and one had a scammer grab a metal rod and threaten the car. These are coordinated 3–6-man teams in near-identical fake uniforms with printed 'PARK' or 'SINAC' lettering, lanyards, radios, clipboards.

For travelers in 2025/2026, the defensive playbook: (1) buy tickets ONLY at sinac.go.cr — since 2023 Manuel Antonio is online-only at $18.08 adult / $5.65 child, cap 2,000/day, closed Tuesdays; anyone selling paper or 'scanning' roadside is a scammer, period; (2) drive past every khaki figure waving you over — the real gate is at the very end where you can't drive further, past a circular turnaround; legit lots (Chalo Parking, $5–$10/day) sit on the LEFT just before the gate; (3) if a scammer stands in the road, lay on the horn and creep forward — they always move; or tailgate a tour shuttle; (4) say 'picking up a friend at Hotel Manuel Antonio' — roadblock crews wave you through; (5) if a scammer damages your rental, drive directly to the new Tourist Police station on Playa Espadilla (opened Sept 2024, 548 m², 16 officers year-round); call 911 for threats or Fuerza Pública non-emergency 2222-1365; (6) never hand over cash to anyone before the SINAC turnstile. How to avoid: Buy park tickets ONLY at sinac.go.cr ($18.08 adult, $5.65 child) — paper tickets at the roadside = 100% scam. Drive to the very end of Route 618 where the circular turnaround sits — official lots (Chalo, etc.) are right there. Lay on the horn and creep forward — scammers always move; or tailgate a tour shuttle through the gauntlet. Say 'going to Hotel Manuel Antonio to pick up a friend' — roadblock crews wave you through. File reports at the new Tourist Police station on Playa Espadilla (opened Sept 2024, 16 officers) or call 911.

Scam alert in Manuel Antonio, Costa Rica — Fake 'SINAC Ticket Booth' Paper Ticket Resellers at the Park Entrance (tourist-trap, severity: high). Since SINAC (Sistema Nacional de Áreas de Conservación) moved Manuel Antonio to online-only ticketing in 2023 at sinac.go.cr (2025/2026 rate: $18.08 adult, $5.65 child 6–12, cap 2,000/day, closed Tuesdays), a secondary scam has replaced the old window line: fake 'ticket booths' near the real gate selling paper or handwritten 'tickets' for $20–$40 USD. Community reports describe a scammer pulling out a 'fake scanner' to 'validate' ticketed guests at a roadside stall. Travelers note the same crew upselling '$60 per person mangrove tours a half-hour away' when tourists refused the parking scam. One traveler wrote: 'They wear uniforms that look like costumes, if you look at them closely. Everyone over there is a vulture.' Community reports confirm the pattern active into 2026. Confederates inside restaurants and gift shops advertise 'Official Park Tickets — Pay Here' with printed signs — never legitimate. Some operators take $40 cash, print a fake QR code, and send tourists to the gate where SINAC rangers reject them; by then the seller has vanished. A real SINAC ticket generates a PDF with a green QR code, the visitor's passport number, the date, and a specific entry-time window; nothing printed by hand on the road is valid.

For travelers in 2025/2026, the defensive playbook: (1) book ONLY at sinac.go.cr — the site is glitchy (travelers confirm it often hangs mid-transaction) but it is the only valid channel; book 7–14 days ahead, especially Dec–April high season and Tuesday-after-reopening days; (2) if sinac.go.cr refuses to complete, use a licensed local operator — reputable options: Jade Tours (guide Julian), Edwin's Manuel Antonio Tours (guide Saul), or your hotel front desk; never a street seller; (3) save the SINAC confirmation PDF offline on your phone — the green QR code is what the turnstile scans; (4) any private guide must hold an ICT (Instituto Costarricense de Turismo) license — verify at visitcostarica.com's directory of 2,500+ certified guides; (5) bring a printed backup QR in case the phone dies, and arrive before 7:30 AM since the park closes to new entries at 2 PM and caps sell out; (6) if approached by any roadside 'ticket' seller, walk away and report to the Tourist Police station on Playa Espadilla. How to avoid: Book online ONLY at sinac.go.cr ($18.08 adult, $5.65 child 6–12) 7–14 days ahead. Save PDF with green SINAC QR + passport number offline on your phone before arrival. Verify any private guide at visitcostarica.com's ICT-licensed guide directory. If SINAC site fails, use Jade Tours, Edwin's Manuel Antonio Tours, or hotel front desk — never street sellers. Arrive at the gate before 7:30 AM; bring printed backup QR in case phone dies.

Scam alert in Manuel Antonio, Costa Rica — Unofficial 'ICT-Certified' Guides at the Park Gate — $60 Shortest-Route Rip-Off (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Community reports describe the canonical case: a guide called 'Glen' (the traveler posted his photo) took $60 per person for a 'wildlife tour,' failed to set up his spotting scope (the traveler suspected it didn't even work), admitted he couldn't operate another guide's scope, took the shortest route through the mangrove to the beach avoiding the sloth and monkey hotspots, and showed no wildlife knowledge. The top community reply: 'if you don't pre-book your guide through the park, you get left with the dudes hanging around for people who didn't pre-plan.' Travelers note that a real guide carries an ICT (Instituto Costarricense de Turismo) license, verifiable in visitcostarica.com's directory of 2,500+ certified naturalist guides. One traveler wrote: 'the Manuel Antonio area was some of the worst scamming/tourist trapping I've ever seen. Constant people lying to my face saying I wasn't allowed to do certain things without paying them.' Community reports document the parallel pattern: unofficial guides cut the 4-hour wildlife tour down to a 1.5-hour dash to the beach to squeeze more groups per day. Going rate at the gate for these unofficial guides is $50–$80 per person; a legitimate ICT-certified private guide booked via Jade Tours, Edwin's, or a hotel runs $30–$45 per person for a proper 2.5-hour tour with a working scope.

For travelers in 2025/2026, the playbook: (1) book via ICT-certified operators before arrival — Jade Tours (guide Julian), Edwin's Manuel Antonio Private Tour (guide Saul — travelers praised showing two- and three-toed sloths, white-faced howler monkeys, basilisks, and frogs), or your hotel front desk; (2) verify any guide's ICT license by asking for their ICT card with photo + ID, or search their name at visitcostarica.com's 'Tour Guides' directory; (3) a guide who won't show ICT credentials is not licensed — walk away; (4) expect $30–$45 pp for a 2.5-hour private tour including entrance handling through their licensed pipeline; anyone demanding $60+ cash at the gate is overcharging; (5) confirm your guide has a working high-magnification spotting scope (essential for sloths 20 m up in the canopy) — no scope means no sloths; (6) specify the Sendero Mirador + Playa Manuel Antonio loop, not the mangrove-to-beach shortcut; (7) underperforming guides should be reported to ICT at 2299-5800 or to the Tourist Police on Playa Espadilla. How to avoid: Pre-book via Jade Tours, Edwin's Manuel Antonio Tours, or hotel front desk — $30–$45 pp typical. Ask to see ICT photo license card; verify name at visitcostarica.com tour-guide directory. Confirm the guide carries a working high-magnification spotting scope before paying. Specify Sendero Mirador + Playa Manuel Antonio loop — skip the mangrove-to-beach shortcut. File ICT complaints at 2299-5800; Tourist Police on Playa Espadilla for aggressive cases.

Scam alert in Manuel Antonio, Costa Rica — Playa Espadilla Beach 'Parking + Umbrella' Cash-Only Intimidation at David's Crew (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Community reports document the beach-side parking racket: a crew led by a man named David charges ₡15,000 colones (~$29 USD) for parking + umbrella + 2 chairs, then refuses to take cards; when one traveler pushed back, 'three or four guys come to start discussing and trying to intimidate you' — especially David. Google reviews cited by travelers describe operators 'throwing stones at cars if you don't pay for parking.' Another report describes a related Easter-weekend variant: parked on Playa Espadilla street after sunset, returned to find a 'traffic cop' removing the license plate as part of a supposed ticket process; stranded without plates until Monday. A counter-voice noted 'parking all over the place by the beach ignoring the parking guys... zero issues' — the 'service' is optional; the coercion is the scam. Further community reports describe: 'the parking attendants are aggressive and will block the street, stand in front of your car, yell, scream and punch or kick your car,' and 'a guy came up demanding money to park there. When we refused he grabbed a metal rod and threatened to vandalize our car.' Two flavors run: (a) aggressive 'pay or your car gets damaged' shakedown on a public street — extortion; (b) legitimate-looking beach service ($15–$30 for parking + umbrella + chairs) where the cash-only ambush lands at pickup. Genuine vendors exist — travelers parked for $10 without incident; others noted the end-of-road circular turnaround has $5–$10 field parking. Correct lots sit at the very end; scammers sit on the beach frontage before the field.

For travelers at Playa Espadilla: (1) carry ₡5,000–₡20,000 in small bills — every beach operator is cash-only; ATM at BAC Credomatic, Manuel Antonio village entrance; (2) type the price into your phone Notes app and have the vendor confirm BEFORE parking, umbrella, or food service; a ₡15,000 quote can't then escalate to ₡30,000; (3) park ONLY at the end-of-road circular turnaround — street-side 'attendants' are the shakedown crew; (4) if pressured by the David crew or any 3–4-man group, walk to the new Tourist Police station on Playa Espadilla (Sept 2024, 548 m², 16 officers 24/7) and file; (5) never pay an unmarked 'traffic cop' on the beach — real Boleta de Citación tickets are paid at Banco de Costa Rica branches, never to the officer; (6) photograph vendor + plate + spot before paying; nearby Playa Biesanz and Playa La Vaca are quieter alternatives. How to avoid: Carry ₡5,000–₡20,000 colones small bills; ATM at BAC Credomatic, Manuel Antonio village entrance. Lock price into your phone Notes app and have vendor confirm BEFORE service. Park only at the end-of-road circular turnaround (correct $5–$10 lots) — not on beach frontage. Never pay a 'traffic cop' on the beach cash — real Boletas are paid at Banco de Costa Rica. Report aggression to the Tourist Police station on Playa Espadilla (Sept 2024, 24/7) or dial 911.

Scam alert in Manuel Antonio, Costa Rica — Tracopa Bus SJO–Quepos Rest Stop Luggage & Overhead-Bin Theft (theft, severity: high). A 2024 community report documented the Tracopa pattern firsthand — on a Tracopa bus heading San José→Quepos, during a short restroom break north of Jacó, 'a group of guys who were passengers on the bus waited until everyone got off for the restroom break then robbed any valuables left on the bus, and had a car waiting for them which they then left in.' A female passenger lost her laptop from the overhead bin. The traveler notes 'there's something of a false sense of security at that particular restroom break, as it's very short and you're always within sight of the bus' — but the thieves are inside the bus, not approaching from outside. Another commenter added: 'These people have come up with some of the most incredible ways to steal from you… anything and everything with you if you want it when you return. I remember when they were doing strong-arm robberies on these buses.' The Tracopa SJO–Quepos route (~3 hours, ₡5,000–₡7,000 one-way at 2025 fares via Terminal Plaza Víquez in San José) is the cheapest way to Manuel Antonio — which is why the operation targets it. Undercarriage luggage is relatively safe (driver locks it); the attack surface is overhead racks and seat pockets where laptops, cameras, passports, and wallets are left during the brief restroom break. The Sept 2024 Playa Espadilla Tourist Police station improves the post-theft response, but the rest-stop gap persists.

For travelers taking Tracopa or any long-distance bus in 2025/2026: (1) never leave ANY valuable in the overhead bin — take your entire daypack (phone, passport, cash, laptop) with you every stop, even a 5-minute restroom break; (2) if you must leave a bag, lock it with a TSA cable lock to the overhead rail — thieves skip locked bags; (3) prefer Tracopa Direct (fewer stops) over the local service — direct skips the Jacó restroom stop; schedules at tracopacr.com; (4) alternative: Interbus, Gray Line, or Easy Ride shared shuttle $49–$65 pp door-to-door SJO→Manuel Antonio, 4 hours, no restroom stops, luggage watched; (5) private transfer $180–$240 USD for 1–4 pax via Monkey Ride, Easy Ride, or hotel — expensive but zero theft risk; (6) budget alternative: Sansa Air SJO→Quepos domestic flight $89–$149 one-way, 25 minutes; (7) if robbed, report to Fuerza Pública in Quepos (911 or the Tourist Police station on Playa Espadilla), get an OIJ case number (800-8000-645) — required for travel insurance claims within 48 hours. How to avoid: NEVER leave valuables on the bus — daypack with passport/phone/laptop comes with you every stop. Lock any bag to the overhead rail with a TSA cable lock — thieves skip locked bags. Prefer Tracopa Direct, Interbus/GrayLine shared shuttle ($49–$65), or Sansa Air ($89–$149) instead. For 2–4 travelers: private transfer $180–$240 via Easy Ride or Monkey Ride — zero theft risk. Report thefts immediately: 911 + OIJ case number at Quepos Fuerza Pública within 48h for insurance.

Scam alert in Manuel Antonio, Costa Rica — White-Faced Capuchin & Raccoon Beach-Theft Distraction — Monkey-Feeding Bag Grab (distraction, severity: moderate). Community reports cover the overlapping wildlife and human theft pattern. A top comment cuts to the truth: 'More likely that a homo sapien will take your stuff on the beach.' Another traveler adds a unique hazard: 'At the MA beach there are Manzanillo trees which can cause a rash if you touch them. There were people sitting under them with clothes draped over branches. Our guide pointed it out to us as an example of what not to do. There are no warning signs.' Community reports document the hybrid human+monkey theft: the white-faced capuchin monkeys at Manuel Antonio's beaches are habituated, aggressive, and trained to target unattended bags — but they're also cover for human thieves. A capuchin causes a scene near one group (grabbing a water bottle, dropping fruit), and a human accomplice lifts a phone or wallet from a different group during the distraction. Raccoons (pizotes and coatis) pull the same trick at dusk. A viral video titled 'Masked thief steals bag off the beach in Costa Rica' shows the human-only variant: a man in a balaclava runs to a blanket on Playa Manuel Antonio and grabs the bag while the owners are 3 m away in the water. The park bans food entirely in 2025 (enforced by SINAC rangers, bag-check at the turnstile) specifically to reduce monkey aggression — but enforcement is spotty and many visitors smuggle snacks in, which trains the monkeys to grab every bag regardless.

For travelers at Manuel Antonio's beaches, the defensive playbook: (1) bring a waterproof 10–20L dry bag that you carry INTO the water on a shoulder strap — passport, phone, cash, hotel key all inside (traveler-recommended); $25 Amazon Basics model is sufficient; (2) leave all non-essential valuables in the hotel safe — don't bring your laptop, camera body, or jewelry to the beach; (3) do NOT bring food into the park — it's illegal, it trains monkeys to associate bags with food, and rangers may refuse entry or confiscate at the turnstile; (4) avoid the tree line at the back of the beach (monkeys and manzanillo tree rash); set up 15+ m from the nearest tree; (5) travel in pairs and rotate a watcher — one person swims while the other sits with the bags, switch after 30 minutes; (6) if a monkey or raccoon approaches, back away 3 m and yell — never try to grab or chase (bites transmit rabies and parasites, require a painful 4-shot vaccine series at Hospital Max Terán Vals in Quepos); (7) if you're robbed by a human, file the report within 24h at the Tourist Police station on Playa Espadilla (Sept 2024, 24/7 English assistance) — required for travel insurance; the OIJ non-emergency line is 800-8000-645 ('800-8000-OIJ'). How to avoid: Waterproof 10–20L dry bag carried INTO the water — passport + phone + cash always with you. Zero food in the park — park rules enforced at turnstile; reduces monkey aggression. Set up 15+ m from the tree line (avoid manzanillo rash + monkey range). Pair rotation — one person watches bags at all times, never leave unattended. Bite / theft reports: Hospital Max Terán Vals Quepos + Tourist Police Playa Espadilla + OIJ 800-8000-645.

Scam alert in Manuel Antonio, Costa Rica — Manuel Antonio Strip Restaurant 'Gringo Menu' & Hidden Service-Charge Upcharge (tourist-trap, severity: low). Community reports anchor the menu-pricing complaint: one traveler was charged $34 for 'a lunch, 1 beer & 1 water bottle' at a Manuel Antonio tourist restaurant where the menu had no prices at all. Travelers document the pattern: English-menu restaurants in Manuel Antonio village charge 50–100% more than the Spanish-menu sodas a few blocks away, then add a mandatory 10% service charge and 13% IVA (VAT), often not printed clearly on the final bill. One traveler clarifies: 'there is no gringo price in the sense that a restaurant won't give a price to me and another to a gringo. In fact that is illegal. What you have is that there's a lot of expensive places.' The mechanisms: (1) English-only menus with prices in USD only — 30–50% higher than the colones equivalent; (2) no prices on the menu at all, verbal quotes, bill doubles at payment; (3) 13% IVA + 10% service added to pre-tax quoted prices (true total 23% above menu); (4) drinks at $6–$10 USD when the local soda sells the same Imperial beer for ₡1,200 (~$2.30); (5) 'catch of the day' with a per-ounce price that reveals a $60 fish at payment. Another traveler reports: 'Had a waiter spend the whole lunch trying to sell me his shitty jewelry' — upsell and menu-price-hike are the same ecosystem. Costa Rica Ley 7472 (consumer protection) requires all prices to be displayed clearly, tax and service included (precio total); a menu without precio total is technically illegal.

For travelers eating in Manuel Antonio in 2025/2026, the playbook: (1) walk past the Route 618 ocean-view decks with English-only menus — equivalent food at a Spanish-menu soda in Quepos (15-min drive) runs 40–60% cheaper (as one traveler put it: 'Try going to a Soda they're cheaper'); (2) 2025 traveler-recommended sodas: Soda Sánchez (Quepos), Soda Restaurante Locos Kepos, Mi Lugar Manuel Antonio (fair-priced ceviche ₡5,000–₡8,000); (3) before ordering ask 'Está incluido el IVA y el servicio?' — Costa Rican law requires yes; any 'service added later' answer = leave, or confirm the final all-in figure in writing; (4) scan the whole menu — any item without a printed price is a trap and grounds to walk out (Ley 7472); (5) for 'catch of the day' ask exact $/ounce AND weight BEFORE ordering; (6) pay credit card (Visa/Mastercard/Amex) not cash — card dispute records protect you; Capital One and Amex handle CR disputes well; (7) file at consumidor.go.cr; post TripAdvisor + Google Maps reviews to warn others. How to avoid: Eat at Spanish-menu sodas (Soda Sánchez Quepos, Locos Kepos, Mi Lugar MA) — 40–60% cheaper. Always ask 'Está incluido el IVA y el servicio?' — required by law to say yes. Walk out of any restaurant with no printed prices (Ley 7472 violation). Pay credit card — Visa/Mastercard/Amex dispute mechanism if overcharged. File at consumidor.go.cr + post TripAdvisor/Google reviews for bad actors.

Scam alert in Marmaris, Turkey — Fake Holiday Rep Excursion Fraud (tourist-trap, severity: high). You check into your Marmaris hotel and the next morning a smartly dressed man appears in the reception area holding a clipboard with the Jet2 or TUI logo. He introduces himself as your tour operator's holiday rep and invites you to a 'welcome meeting.' He offers excursion packages — boat trips, Dalyan mud baths, Ephesus tours — at what seem like reasonable prices. A family of four pays £320 for several trips (£80 per person). When they contact Jet2, the airline confirms they don't have a rep in Marmaris. The excursions never materialize, or they're substandard knockoffs of what was promised. The hotel claims no knowledge. This specific scam was documented in detail by the travel blog Sixty Rocks, who wrote 'The Fake Jet2 Rep Scam — What Really Happened at Our Marmaris Hotel.' The TripAdvisor Marmaris forum has dedicated threads including 'Fake Holiday Reps' and 'Love holidays scammers' with multiple families reporting nearly identical experiences. When the victim in the Sixty Rocks case had the hotel call the scammer to cancel, the scammer refused. Local tour operators on the street were offering identical trips for a fraction of the price, with child discounts the fake rep never offered. The key defense is simple: legitimate tour operators never approach you in your hotel lobby uninvited. Real Jet2, TUI, and other operator reps are identified on your booking paperwork before departure, and you can verify their identity through the operator's app or customer service line. How to avoid: Verify any claimed tour operator rep through the operator's official app or customer service number before buying anything Your genuine rep will be identified in your pre-departure paperwork — check before you travel Book excursions through verified local operators with TripAdvisor reviews or through your tour operator's official app Never pay cash without a proper printed receipt from a registered business Ask the hotel reception directly whether the person is an authorized rep — but verify independently as some hotels are complicit

Scam alert in Marmaris, Turkey — Bar Street Bill Inflation and Drink Spiking (tourist-trap, severity: high). You head to Marmaris Bar Street, a neon-lit strip of clubs and bars that's a rite of passage for British tourists. Promoters on the street offer 'free entry' and cheap drink deals. Inside, the first round seems fairly priced. But the drinks keep flowing, and when the bill arrives at closing, it's 1,200 Turkish lira for what you thought was four vodkas — plus a 500-lira 'service charge' that was never mentioned. You're charged £58 for four vodka mixers that should have cost half that. In the most alarming reports, unfamiliar people join your table and buy you drinks that turn out to be spiked, leading to memory loss and, in some cases, robbery. TripAdvisor's Marmaris forum is filled with Bar Street complaints. One thread titled 'Reataurant/Bar scams' documents patrons being overcharged and asked to pay undisclosed service charges. Another visitor reported being spiked after unfamiliar people joined their table — they lost consciousness after finishing a drink and subsequently got into a fight. The situation became severe enough that fourteen bars in Marmaris were shut down following reports of harassment, with Turkish media outlet Turkiye Today reporting on 'disturbing footage of sexually aggressive dance shows and inappropriate conduct by bar staff.' Marmaris has legitimate, enjoyable nightlife, but stick to venues with posted prices, keep your drink in sight at all times, and pay per round rather than running a tab. How to avoid: Choose bars with clearly posted price lists and pay per round rather than running a tab Never accept drinks from strangers or leave your drink unattended — keep it in your hand at all times Go out with friends and agree to watch each other's drinks throughout the evening If you feel unexpectedly intoxicated, tell your friends immediately and leave the venue together Check TripAdvisor reviews for specific Marmaris bars before going out to avoid venues with complaints

Scam alert in Marmaris, Turkey — Boat Trip All-Inclusive That Isn't (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). You book an 'all-inclusive' boat trip from the Marmaris harbor for 600 lira per person, expecting a full day of swimming, lunch, and unlimited drinks. Once on the boat, the crew confiscates all the food and water you brought and tells you it's 'for safety reasons.' Then they proceed to sell their own food and drinks at premium prices — fries for 100 lira, water for 50 lira. Cocktails displayed on large posters behind the bar are 'not available' when ordered. The 'all-inclusive' lunch turns out to be a small portion of rice and grilled chicken. One TripAdvisor reviewer of the Orca II Boat in Marmaris titled their review 'Not worth it and a scam,' describing how staff 'remove all your food and drink then proceed to bombard you to buy their food and drink' and compared it to a 'prison boat.' Another reviewer noted that despite the trip being sold as all-inclusive, multiple items were charged separately. The fake advertising about available drinks — posters showing cocktails that staff claim they can't make — is a deliberate bait-and-switch. The standard price for a legitimate full-day group boat trip in Marmaris should be 15-35 euros per person for a 6-8 hour experience. Reputable operators with hundreds of positive reviews exist — check TripAdvisor and confirm in writing exactly what 'all-inclusive' covers before boarding. How to avoid: Get written confirmation of exactly what 'all-inclusive' covers before paying — meals, specific drinks, snorkeling equipment Book through operators with hundreds of TripAdvisor reviews rather than street agents Ask specifically whether you can bring your own food and water aboard Compare prices with at least three operators — a legitimate all-inclusive day boat costs 15-35 euros per person Read the most recent reviews, not just the overall rating, as quality can change between seasons

Scam alert in Marmaris, Turkey — Taxi Meter Manipulation and Route Padding (transport, severity: moderate). You flag a taxi in Marmaris center for the ride back to your hotel in Icmeler, about 8 kilometers away. The meter starts at a normal rate, but you notice it's climbing unusually fast. What should be a 60-80 lira ride shows 180 lira when you arrive. The meter was legitimate — but programmed to a higher tariff rate. Turkish taxi meters can store multiple tariff rates, and switching between them requires only a button press. This form of meter manipulation is extensively documented across Turkey's tourist destinations by Chasing the Donkey, The Istanbul Insider, and Inspired to Explore. While most examples focus on Istanbul, the same meters and tactics are used in resort towns like Marmaris. Common variations include not resetting the meter from a previous ride (starting your fare from a higher point), inflating the rate based on luggage or number of passengers, and taking circuitous routes that add distance. The recommended app-based alternatives in Marmaris are BiTaksi and the local hotel shuttle services. If using a street taxi, watch the meter at the start — it should begin at the minimum fare (the 'açılış' rate). For the Dalaman Airport to Marmaris transfer (roughly 90 km), pre-book a transfer at a fixed rate rather than taking a taxi, which can charge wildly variable amounts. How to avoid: Check that the meter resets to the minimum opening fare when your ride begins Have Google Maps running on your phone so you can see the route in real time Use BiTaksi app or hotel shuttle services for transparent pricing For the Dalaman Airport to Marmaris transfer, pre-book through your hotel or a licensed transfer company at a fixed rate Learn the approximate fare for common routes (Marmaris center to Icmeler should be about 60-80 TRY) and challenge overcharges

Scam alert in Marmaris, Turkey — Jet Ski and Water Sports Damage Charge (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). You rent a jet ski on Marmaris beach for 30 minutes at 400 lira. Before you go out, the operator gives you a cursory walkthrough but no written condition report or contract. After your ride — which was uneventful — the operator 'discovers' a scratch on the jet ski that he claims wasn't there before. He demands 2,000 lira for the damage. Without documentation of the jet ski's pre-ride condition, it's your word against his. This damage-charge scam at Turkish beach resorts is a variation of the rental car scam documented across Turkey's tourist destinations. Property Turkey and Chasing the Donkey both warn about water sports operators who extract inflated damage payments from tourists who cannot prove pre-existing wear on the equipment. The scam is particularly effective because jet skis, unlike cars, have no standardized condition report or insurance framework for tourists. The defense: photograph or video the equipment from all angles before using it, insist on a written rental agreement that documents the current condition, and only rent from operators with established TripAdvisor or Google reviews. If confronted with a spurious damage claim, offer to call the police (155) to mediate. How to avoid: Photograph or video the equipment from all angles before using it, with the operator present Insist on a written rental agreement that notes the current condition of the equipment Only use operators with established online reviews (TripAdvisor, Google) If accused of damage, offer to call the Jandarma (military police, 156) to mediate — this often resolves spurious claims Pay by credit card rather than cash so you can dispute fraudulent charges later

Scam alert in Marmaris, Turkey — The Carpet and Leather Shop Lure (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). A shopkeeper calls out 'hello my friend, where are you from?' and before you know it, you are sitting in his shop drinking apple tea while he rolls out carpets. The tea is genuine Turkish hospitality, but the prices are five times what you would pay at a bazaar in Istanbul. After forty-five minutes of presentation, the social pressure to buy something is immense. The municipality has actually taken action to close shops in Marmaris that harass tourists, as reported in a Reddit thread, but the practice persists in side streets away from enforced zones. How to avoid: Politely decline the tea invitation if you are not genuinely interested in buying If you enter a shop, it is perfectly acceptable to look and leave without purchasing Ask for prices before any product demonstration begins Compare carpet and leather prices at shops with fixed price tags before considering bazaar purchases The tea is free regardless — you are never obligated to buy after accepting hospitality in Turkey

Scam alert in Marrakech, Morocco — 'That Way's Closed' Fake Guide (counterfeit, severity: high). You're consulting your map on the edge of Djemaa el-Fna, trying to find the route to the Bahia Palace through the souks, when a friendly man taps you on the shoulder and says 'sorry, that street is closed today — festival.' He offers to show you an alternate route. Twenty confusing turns through the medina later, you're in a carpet shop owned by his cousin, and the 'guide' is now expecting 200 dirhams for his trouble. This is Marrakech's most infamous scam, documented relentlessly in traveler forums. One traveler wrote: 'Every day was relentless scamming of road closed or we are from your hotel — it got so I couldn't enjoy being outside.' How to avoid: Download offline maps (Maps.me or Google Maps offline) before entering the medina If someone says a street is closed, verify independently by walking toward it yourself Say 'la, shukran' (no, thank you in Arabic) and keep moving without engaging Book official guides through Riad Marrakech or the ONMT tourist office — they have ID badges If you reach a shop, you're under no obligation to buy anything — just leave politely

Scam alert in Marrakech, Morocco — Henna Tattoo Ambush (distraction, severity: moderate). A woman in traditional dress smiles at you near the Koutoubia Mosque and grabs your wrist, saying 'a gift, a gift — for luck, no money.' Before you can pull away, she's already applying henna paste to your hand in an intricate pattern. When she finishes, the gift is suddenly 300 dirhams (about $30) and she calls over two male relatives to make sure you pay. Traveler forums are full of these stories — one traveler described being physically held by the wrist: 'She wouldn't let go until I paid. My boyfriend had to step in. The police just watched.' How to avoid: Keep your hands in your pockets or crossed over your chest near Djemaa el-Fna Firmly say 'la' (no) and step back the moment someone reaches for your hands If you want a henna tattoo, book it through your riad or go to an established shop with prices posted If already trapped, negotiate down to 50 dirhams maximum — never pay the initial demand Walk toward tourist police (identifiable by blue uniforms) if things feel threatening

Scam alert in Marrakech, Morocco — Snake Charmer / Monkey Photo Trap (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). The snake charmers and Barbary macaque handlers on Djemaa el-Fna look like the ultimate photo opportunity. A charmer catches your eye and gives a nod — you take out your phone for a quick shot and suddenly a cobra is draped around your neck by a handler who appeared from nowhere. Now there are three men surrounding you demanding 200 dirhams for the 'special photo experience.' Refusing means escalating pressure. A traveler post described it perfectly: 'The monkeys were placed on our shoulders before we could say anything. The whole thing was choreographed to the second.' How to avoid: Keep your phone out of sight and avoid eye contact with performers on Djemaa el-Fna If you want the photo, agree on a price in dirhams BEFORE any animal or prop touches you The going rate for a negotiated photo is 20–30 dirhams — not 200 Walk in the outer ring of the square where performers are less concentrated Say clearly: 'bikam?' (how much?) before engaging — if they can't quote a price, walk away

Scam alert in Marrakech, Morocco — Fake Argan Oil and Spice Shop (counterfeit, severity: moderate). A charming young man outside the Souk el-Attarine offers to show you a 'women's cooperative' selling authentic argan oil and spices. The shop looks legitimate, even has certificates on the wall. You buy 500ml of 'pure' argan oil for 300 dirhams. At home, you discover it's a diluted product worth maybe 50 dirhams — the certificates were props, and the 'cooperative' was a private shop with a markup of 500%. Travelers note: 'The rug and argan scams are the biggest money ones — they target people who want to support local women but end up funding a middleman.' How to avoid: Buy argan oil only from shops recommended by your riad or from the official AMONT cooperatives Genuine argan oil is never cheap — expect to pay 150–250 dirhams for a small authentic bottle Don't follow strangers to any shop — decide your shopping destinations before entering the souks Real women's cooperatives are usually outside the medina in quieter neighborhoods Use smell and texture tests: real argan oil has a nutty scent and isn't perfectly clear

Scam alert in Marrakech, Morocco — Petit Taxi Meter Scam (transport, severity: moderate). You hail a red petit taxi outside Djemaa el-Fna heading to your riad in Gueliz. The driver says the meter is 'broken' but quotes you 100 dirhams flat — about four times the metered fare for the same ride. When you insist on the meter, he waves his hand dismissively and says 'tourist price, very normal.' A later check of traveler forums reveals the metered fare for most cross-city trips in Marrakech should be 15–30 dirhams. Another common trick: the driver stops mid-route and demands extra money before continuing, knowing you're lost in an unfamiliar neighborhood. How to avoid: Always insist on the meter — say 'al-addad, min fadlak' (the meter, please) If the meter is claimed broken, exit and find another taxi — there are always more Agree on a price in dirhams before entering if no meter is available, and show it written Use Careem or inDrive app in Marrakech for fixed-price rides with upfront quotes Ask your riad what the fair price is for your destination before leaving — they'll know the going rate

Scam alert in Marrakech, Morocco — Restaurant Menu Switch (overcharging, severity: moderate). The rooftop terrace directly above Djemaa el-Fna offers the best view in Marrakech, and the waiter hands you a reasonable-looking menu. You order tagine and mint tea. When the bill arrives, there's a 'tourist menu' price — nearly double what was on the menu you ordered from. The waiter explains the menu you held was 'the old menu' and that there's now a 'terrace supplement.' Some restaurants near the square have two menus: one shown to tourists and one for negotiated regulars. A Redditor reported: 'We definitely got scammed at the food stalls in the medina but overall had a great time — just know what you're getting into.' How to avoid: Take a photo of the menu when you first receive it so you have a record of prices Confirm the total before ordering: 'So this meal will be approximately X dirhams, correct?' Eat away from the main square — restaurants two blocks off Djemaa el-Fna are cheaper and often better Check recent Google Maps reviews — scam restaurants get called out specifically Ask for an itemized receipt and compare it line by line to what you ordered

Scam alert in Marrakech, Morocco — Bracelet Forced Sale (distraction, severity: low). You're walking through the narrow lanes near Bab Doukkala when a teenage boy puts a leather bracelet around your wrist with a cheerful 'welcome, my friend — it's a gift from Morocco!' Before you can react, he's tied it with a knot and is explaining the 'traditional meaning.' Now he wants 50 dirhams for the bracelet he 'gave' you. If you try to return it, he insists it's bad luck. Multiple traveler-forum threads describe this as one of the most common low-stakes scams targeting tourists in the medina — annoying rather than dangerous, but worth knowing. How to avoid: If someone reaches for your wrist, step back immediately and say 'la' firmly If a bracelet is already on you, untie it calmly and hand it back without paying Don't feel guilty — saying no to an unsolicited item is completely reasonable Walk with a purpose and don't make eye contact with people selling items on the street Traveling with others makes you a less attractive target for bracelet scammers

Scam alert in Marseille, France — Friendship Bracelet/String Scam (distraction, severity: low). Someone approaches you in a friendly manner on Vieux-Port and loops a colored string or bracelet around your wrist before you can refuse. Once it’s tied, they call it a ‘gift’ and aggressively demand cash — typically €5–€20. They may physically grab your wrist to tie it, and if you try to walk off without paying, they make a scene to pressure you into handing over the money. How to avoid: Keep your hands in your pockets when walking through Vieux-Port and La Canebière. Say *non merci* firmly and keep moving. Do not stop to engage. If they grab your wrist, pull your hand away and walk toward a busy shop or café — they rarely follow.

Scam alert in Marseille, France — Gold Ring Scam (distraction, severity: low). A passer-by ‘finds’ a gold ring on the ground near you and picks it up, showing it to you and claiming it’s yours or that you must have dropped it. When you say it’s not yours, they offer to let you have it as it ‘must be your lucky day.’ They then ask for a reward or ‘finder’s fee’ for their ‘honesty.’ The ring is actually cheap brass or gold-plated and worthless, worth perhaps a few cents. How to avoid: Ignore anyone who approaches claiming to have found something valuable. Say ‘Non, ce n’est pas à moi’ (No, it’s not mine) and walk away. Never accept items from strangers. Do not engage in conversation about found items.

Scam alert in Marseille, France — Pickpocketing (pickpocket, severity: high). Marseille has significant pickpocket activity, especially in tourist areas. Thieves work in groups using distraction techniques. Common methods: children swarming tourists near Gare Saint-Charles while accomplices lift valuables; one person asking for directions while another picks the pocket; staged bumps and commotions; and tight crowding at Metro doors timed so the thief grabs and steps off as the doors close. The concentration around Gare Saint-Charles is particularly heavy. How to avoid: Wear a cross-body bag in front, not behind. Keep phones out of back pockets. Never sling a bag over a chair back at outdoor tables. Use a money belt for large amounts of cash and cards. Be extra vigilant when metro doors open and close. Avoid displaying expensive watches, cameras, or jewelry. Keep only what you need for the day; leave valuables in hotel safe.

Scam alert in Marseille, France — Fake Charity Petition Scam (pickpocket, severity: moderate). A person approaches with a clipboard, often claiming to be deaf-mute, and asks if you speak English. They then request you sign a ‘petition’ for a charity, supposedly supporting deaf or disabled people. The petition is in English (a red flag in France) and looks official. After signing, they demand a donation, pointing to text on the paper claiming you agreed to donate when you signed. While you’re distracted signing, an accomplice may be going through your pockets or bag. Even if there’s no accomplice, you may feel pressured into giving money for a fake cause. How to avoid: Never stop for clipboard petitioners. Say ‘Non’ firmly and keep walking. Never sign anything on the street. Keep hands in pockets and maintain distance. If approached, check that your belongings are secure immediately.

Scam alert in Marseille, France — Three Card Monte / Shell Game (street-scam, severity: moderate). You encounter a group gathered around someone playing a simple card game (find the queen) or shell game (find the ball under the cup). The game looks easy to win, and you watch people (who are actually accomplices called ‘shills’) winning money easily. When you try to play, you lose every time because the operator uses sleight of hand to cheat. The game depends on a lookout watching for police, a ‘roper’ to bring in players, and shills who pretend to win. The moment you put down money, it’s gone. Some operations may become aggressive if you try to leave without paying. How to avoid: Never play street gambling games — they are always rigged. Do not stop to watch. Remember that bystanders are likely accomplices. The shell game is fraud in France.

Scam alert in Marseille, France — Taxi Overcharging / Unlicensed Taxi Scam (transport, severity: moderate). Unlicensed taxi drivers or unscrupulous licensed drivers target tourists arriving at the airport or train station. They may refuse to use the meter, quote a fixed price that’s significantly inflated, take unnecessarily long routes, or claim the meter is broken. Some unlicensed operators solicit fares inside terminals. At night, prices can be quoted at 2-3x the normal rate. Official airport-to-city fare should be approximately 50 euros daytime and 60 euros at night. How to avoid: Use only official taxis from designated ranks (outside Arrivals Hall at airport). Confirm the fare before getting in. Insist on the meter being used. Know the approximate fare in advance (€50 day/€60 night airport to center). Use ride-sharing apps like Uber for transparent pricing. Note driver ID and license plate if overcharged — report to police.

Scam alert in Marseille, France — Restaurant Overcharging (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Restaurants in tourist areas use a familiar playbook: posted prices that don’t match the bill; verbal ‘specials’ that turn out to be expensive; items added that you didn’t order; bottled water served automatically when you ask for water; pressure for American-style tips despite service being included; only medium or large sizes offered at inflated prices; and a different, higher-priced menu for tourists than for locals. One documented Marseille case showed a €28 menu where 9 of 13 dishes required a €5–€10 supplement each. How to avoid: Ask for the French menu and compare prices. Request ‘une carafe d’eau’ (pitcher of tap water) — it’s free. Verify prices for specials before ordering. Review the bill carefully (‘l’addition’) against what you ordered. Tipping is not required in France — service is included. Choose restaurants away from main tourist thoroughfares. Read recent online reviews.

Scam alert in Marseille, France — ATM Skimming / Card Trap Scam (financial-fraud, severity: high). Criminals fit skimming hardware onto ATMs to capture your card data and PIN: an overlay over the card slot reads the magnetic stripe, a fake keypad or pinhole camera records your PIN, and in the card-trap variant a false insert jams the card inside. In that version, a ‘helpful’ stranger appears and watches you re-enter the PIN a few times; once you leave to find help, they retrieve the card and use it with the code they just learned. How to avoid: Use ATMs inside bank branches during business hours. Cover the keypad completely when entering your PIN. Wiggle the card slot and the keypad before inserting your card — skimmers are usually loosely attached. If your card gets stuck, do not leave the machine; call the bank number printed on it. Decline help from any stranger at an ATM, and enable transaction alerts before you leave home.

Scam alert in Marseille, France — Fake Police Scam (impersonation, severity: high). Two people in official-looking uniforms or plain clothes approach you, flash fake badges quickly, and claim to be ‘Tourist Police’ or plainclothes officers. For travelers: (1) ALWAYS verify the payee name on your banking app before tapping confirm — a legitimate Jonker Walk food stall will show the registered business or owner's full Malay name, not an unrelated personal account; (2) pay in cash (RM10 / RM20 notes) for every stall transaction under RM50 — keeps the fraud surface near zero; (3) if a stranger asks you to DuitNow-transfer on their behalf for cash, REFUSE — community reports confirm this is always a scam; (4) peel back any QR sticker that looks freshly stuck or slightly misaligned — legitimate stickers are usually laminated behind plastic; (5) take a photo of the QR decal before scanning at stalls you're unsure about so your bank can trace a dispute; (6) NEVER accept a screenshot as proof of incoming payment — only a real-time push notification on your own bank app counts; (7) report suspicious QR stickers to MBMB enforcement or the vendor's parent chain (7-Eleven, KK Super Mart, Caltex); (8) save the National Scam Response Centre hotline 997 and MOTAC tourist line 1300-88-5050 for immediate freezes. How to avoid: Verify payee name on banking app before confirming — not just the amount Pay cash (RM10 / RM20) for stall transactions under RM50 NEVER DuitNow-transfer on behalf of a stranger offering 'cash back' Peel-test QR stickers that look freshly stuck — legitimate ones are laminated Only a push notification on your own bank app is real proof of payment National Scam Response Centre 997; MOTAC tourist line 1300-88-5050

Scam alert in Mexico City, Mexico — CDMX Express-Kidnapping (Secuestro Exprés) at ATMs & Forced-Withdrawal (tourist-trap, severity: high). Express kidnapping (secuestro exprés) is Mexico City's highest-financial-risk tourist crime — a short-duration abduction (2–8 hours) during which the victim is forced to make multiple ATM withdrawals up to daily limit across accounts. Community reports document the police-shakedown overlap (sometimes the 'police' are the perpetrators). The 2025 pattern: (a) taxi pickup from Polanco or Roma bar — driver claims 'ATM nearby for cash' and takes you to a compromised ATM in a quiet location; (b) 2–3 accomplices appear, force tourist into a car, drive to multiple ATMs (HSBC, Banamex, Santander) forcing max withdrawals; (c) phone is taken, banking apps used to transfer funds; (d) some crews use Uber/Didi drivers as tip-offs — the Uber driver picks up then calls the crew; (e) ATMs at street corners are sometimes physically tampered with to hold cards + capture PINs. A widely circulated traveler tip warns: never accept ATM on-screen prompts asking 'would you like a conversion rate?' — these are DCC fraud prompts that inflate rates 8–15%. For older travelers: (1) use ONLY ATMs INSIDE bank branches (HSBC, Banamex, Santander, BBVA, Citibanamex) during BUSINESS HOURS (9 AM–4 PM Mon–Fri); (2) NEVER withdraw from a standalone street ATM, especially at night; (3) set LOW daily withdrawal limits (MX$3,000 / US$175 max per day) in your bank app BEFORE travel; (4) enable real-time transaction alerts; (5) carry ONE dedicated travel debit card, not your primary account card; (6) if taxi driver suggests 'ATM nearby', REFUSE and ask to go directly to hotel; (7) NEVER withdraw more than MX$1,000 at a time; small multiple withdrawals are safer than one large; (8) REFUSE every ATM prompt asking 'conversion rate to your home currency' — always say 'NO / PROCEED IN MX$'; (9) if you sense pre-kidnap behavior (being followed, driver making phone calls), go to the nearest hotel lobby, bank branch, or Oxxo convenience store — 'refuge in place'; (10) US Embassy 24-hr emergency +52 55 8526 2561. How to avoid: ONLY bank-branch ATMs during business hours (9 AM–4 PM Mon–Fri) NEVER withdraw from standalone street ATMs, especially at night Low daily withdrawal limit MX$3,000; real-time alerts enabled REFUSE 'home currency rate' ATM prompt — always proceed in MX$ Dedicated travel debit card; US Embassy 24-hr +52 55 8526 2561

Community reports corroborate a broader 2025 card-cloning pattern across CDMX. The 2025 scams: (a) 'Sitio' taxi counters INSIDE terminal selling rides at MX$400–$800 to central areas when the real Uber/Didi rate is MX$120–$250 and legitimate airport-taxi equivalents are MX$180–$280; (b) counterfeit bus-ticket resellers outside terminal selling 'ADO/OCC Primera Clase' tickets at 30% discount — tickets are either fake barcodes or for a different date; (c) credit-card cloning at unofficial 'sitio' counters — card handed over 'for deposit', swiped through skimmer; (d) ADO/OCC bus-bag-theft — thieves wearing bus-line uniforms approach passengers in the waiting area offering to 'help with bags'; (e) WhatsApp-only 'cheap bus tickets' from scalpers outside terminal entrances. For older travelers: (1) exit TAPO/Central del Norte terminals and book Uber/Didi on the MAIN STREET outside, NOT from the taxi queue — real app rates are MX$120–$250 to central; (2) buy bus tickets ONLY from official counter windows inside terminal OR directly on ADO.com / Primera Plus website — NEVER from resellers outside the terminal or WhatsApp contacts; (3) NEVER hand your credit card to any taxi 'sitio' counter — use in-app payment only; (4) if you must use a sitio, ask for the PRINTED flat-rate sheet and pay the exact amount in cash; (5) keep bags between your feet or across your chest — do not accept 'help with bags' from anyone not explicitly ADO/OCC uniformed staff WITH a visible ID badge; (6) travelers who have been targeted specifically warn: never follow a 'driver' away from the main terminal entrance; (7) TAPO has an Uber pickup signposted zone — use it. How to avoid: Book Uber/Didi on MAIN STREET outside terminal — MX$120–$250 Buy bus tickets ONLY at official counter OR ADO.com/Primera Plus NEVER hand credit card to sitio counter — in-app or cash only Refuse 'help with bags' except from badged ADO/OCC staff Use TAPO's signposted Uber pickup zone — not the taxi queue

Scam alert in Milan, Italy — The Duomo Bracelet & "3-Euro Selfie" Trap (street_scam, severity: high). Men in Piazza del Duomo and the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II flick friendship bracelets onto tourists' wrists or offer to take their photo 'only 3 euros,' then demand €20+ or pass the phone to an accomplice. Milano Today's viral 'truffa dei selfie' video documents the €3 selfie pitch; Corriere della Sera published a British tourist's TikTok warning recounting the same pitch at Castello Sforzesco and the Duomo. Il Giorno documents 100 Antiborseggio arrests in 100 days in 2025 working this exact 200-meter radius. How to avoid: Treat bracelet and selfie men as invisible — do not stop, do not make eye contact, do not reply. Keep arms close to your torso crossing Piazza Duomo (bracelet only works if you reflexively catch). Never hand your phone to a stranger. If a bracelet is tied on, walk away with it on your wrist — do not pay. Shout 'polizia!' if someone refuses to release your arm; plainclothes Antiborseggio patrol the Duomo.

Scam alert in Milan, Italy — The M1 / M3 Metro Pickpocket Ring at Duomo (pickpocket, severity: high). Three-to-five-person teams swarm passengers on the M1 red and M3 yellow lines — especially Cairoli–Duomo and the Duomo mezzanine — using a 'fall and help' distraction while accomplices unzip bags. A firsthand traveler-forum victim post titled 'I was pickpocketed on the train from Cairoli to Duomo' documents the domino-push MO. Corriere Milano published a September 2024 first-person account. Repubblica April 2023 records a 34-year-old punched in the eye at the Duomo mezzanine for warning passengers. Milan's own metro PA now warns 'attenzione, pickpocket!' How to avoid: Wear backpacks on your chest, not your back, on M1 and M3. Keep phone/wallet in inside jacket or front trouser pockets. Buy tickets only from ATM Milano machines, newsstands, or contactless gates — never from anyone 'selling' tickets near machines. If a group clusters around you as doors close, step off and take the next train. Shout 'polizia!' and press the platform intercom if pickpocketed; Polmetro patrols Duomo in plainclothes.

Scam alert in Milan, Italy — Milano Centrale Platform & Luggage-Theft Teams (pickpocket, severity: high). Coordinated teams work Milano Centrale platforms, concourse, and the Galleria delle Carrozze, with fake 'helpers' offering to carry bags or operate ticket machines. A traveler-forum thread titled 'Milano centrale pick pocketing is real' documents a three-person team (two girls + one man) testing a father's backpack zipper within seconds of entering the station. Milano Today documents arrests: three Roma women who pickpocketed Japanese tourists at the Centrale metro; a 22-year-old Moroccan man caught snatching a bag inside the station; a three-year sentence for a July 2016 daylight assault in Via Napo Torriani (near Hotel Berna). How to avoid: Never let anyone touch your luggage inside Milano Centrale — politely refuse all 'help.' On Frecciarossa/Italo, put luggage on the end-of-carriage rack you face rather than overhead. Take only official white Taxi Blu (02.4040) or Autoradio (02.8585) from the signed rank; ignore any 'taxi?' offers inside the hall. Use only operator-logo machines for tickets. Avoid walking Via Napo Torriani alone with luggage in daylight.

Scam alert in Milan, Italy — The Via Dante "Tre Campanelle" Shell Game (scam_game, severity: high). Crews run the 'three bells' shell game and three-card variants on Via Dante, Via Torino, Piazza Cordusio and under the Castello Sforzesco drawbridge, with paid shills as 'winners' luring tourists to bet. A Repubblica Milano April 1, 2026 report documents a tourist losing €500 to the scam on Via Dante; Corriere Milano's September 29, 2025 feature records 125 people denounced by local police in four months between Via Torino and Via Dante, stopped with up to €4,000 in victims' cash. Milano Today documents a Castello Sforzesco three-card variant that ran combined with pickpocketing a US couple — producing five arrests. How to avoid: Recognize the shape on sight — a small crowd around a low table on Via Dante, Via Torino, Cordusio or the Castello approach is almost always tre campanelle. Do not slow down, do not look, do not join. If a stranger steps up beside you and narrates the game, step back two meters — they are there to pickpocket you. Never bet; the operator and the player both commit offenses under Italian law. Report active games to polizia locale at 02.0208. Call 112 immediately if you've lost money — recovery window is minutes.

Scam alert in Milan, Italy — The Malpensa / Linate Taxi Overcharge (transport, severity: high). Drivers at Malpensa, Linate and Orio al Serio charge 2–2.5x the posted fixed fare (Malpensa €95, Linate €65 to central Milan in 2025), switch to long-distance tariffs mid-trip, or claim the card reader is 'broken.' A firsthand traveler-forum victim paid €250 from Malpensa (vs €105 then-fixed), with two other Milan-airport victims chiming in below the same comment. Milano Today documents an unlicensed driver without a valid license caught working Malpensa. A 'friendly stranger' variant targets solo travelers inside the MXP arrivals hall. How to avoid: Take the Malpensa Express to Cadorna or Centrale (€13 standard, €20 non-stop; 43–52 min); Linate is €2.20 on M4 metro. For taxis, confirm the posted fixed fare aloud before closing the door ('novantacinque euro, corretto?'). Use only white Taxi Blu or Autoradio at the signed rank. Use FreeNow or itTaxi app for fare-transparent bookings. Refuse ATM detours — Italian law requires card acceptance. If overcharged, pay by card and dispute; Amex chargeback has been documented as working.

Scam alert in Milan, Italy — The Fake Plainclothes-Police ID Check (money, severity: high). Men posing as plainclothes police flash laminated badges, claim to be checking for 'counterfeit notes,' and pocket cash and watches during the 'verification.' Repubblica Milano's January 2017 cronaca documents a Russian tourist couple losing €10,000 in cash and two luxury watches to this MO. Corriere Milano's July 2019 report documents an 11-person crew specializing in Milan fake-police robberies. Milano Today documents a married-couple 'Bonnie e Clyde' crew who ran the scam across Italy with specific Milan incidents. How to avoid: Never hand over wallet, passport, or valuables to anyone not in full uniform inside a police station. Ask to be 'accompanied to the police station' for the check — real officers agree; scammers make excuses. Demand to see the badge at reading distance; compare to Polizia di Stato tessera images on poliziadistato.it. Walk toward a crowded area or a real carabiniere; call 112 while walking. Keep daily wallet separate from passport and main cards.

Scam alert in Milan, Italy — The Navigli Aperitivo Tourist-Trap Bill (overcharging, severity: moderate). Canal-side Navigli aperitivo spots apply unadvertised per-person coperto above €3, auto-applied 10–15% 'servizio' on foreign cards, unrequested pane/acqua/antipasti, and a 'turista menu' at 2–3x local prices. A traveler-forum Navigli recommendations thread contains a flat Milanese warning: 'the Navigli area became a real tourist trap, you still can find quality but they will be priced.' The same Quadrilatero tourist-trap density is documented by Corriere's cronaca archive in the Duomo cluster. Italian law (DL 206/2005) requires publicly displayed price-marked menus; missing fish/steak prices is the clearest tell. How to avoid: Walk one block off the Naviglio Grande towpath — Via Vigevano and Via Savona are locally recommended. Photograph the posted menu outside before sitting. Ask at seating: 'mi conferma il coperto e se c'è servizio?' Pay by card (legal requirement, chargeback path). Prefer handwritten daily boards with 3–5 primi/3–5 secondi. Trust Italian-language Google reviews sorted Most Recent over English.

Scam alert in Milan, Italy — Counterfeit Designer Goods (and the Buyer's Fine) (money, severity: low). Street vendors sell counterfeit 'Louis Vuitton,' 'Prada,' 'Gucci' bags on blankets near the Duomo, Via Torino, Navigli and Castello Sforzesco — but the buyer, not just the seller, faces administrative fines of €100–€7,000 per item under Italian Law 80/2005 / DL 35/2005. A traveler-forum thread documents pricing logic ('they size you up and quote a price') and quality ('you'll be lucky to get a season out of them'). Guardia di Finanza runs ongoing Milan seizure operations; buyer fines have been written at Malpensa and Linate customs.
