The 2025 scams: (a) arrivals-kerb 'taxi' sign-holders quoting MX$500–$800 (2–3x real rate); (b) 'Hotel transfer VIP' claimed at MX$1,200 for a standard sedan ride; (c) private driver insisting 'Uber doesn't work here' — Uber IS available in Oaxaca with 5–15 min wait; (d) 'combined airport + Monte Albán tour package' bait bundled at MX$2,000 with excuse 'already booked'; (e) Didi cancellation scam — same pattern as documented in Mexico City community reports; (f) hotel-side bellhop kickbacks directing guests to 'recommended driver' at 1.8x rate. For older travelers: (1) book Uber or Didi on airport Wi-Fi AFTER luggage — typical fare MX$180–$250 for the 20-min ride to Centro; (2) if Uber is slow, the official Transporte Terrestre booth inside arrivals IS legitimate at MX$220–$280 flat-rate prepaid (look for uniformed staff + printed receipts); (3) the combi (shared van) to Centro is MX$60–$75 per person — cheap budget option; (4) IGNORE every 'taxi' sign-holder at arrivals kerb quoting MX$500+; (5) your hotel likely includes free airport pickup with advance email — use this; (6) for return to OAX, pre-book Uber or the night before at Rp ... err MX$180–$250 from Centro; (7) Oaxaca is compact — once in Centro Histórico, most sights are walkable; use Uber for evening returns to hotel if dining far out; (8) save Oaxaca Tourist Police: +52 951 501 5000 ext. 23406 (English available). How to avoid: Book Uber/Didi on airport Wi-Fi — MX$180–$250 to Centro (20 min) Official Transporte Terrestre booth inside arrivals IS legit (MX$220–$280) Budget: combi shared van MX$60–$75 per person (30 min) Use hotel's free airport pickup (advance email booking) Oaxaca Tourist Police English: +52 951 501 5000 ext. 23406

Scam alert in Oaxaca, Mexico — Oaxaca Día de los Muertos / Guelaguetza Festival Price-Gouging & Airbnb Cancellations (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Oaxaca's Día de los Muertos (Oct 28 – Nov 3) and Guelaguetza festival (July) are Mexico's most-iconic cultural celebrations — and host 2025 price-gouging + booking-cancellation scams. Community reports document specific 2025 cancellation scams, and English event guides for first-time solo visitors give useful planning baselines. The 2025 scam pattern: (a) Airbnb cancellation + re-list at 3–5x price — hosts cancel confirmed bookings made 6+ months ahead (without compensation), relist same property at MX$8,000–$15,000 per night for the Día festival window; (b) 'exclusive rooftop viewing package' sold at MX$3,500 per person for the Zócalo parades (which are free public events visible from any sidewalk); (c) 'VIP cemetery tour Xoxocotlán MX$2,500' when public cemetery visits are free and local tours cost MX$400–$600; (d) fake 'festival parade ticket' resellers on WhatsApp selling non-existent 'front-row' access; (e) restaurants posting 'festival menu' at 2–3x normal prices with MX$1,200 mole negro; (f) 'official comparsa dancer photo session' at MX$500 per photo — these are local community members, not professional performers; tipping MX$50–$100 at their discretion is fair. For older travelers: (1) book accommodations 9–12 MONTHS ahead of Día de los Muertos (Oct 28 – Nov 3) via Booking.com, Hyatt, or Marriott directly — platform-protected bookings have recourse against cancellation scams; (2) Airbnb cancellation has limited recourse — community reports document specific cancelled-booking cases; prefer hotel chains for guaranteed booking; (3) REFUSE every 'exclusive rooftop viewing package' and 'VIP cemetery tour' — the parades and cemeteries are FREE PUBLIC events; (4) for a guided Día experience, book ONLY via reputable English-speaking operators (Horus Tours, Coyote Aventuras) at MX$600–$1,000; (5) budget for festival-surcharge meals (restaurants legitimately raise 20–30% during Día); skip the MX$1,200 mole negro; (6) bring plenty of small bills for vendor tipping (MX$50–$100 to performers is generous); (7) respect altars and graveside rituals — photograph from distance, ask permission for close shots; (8) plan to arrive Oct 26–27 and depart Nov 4–5 for full festival without peak-price crush. How to avoid: Book accommodations 9–12 months ahead via Booking.com/Hyatt/Marriott REFUSE 'exclusive rooftop' and 'VIP cemetery tour' — events are FREE Guided Día experience: Horus Tours or Coyote Aventuras MX$600–$1,000 Airbnb Día has high cancellation risk — prefer hotel chains Arrive Oct 26–27, depart Nov 4–5 to avoid peak-price crush

Scam alert in Oaxaca, Mexico — Oaxaca Rental-Car Card-Cloning & Mitla-Approach Highway Scam (transport, severity: high). Oaxaca rental-car agencies have a documented 2025 credit-card cloning + deposit-refusal pattern. Community reports document the pattern consistently and cover the broader 2025 tourist-targeting context. The highway variant mirrors Yucatán's 'Mi Lindo Yucatán' pattern documented in Chichén Itzá area reports. The 2025 scams: (a) rental-car 'security deposit MX$8,000–$15,000' charged to credit card — deposit is either 'held' for 30–60 days (accruing interest + foreign fees) or never refunded; (b) fake 'pre-existing damage' claims on vehicle return — dent or scratch that wasn't photographed at pickup; (c) Mitla-approach 'highway restaurant' tourist-trap where drivers are directed to stop — 2–3x restaurant prices + commission to driver; (d) 'required insurance' upsold at MX$800/day on top of base rate — most US and Canadian credit cards include rental insurance for Mexico (verify yours); (e) 'mandatory toll fee MX$400' added at return (tolls on Route 190 are legitimate but max MX$80–$120 each way); (f) unlicensed 'budget rental' agencies on Alcalá street that don't accept insurance documents. For older travelers: (1) book rental cars ONLY via verified agencies with Google 4.5+ reviews (Hertz Oaxaca, Europcar, Budget, Expedia Cars) at the AIRPORT not city offices; (2) photograph EVERY scratch, dent, tire condition, mileage BEFORE driving off — timestamp all photos; require an inspection form signed by the agent; (3) verify your credit card's rental insurance coverage in Mexico BEFORE declining agency insurance (MX$800/day is significant); (4) REFUSE 'security deposit' above US$500; if required, use a credit card WITH dispute protection — never debit card; (5) on the Mitla-approach route 190, DO NOT stop at any restaurant the driver 'recommends' — eat in Mitla or Teotitlán at Google 4.5+ verified spots; (6) keep ALL toll receipts to verify final charges; legitimate tolls on Route 190 Oaxaca–Tehuantepec are MX$60–$120 each way; (7) consider Uber/Didi between city and valley sites instead of rental car — MX$250–$400 each way is often cheaper and zero-risk; (8) if defrauded, file denuncia at Oaxaca MP (+52 951 514 3822) within 48 hours for chargeback documentation. How to avoid: Book verified agencies (Hertz, Europcar, Budget) at AIRPORT only Photograph every scratch/tire/mileage BEFORE driving off (timestamped) Verify credit-card rental insurance in Mexico BEFORE declining Refuse security deposits above US$500; credit card only (dispute-able) On Route 190, don't stop at 'recommended' restaurants; eat in Mitla

Scam alert in Okinawa, Japan — The Matsuyama Kyabakura / Bottakuri Bar Overcharge (nightlife, severity: high). You're walking through Matsuyama in Naha after dinner and a hustler in a suit pitches 'great bar upstairs, ¥3,000 set.' You take the elevator to the fourth floor, the room is dim, and the door clicks shut behind you. A bottle of 'champagne' arrives unrequested. Ninety minutes later the bill is ¥821,000 — the exact amount in a March 2021 documented case for seven bottles of champagne and six juices. July 2023 police raids on Matsuyama found 18 establishments paying yakuza protection money, and the entire district sits on the Okinawa Prefectural Police caution list. How to avoid: Never take an elevator to an upstairs bar you were pulled into from the street in Matsuyama. Stay on Kokusai-dori — it is well-lit, ground-floor, and tourist-safe. If you're already inside and staff ask for your card before showing a printed menu with prices, stand up and leave; no order placed means no legal claim. If the door is blocked, dial 110 — Okinawa Prefectural Police run a dedicated bottakuri response unit for Matsuyama. Freeze the card from your issuer's app at the first sign of coercion.

Scam alert in Okinawa, Japan — The Makishi Public Market Cooking-Fee Bait-and-Switch (sightseeing, severity: moderate). Fish vendors at Makishi Public Market quote unpriced seafood then charge ¥550-per-person cooking fees upstairs, including for non-eating family members. February 2026 review documented charging for 5 people when only 2 were eating. Prices change based on customer nationality with no posted rates. How to avoid: Get fish prices in writing before purchase leaves counter. Confirm cooking-fee headcount in advance. Walk away from stalls refusing written pricing. Use Tomari Fish Market instead where prices are posted. Demand itemized receipt.

Scam alert in Okinawa, Japan — The Naha Airport Shirotaku and Long-Distance Taxi Overcharge (transport, severity: moderate). Illegal white-plate taxis (shirotaku) at airport arrivals refuse meters and charge 1.5× normal fares with no receipt. Even licensed Stand No.8 is rated 2.3 stars with drivers inflating fares via unnecessary expressway detours and forcing large taxis instead of medium vehicles. How to avoid: Use Yui Rail monorail instead (¥270-330). Queue at Stand No.6 or No.7, not Stand No.8. Insist drivers use meters before departure. Book hotel transfers or use Go taxi app. Never follow unofficial curbside ride offers.

Scam alert in Okinawa, Japan — The Rental Car "Neighbor Gas Station" Fuel Overcharge (transport, severity: moderate). Rental car return counters direct customers to adjacent gas stations charging ¥197/L when market price is ¥165/L, creating ¥15-20/L premiums with no opportunity to comparison shop. Staff map specifically routes returns to overpriced partner stations. How to avoid: Fill up at ENEOS or Cosmo stations 2+ km away. Check prices via GoGo.gs before returning. Photograph fuel gauge at pickup and return. Photograph all car panels at pickup for damage disputes. Decline optional insurance upsells.

Scam alert in Okinawa, Japan — The Kokusai-dori Souvenir Fake-Discount and Hidden Table Charge (sightseeing, severity: low). A souvenir shop on Kokusai-dori displays a Shisa lion-dog figurine with '¥4,980' crossed out in red marker and '¥1,980 — today only' written above it. The ¥4,980 was never the real price; the same figurine is ¥1,680 at Ryubo Department Store four blocks away and ¥1,280 at Naha Airport. Down the street, a restaurant with English photos in the window seats you, brings an unrequested plate of tofu and vegetables, and later charges ¥550 per person for 'otoshi' that wasn't on the outside menu. A ¥2,000 lunch ends at ¥4,500 for two people. How to avoid: Before buying any souvenir on Kokusai-dori over ¥1,000, check the same item on Amazon Japan or at Ryubo — if the Kokusai-dori price is more than 30% above Ryubo's, walk away. Naha Airport is usually cheaper still. For restaurants, ask 'otoshi wa arimasu ka?' (お通しはありますか？ — 'is there an otoshi charge?') before you sit down, and if the answer is yes, ask the price. Eating one block off Kokusai-dori, in the covered Heiwa-dori arcade or on Ukishima-dori, typically runs 30–40% less for the same dish.

Scam alert in Okinawa, Japan — The US Military Card-Fraud and Juicy-Bar Targeting (nightlife, severity: moderate). November 2024 Stars & Stripes reported 23 credit/debit card fraud cases at Kadena Air Base with charges appearing within 24 hours of Exchange/commissary purchases. Chatan and Kin-town juicy bars target service members with champagne pushes and drink-spiking, with specific establishments on III MEF off-limits lists. How to avoid: Check MCIPAC-MCBB Bulletin 5800 off-limits list before visiting entertainment districts. Use credit over debit off-base. Set transaction alerts on all military banking. Pay cash at small bars. Leave immediately if drink tastes wrong and contact base clinic or call 110.

Scam alert in Okinawa, Japan — The Yonaguni and Rural Okinawa Ore-Ore Police-Impersonation Fraud (money, severity: moderate). Fake police officers call hotel rooms claiming accounts are used for fraud, directing transfers to fake safe accounts. A September 2024 tourist from Niigata lost ¥19 million; a Yonaguni visitor lost over ¥10 million. January-February 2026 saw 85 fraud cases with ¥400 million in losses. How to avoid: Hang up immediately on cold police calls—Japanese police never call about accounts. Dial 110 independently to verify. Never transfer money to phone-identified accounts. Alert hotel staff of alarming calls. Never accept offers to visit ATMs from taxi drivers or strangers.

Scam alert in Osaka, Japan — Kuromon Market Tourist-Tier Pricing (sightseeing, severity: moderate). Vendors at Kuromon Market systematically overcharge foreign tourists for seafood and wagyu. Prices are hidden, displayed only in foreign currencies, or obscured behind secondary signs. A 2024 investigation documented ¥30,000 for four crab legs and ¥3,500 for a single shrimp, though prices moderated after market association intervention. About 25 of 150 stalls carry the overcharging reputation. How to avoid: Ask exact total price in Japanese before ordering and walk away if staff dodge the question. Eat at Tenjinbashisuji Shopping Street or standalone sushi restaurants on Tabelog instead. Photograph price signs before ordering. Verify the shop displays the association's fair-price flyer.

Scam alert in Osaka, Japan — Dotonbori Wagyu Hamburger Bait-and-Switch (nightlife, severity: high). Street hustlers lure tourists into unmarked restaurants with laminated menus advertising A5 wagyu. Once seated, staff claim card-only payment via portable readers with no cash register. Cold, poor-quality meat arrives and the bill—around ¥29,568—is already processed. October 2025 Reddit post documenting this drew 800+ upvotes confirming the pattern. How to avoid: Never follow street hustlers in Dotonbori. Pre-select wagyu restaurants on Tabelog with 4.0+ stars and 100+ Japanese reviews. Legitimate places have visible cash registers and published prices. If trapped, stand and leave before ordering; staff cannot legally force payment without an order.

Scam alert in Osaka, Japan — Minami/Kitashinchi Girls-Bar Bottakuri (nightlife, severity: high). Hustlers offer girls bars at ¥3,000 per hour. Bills escalate to ¥300,000–¥950,000 after staff pressure customers to order expensive champagne bottles (¥200,000+). Door staff block exits; ATM withdrawal is 'suggested.' A January 2025 Suita case involved ¥950,000 charges and a January 2019 case resulted in police arrest after customers were beaten over payment disputes. How to avoid: Never enter bars recruited from the street. Book Tabelog-listed venues with published prices and 20+ Japanese reviews. Leave before accepting food or drink if no menu appears. Say '警察を呼んでください' (call police) and dial 110 if challenged. Never let staff accompany you to ATMs.

Scam alert in Osaka, Japan — Midosuji Line Panhandle Scam (money, severity: low). You're on the Midosuji Line between Namba and Umeda and a well-dressed young man sits next to you. 'Sorry, can I practice my English?' Two minutes later the story lands: his wallet was stolen at Kansai Airport, his hotel won't let him in without ID, the police 'can't help foreigners,' and he just needs ¥5,000 to ¥10,000 for cab fare home. A July 2025 Reddit thread documented the exact script, and a nearby Japanese commuter in the same thread confirmed the operator had been working the Midosuji Line for months — tourists see the sequence once, but he runs it many times a day. How to avoid: Genuine Japanese homeless almost never approach strangers, and genuinely stranded tourists go to the koban outside every major Osaka Metro station (there's one at the south exit of Namba Station and one at the north exit of Umeda Station). If a stranger on the train opens with 'can I practice my English?' and the conversation turns to money in under three minutes, stand up at the next stop, walk off, and don't explain yourself. If they follow you off the train, walk straight into the station koban — which will end the approach instantly.

Scam alert in Osaka, Japan — Kansai/Itami Airport Unofficial Taxi (transport, severity: moderate). Suited men approach in arrivals offering 'flat-rate' taxi service bypassing official queues. White license plates indicate unauthorized shiro-taku drivers. Initial quotes (¥8,000) inflate to ¥15,000–¥32,000 with surprise tolls and night-service fees. A 2024 case charged ¥11,640 on a ¥3,000 route; another saw ¥32,000 versus the legal ¥20,000–¥22,000 fixed rate. How to avoid: Walk directly to official taxi ranks—ignore anyone approaching in arrivals. Take Nankai Rapi:t (¥1,450) or JR Kansai-Airport Rapid (¥1,210) instead. Check that license plates are green (緑ナンバー)—white plates mean the driver is unlicensed. Photograph receipt, plate, and driver ID if charged unexpectedly and file a Kansai Transport Bureau complaint.

Scam alert in Osaka, Japan — Counterfeit Brand Goods in Shinsaibashi/Amemura (counterfeit, severity: moderate). Luxury items (Louis Vuitton wallets at ¥8,000, Moncler jackets at ¥15,000) sold from back-street shops are counterfeit. A 2024 Mainichi investigation documented the Tsuruhashi area nicknamed '鶴橋偽ブランド通り' where sellers ask 'You're not the police, right?' before revealing stock. Osaka Customs blocked ~9,600 counterfeits in FY2024; Japanese counterfeiting carries 10-year prison and ~$73,000 USD fines. How to avoid: Prices 10–20% below retail are counterfeit. Buy only from official boutiques or major department stores (Hankyu, Daimaru, Takashimaya). Use secondhand authenticators with 50+ Japanese reviews (Komehyo, RagTag). Avoid Expo 2025 Myaku-Myaku merchandise from unofficial stalls. Do not export counterfeits—customs in EU, UK, US, Australia, South Korea will seize goods and levy fines.

Scam alert in Osaka, Japan — Osaka Expo 2025 Fake-Ticket Fraud (money, severity: moderate). Osaka Expo 2025 ran from April to October 2025 and drew over 28 million visitors. During the run, fake websites mimicked the official Expo site, harvested card details, and sold counterfeit tickets whose QR codes failed at the gates; a March 2025 Trend Micro report flagged multiple fraudulent domains, and NHK and the Expo Association issued repeated warnings through the summer. Since the Expo closed, the same operators have pivoted to selling counterfeit Myaku-Myaku mascot merchandise through look-alike shops. A typical victim is charged around ¥7,500 to ¥15,000 for a 'limited-edition' plush that either never arrives or arrives as a poor knockoff from a foreign warehouse. How to avoid: Expo 2025 closed in October 2025—any site selling 'Expo tickets' in 2026 is a scam. Buy Myaku-Myaku merchandise only from official licensees (Osaka Tourism Bureau shops and major department stores such as Hankyu, Daimaru, or Takashimaya). Never click Expo-themed ads on social media. If you've already paid a suspicious site, file a chargeback with your card issuer within 60 days and report the site to the Consumer Affairs Agency hotline on 188.

Scam alert in Osaka, Japan — Dotonbori Pickpocketing and Phone-Hold Distraction (other, severity: high). Thieves target dense crowds at Dotonbori's Ebisu Bridge Glico sign photo spot (500+ tourists) and Namba Walk. Phones in back pockets vanish; a classic distraction involves asking you to hold someone's phone while taking a photo—while distracted, an accomplice rifles your bag. A 2025 NTV report featured a 41-year-old serial thief rearrested after CCTV caught him stealing a ¥35,000 wallet from a backpack; he told police 'Japanese people are easy targets.' How to avoid: Wear a cross-body bag with zipper forward or money belt under clothes. Never put valuables in back or open jacket pockets. At Glico Bridge, stand with back to wall, not in crowd center. Don't hand your phone to strangers—ask uniformed staff instead. On Midosuji Line during rush hour, wear backpack on front. Report theft to nearest koban immediately for insurance purposes.

Scam alert in Ottawa, Canada — Fake Parliament Tour Reseller — Real Tours Are FREE (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Tours of Canada's Parliament (Centre Block, currently under restoration so tours run at the Senate of Canada Building and West Block until 2030) are completely FREE — no tickets required, just sign up at the Parliament Visitor Welcome Centre (90 Wellington Street) or pre-register at parl.gc.ca. The scam: fake websites and third-party 'guided Parliament tour' aggregators sell 'skip-the-line Parliament VIP tours' or 'private guided experiences' at $40–$120 per person for what is a free official Parliament tour available daily. Tout offers near Parliament Hill sell 'Ottawa Parliament + Tulip Festival + Rideau Canal' bundles at $150–$250 per person where each component is free or $5–$15. The pattern is similar to the fake Sagrada Família and fake Alhambra ticket sites documented in Spain — tourists who don't realize the underlying attraction is free pay third-party 'resellers' for tickets that aren't tickets at all. Real Parliament tours can be reserved up to 30 days ahead at the Parliament of Canada website (parl.gc.ca/Visit) or walked up at the Visitor Welcome Centre during operating hours. For older travelers visiting Ottawa, the practical playbook: (1) Parliament tours are FREE — book at parl.gc.ca/Visit or call +1-613-996-0896 for assistance; (2) the Visitor Welcome Centre at 90 Wellington Street is the only legitimate booking location for walk-up tours; (3) decline ALL 'skip-the-line Parliament' or 'VIP Parliament tour' offers from third-party sites or street touts; (4) the Library of Parliament (the round building behind Centre Block) is included on the official tour and is genuinely impressive; (5) for older travelers, the tour involves moderate walking and stair-climbing — the Parliament Visitor Welcome Centre has accessibility accommodations available with advance request; (6) the Centennial Flame in front of Parliament is a free outdoor monument; the Changing of the Guard ceremony (June 24 - August 22, 10 AM daily, Parliament Hill front lawn) is FREE; (7) check the parl.gc.ca/Visit page for the current tour location (rotates between Senate building and West Block during Centre Block restoration). How to avoid: Parliament tours are FREE — book at parl.gc.ca/Visit or call +1-613-996-0896 Visitor Welcome Centre at 90 Wellington Street for walk-up tours Decline ALL 'skip-the-line Parliament' offers from third-party sites or touts Changing of the Guard (June 24 - Aug 22, 10 AM daily) is FREE on Parliament Hill front lawn Check parl.gc.ca/Visit for current tour location during Centre Block restoration

Scam alert in Ottawa, Canada — Ottawa Tulip Festival Vendor & Bus Tour Markup Fraud (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). The Canadian Tulip Festival (annual mid-May, Ottawa) is North America's largest tulip festival — 1 million tulips bloom across Commissioners Park, Major's Hill Park, and Dow's Lake. Festival admission is FREE (the tulip displays are in public parks). The scam genre: third-party 'Tulip Festival VIP shuttle' packages at $80–$150 per person that bundle the FREE festival viewing with a paid bus shuttle and 'guided tulip tour' (where there's nothing to guide — the tulips are self-explanatory at marked viewing locations). The specific patterns: (1) bus tour 'Tulip Festival package' at $80–$150 per person for what's a $4 OC Transpo bus + free festival viewing; (2) 'tulip vendor' stalls selling 'bulb gift packs' at $25–$50 for products that wholesale at $5–$10 per dozen at any Ottawa garden center; (3) 'official Tulip Festival merchandise' counterfeit t-shirts, scarves, mugs at $30–$60 (the legitimate Canadian Tulip Festival merchandise tent sells official products at $20–$45 with authentic licensing); (4) 'private Tulip Festival photographer' offers at the viewing locations demanding $25+ per shot. For older travelers visiting Ottawa during Tulip Festival (mid-May), the practical playbook: (1) Tulip Festival admission is FREE — the displays are in public parks; (2) for transport between viewing locations, OC Transpo buses (Routes 6, 7, 16) cost $4 single ride or $11.25 day-pass — connects Commissioners Park, Major's Hill Park, and Dow's Lake; (3) decline 'Tulip Festival VIP shuttle' packages at $80+ — the math is 10x bus fare for no added value; (4) for tulip bulbs as gifts, buy at any Ottawa garden center (Ritchie Feed & Seed, Peter Knippel Garden Centre) at $5–$10 per dozen; (5) decline 'private photographer' offers — the tulips look great with phone cameras; (6) for older travelers with mobility concerns, Commissioners Park has accessible paved walkways throughout; Major's Hill Park has steeper terrain; (7) the festival is most spectacular in the morning (8-10 AM) before crowds peak; the Tulip Festival opening weekend draws the largest crowds and worst overpricing. How to avoid: Tulip Festival admission is FREE in public parks (Commissioners, Major's Hill, Dow's Lake) OC Transpo Routes 6, 7, 16 connect viewing locations ($4 single / $11.25 day-pass) Decline 'Tulip Festival VIP shuttle' packages at $80+ For tulip bulb gifts, buy at Ritchie Feed & Seed or Peter Knippel Garden Centre Visit 8-10 AM for fewer crowds and best photo light

Scam alert in Ottawa, Canada — ByWard Market Restaurant Tourist-Trap & Beavertails Markup (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). ByWard Market is Ottawa's iconic 200-year-old market district — restaurants, vendors, and cafes serving the Parliament/government workforce by day and tourists by night. The scam genre is the standard Canadian tourist-strip pattern: George Street pub-row pricing inflation ($35–$50 per entrée for what's $20–$30 in residential Ottawa neighborhoods), 'Ottawa Beavertails' stand markups ($12–$18 for the iconic deep-fried pastry that costs $7–$10 at the original Beavertails outlets in residential areas), and tourist-menu inflation at restaurants directly facing the William Street market entrance. The patterns: (1) George Street pubs charging $35–$50 per entrée + automatic 18% gratuity for parties of 4+ without disclosure; (2) ByWard Market 'tourist Beavertails' at $12–$18 (legitimate residential Beavertails outlets in The Glebe or Westboro: $7–$10); (3) 'Ottawa craft beer flight' at $25–$35 (residential Bridgehead Coffee, Beyond the Pale, Dominion City: $12–$18); (4) 'maple syrup gift bottle' at $25–$40 (legitimate Ottawa Farmers' Market: $10–$15 per 250 ml, comparable to Quebec City pricing). For older travelers visiting Ottawa, the practical playbook: (1) avoid George Street pub-row for sit-down meals — walk 5 minutes to honest-priced ByWard Market venues: Le Cellier (Murray Street, classic French Canadian, $28–$42 mains), Fairouz (Mediterranean Levantine, $22–$32), Mooshu Ice Cream Pancakes (Asian fusion, $18–$28); (2) for Beavertails, walk to The Glebe (Bank Street) or visit the residential original Beavertails store on Wellington Street West for $7–$10 prices; (3) for craft beer, visit the actual breweries (Bridgehead Coffee + Beyond the Pale + Dominion City) for honest tasting flight prices; (4) for maple syrup, buy at Ottawa Farmers' Market (Saturday mornings, Lansdowne Park) at $10–$15 per 250 ml; (5) confirm credit-card processing fee policy and gratuity policy at seating; (6) check the bill for pre-added gratuity before tipping; (7) for the most authentic Ottawa food scene, take OC Transpo Route 1 to The Glebe or Westboro neighborhoods. How to avoid: Walk 5 min off George Street to: Le Cellier, Fairouz, Mooshu (honest-priced) For Beavertails, walk to The Glebe (Bank Street) or original Wellington Street West store Visit actual breweries: Bridgehead Coffee, Beyond the Pale, Dominion City for honest flights Buy maple syrup at Ottawa Farmers' Market (Saturday mornings, Lansdowne Park) Confirm gratuity and credit-card-fee policy at seating; refuse if not disclosed

Scam alert in Ottawa, Canada — YOW Ottawa Macdonald-Cartier Airport Taxi & Uber Cancel-And-Cash (transport, severity: minor). Ottawa Macdonald-Cartier International Airport (YOW) is 12 km southeast of downtown Ottawa. Legitimate licensed taxi fare is $30–$40 metered to downtown — relatively short trip and modest pricing compared to other Canadian capitals. The scam variants follow the broader Canadian airport-taxi pattern: (1) 'fixed price' quotes of $50–$70 for the standard $30–$40 trip; (2) Uber drivers with the cancel-and-cash variant (similar to Halifax YHZ and Calgary YYC patterns); (3) hotel-concierge 'private transfer' upsells at $70–$100 for the same trip. The scam mechanics at YOW: (1) the 'fixed price' taxi pitch in the ground-transportation zone — $50–$70 quoted for the $30–$40 metered trip down Airport Parkway; (2) the cancel-and-cash Uber variant (cross-Canadian pattern documented at Halifax and Calgary airports) where the driver collects $60–$80 cash and cancels the app ride, erasing the record; (3) government-conference and Tulip Festival weeks (May) and Winterlude (February) drive higher scam attempts as tourist demand peaks; (4) hotel-concierge 'private transfer' upsells at $70–$100 often route to the same taxi fleet at markup. For comfort-focused older travelers, OC Transpo Route 97 at $4.25 is the cheapest option but requires a transfer at South Keys; the YOW Airport Express Bus (Route 97) is acceptable with overhead luggage racks. For older travelers arriving at YOW, the practical playbook: (1) the YOW-to-downtown metered taxi is $30–$40 — refuse any quote above $50; (2) for Uber, NEVER cancel the booking at the driver's request — if a driver asks to cancel and pay cash, immediately exit and request another Uber driver; (3) OC Transpo Route 97 from YOW to downtown is $4 with Presto card or $4.25 cash, runs every 30 min — the cheapest and most overcharge-proof option (90-min total transit including transfer at South Keys Station to O-Train Line 1); (4) the OC Transpo-O-Train combo is the cheapest but slowest option; for older travelers with luggage, the YOW Airport Express Bus (Route 97) is acceptable; (5) for late-night arrivals, pre-book Capital Taxi (+1-613-744-3333) or Blue Line Taxi (+1-613-238-1111) for guaranteed pickup; (6) verify Uber driver and vehicle match the app BEFORE entering the vehicle; (7) tip via the Uber app rather than cash to avoid tip-skimming concerns per the cross-Canadian Uber pattern. How to avoid: YOW-to-downtown metered taxi is $30–$40 — refuse quotes above $50 NEVER cancel Uber booking at driver's request; exit and request another driver OC Transpo Route 97 + O-Train Line 1 ($4 Presto / $4.25 cash) for budget travel Pre-book Capital Taxi (+1-613-744-3333) or Blue Line Taxi (+1-613-238-1111) for late-night Verify Uber driver and vehicle match the app BEFORE entering vehicle

Scam alert in Ottawa, Canada — Rideau Canal Skating 'Pass' & Winterlude Festival Vendor Fraud (tourist-trap, severity: minor). The Rideau Canal Skateway (UNESCO World Heritage canal that becomes the world's largest skating rink January-February) is FREE — there's no admission, no skating pass, no parking fee for the canal-side lots. Winterlude (Ottawa-Gatineau winter festival, early February) is also FREE — ice sculptures in Confederation Park, snow slides at Jacques-Cartier Park (Gatineau), all free. The scam genre is small but persistent: tout offers selling 'Rideau Canal skating pass' or 'Winterlude VIP pass' at $30–$60 per person for what is completely free, and counterfeit 'official Winterlude' merchandise. The specific patterns during winter: (1) tout flyers near the canal selling 'Rideau Canal skating day pass' at $30–$60 (the canal is free); (2) 'BeaverTails Pass' bundles at $40+ that 'guarantee' BeaverTails — but BeaverTails are sold individually at $7–$10 from canal-side stands; (3) 'Winterlude VIP package' at $80–$150 per person bundling FREE festival access with a 'private guided ice sculpture tour'; (4) skate rental from non-NCC (National Capital Commission) operators at $30–$50 (the official NCC skate rental at Dow's Lake Pavilion is $14 adult). For older travelers visiting Ottawa in winter (January-February), the practical playbook: (1) Rideau Canal Skateway is FREE — just show up and skate; check ncc-ccn.gc.ca for daily ice conditions; (2) Skate rental at Dow's Lake Pavilion (NCC official) is $14 adult, $9 youth — refuse third-party 'rental' offers at $30+; (3) Winterlude festival admission is FREE — confederationpark.ca for daily program; (4) for BeaverTails along the canal, buy at the official BeaverTails stands at Dow's Lake or 5th Avenue ($7–$10) — refuse 'pass' bundles; (5) for ice sculpture viewing, the official Winterlude ice sculptures at Confederation Park have free interpretive signage; decline 'guided tour' offers; (6) for older travelers with mobility concerns, the canal has access ramps at Dow's Lake, 5th Avenue, and Bank Street; (7) carry layered cold-weather clothing — Ottawa winter temperatures drop to -25°C to -35°C with wind chill; the Rideau Canal Skateway closes for warm-weather days. How to avoid: Rideau Canal Skateway is FREE — just show up and skate; check ncc-ccn.gc.ca for ice conditions Official NCC skate rental at Dow's Lake Pavilion: $14 adult, $9 youth Winterlude admission is FREE — confederationpark.ca for daily program Buy BeaverTails at official Dow's Lake or 5th Avenue stands ($7–$10) Carry layered cold-weather clothing for -25°C to -35°C wind-chill conditions
