Community reports from 2014–2026 cover the Recife/Olinda baseline, Northeast Brazil itineraries, first-visit perspectives, and the broader Pernambuco regional landscape. The 2025 scam patterns: (a) Alto da Sé (Olinda's iconic hilltop viewpoint with 360° Recife panorama) — 'mandatory local guide R$100' demanded by self-appointed Pelourinho-style touts at the viewpoint plaza; no guide is required — Olinda is a free public UNESCO town walkable in 2–3 hours; (b) hotel-concierge 'Olinda + Recife Antigo combined day-trip R$350 per person' kickback markup (real DIY: R$60–R$90 Uber round-trip + free walking = R$100 per couple); (c) 'private heritage tour with English-speaking guide R$250 per person' (Free Walker Tour Olinda offers donation-based tours at R$30–R$50 voluntary per person); (d) commission-restaurant lunch stops at Recife-side tour-operator routes — 'Mariscada Pernambucana lunch R$200 per person' at commission-kickback restaurants vs R$80–R$130 at authentic Olinda spots; (e) 'commission-shop atelier visit R$100 mandatory' at Olinda artisan workshops on tour routes; (f) 'photo with frevo dancer R$80' at Alto da Sé (legitimate frevo street performances are tip-based at R$5–R$20 voluntary); (g) Olinda Carnaval (one of Brazil's most authentic) attracts fake-ticket resellers per community reports — there are NO tickets for Olinda street Carnaval; it's free public access to all blocos. For travelers: (1) Olinda is best done DIY — take Uber from Recife to Praça do Carmo / Alto da Sé R$30–R$50 (15 min); (2) Olinda is a small UNESCO old town walkable in 2–3 hours — main sights: Alto da Sé viewpoint, Mosteiro de São Bento (gilded interior, free entry), Igreja da Sé (Cathedral), Casa do Carnaval, Largo do Boa Hora; (3) NO mandatory guide is required anywhere in Olinda; if you want a guide, book FREE Walker Tour Olinda (donation-based R$30–R$50 voluntary at end) or licensed PE Tourism Office guides at the Praça do Carmo information center R$80–R$150 PER GROUP (4–8 people); (4) REFUSE every 'mandatory local guide R$100' Alto da Sé tout — they have no authority; (5) eat at AUTHENTIC Olinda spots: Restaurante Oficina do Sabor (Rua do Amparo, Pernambuco classic, Google 4.5+, R$70–R$150 per meal), Restaurante Goya (Largo da Misericórdia, Pernambuco regional, R$60–R$120), Don Francisco Bistrô (Rua do Amparo, contemporary, R$80–R$180); (6) for the iconic Olinda photo (Alto da Sé sunset over Recife skyline), arrive 5 PM weekday for the best views with sparser crowds; (7) Olinda Carnaval (Feb–Mar) is FREE public access — refuse every 'Olinda Carnaval VIP ticket R$500+' offer; book Recife/Olinda accommodation 6+ months ahead for Carnaval dates; (8) DEATUR Olinda +55 81 3429 0008 (Praça do Carmo); the town is generally safe daytime but avoid late-night walking in narrow lanes. How to avoid: DIY: Uber Recife-Olinda R$30–R$50 (15 min); walkable 2–3 hours NO mandatory guide; Free Walker Tour Olinda R$30–R$50 voluntary OR PE Tourism R$80–R$150/GROUP Eat: Oficina do Sabor, Restaurante Goya, Don Francisco Bistrô R$60–R$180 Frevo street performance: tip R$5–R$20 voluntary, refuse R$80 demands Olinda Carnaval is FREE; refuse 'VIP ticket' offers

Scam alert in Recife, Brazil — Recife Boa Viagem Restaurant Couvert + Serviço Padding & 'Frutos do Mar Market Price' Trap (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Recife's Boa Viagem beachfront and Recife Antigo dining hubs host a 2025 couvert artístico + serviço padding ecosystem common to Brazilian coastal cities, plus a specific 'frutos do mar peso variável' (variable-weight seafood platter) overcharge pattern. Community reports from 2014–2026 cover Recife-baseline itineraries, Northeast Brazil itineraries, first-time visits, and the cross-region Brazilian couvert / serviço abuse pattern. The 2025 scam patterns: (a) Boa Viagem beachfront restaurants with 'couvert artístico R$25–R$60 per person' for live music that's a single guitarist for 30 min — legitimate is R$10–R$25 disclosed BEFORE seating; (b) 'serviço 13–15%' instead of standard 10% (Brazilian Lei 13.419/2017 makes serviço OPTIONAL — you can refuse); (c) 'taxa de couvert + serviço' double-charging (illegal per PROCON PE); (d) 'frutos do mar para 2' (seafood platter for 2) market-price quoted at R$350–R$600 without weight or species disclosed (real R$150–R$280 at authentic spots with same items); (e) 'lagosta peso variável' market-price lobster at R$800–R$1,400 per kg without weight disclosed; (f) 'agua mineral R$18' (real R$5–R$10); (g) 'caipirinha de cachaça artesanal R$45' from house cachaça (real R$18–R$30); (h) Recife Antigo USD-only menus at 2–3× local prices for Pernambucano dishes; (i) bill-switcheroo where R$ amount on receipt differs from card by R$50–R$200; (j) Marco Zero Sunday-market food stalls overcharging tourists 1.5–2× weekday rates. For travelers: (1) eat at AUTHENTIC Pernambucano spots: Restaurante Oficina do Sabor (Olinda, Pernambuco classic, Google 4.5+, R$70–R$150 per meal), Beijupirá (Boa Viagem, contemporary Northeast cuisine, R$100–R$250), Veggie Lab (Boa Viagem, vegetarian-friendly Pernambucano, R$60–R$130), Restaurante Leite (Recife Antigo, traditional Brazilian since 1882, R$80–R$180), Pernambucanas Casa da Tia Anastácia (Boa Viagem, working-class authentic, R$50–R$100); (2) BEFORE sitting, ASK for menu and CONFIRM (a) couvert artístico R$ amount per person (legitimate R$10–R$25), (b) serviço % policy (10% standard, OPTIONAL by Brazilian law), (c) credit-card surcharge — photograph the menu; (3) for FRUTOS DO MAR PARA 2 (seafood platter for 2 — Pernambuco's signature dish), agree the EXACT items + weight + price IN WRITING BEFORE cooking — fair platter R$150–R$280 with shrimp + mussels + clams + fish; refuse 'market price R$350–R$600' without itemisation; (4) for lobster, agree weight × R$400–R$700 per kg in writing; (5) 'serviço' is OPTIONAL by Brazilian Lei 13.419/2017 — tip 10% if happy, refuse if poor service or padded; (6) for water, order 'água sem gás copo' (free tap water) at most spots; (7) for caipirinha, expect R$18–R$30 at reputable spots — anything above R$50 is tourist-trap; (8) PROCON PE can be contacted via 151 or procon.pe.gov.br for any abusive bill. How to avoid: Eat: Oficina do Sabor (Olinda), Beijupirá, Veggie Lab, Restaurante Leite, Tia Anastácia BEFORE sitting confirm couvert + serviço + card surcharge in writing Frutos do Mar para 2: agree items + weight + price IN WRITING (R$150–R$280 fair) Lobster: agree weight × R$400–R$700/kg in writing PROCON PE: 151 or procon.pe.gov.br for abusive bills

Scam alert in Recife, Brazil — Recife Carnaval Frevo Booking Fraud & Galo da Madrugada Counterfeit-Ticket Scam (tourist-trap, severity: high). Recife / Olinda Carnaval (4–7 day event in Feb, Brazil's most authentic frevo + maracatu street Carnaval — the Galo da Madrugada bloco is Guinness-recorded as the world's largest Carnaval bloco with 2.5+ million participants) drives accommodation prices 5–10× normal — and a 2025 cancel-and-relist + counterfeit-Camarote-ticket fraud ecosystem mirrors the Salvador / Rio pattern. Community reports from 2025–2026 compare Brazilian Carnaval cities, plan for 2026, and debate whether Carnaval is worth it for non-drinkers. The 2025 scam patterns: (a) Booking.com / Airbnb 'phantom listings' for Recife / Olinda Carnaval — high-quality photos of properties that don't exist or are already booked; tourist pays in advance, arrives, finds no property; (b) confirmed-booking cancellation 30–60 days before Carnaval with re-listing at 5–10× original price; (c) WhatsApp 'private Olinda Centro apartment for Carnaval R$5,000/night' demanding 100% PIX upfront — irreversible Brazilian payment; (d) 'Camarote VIP ticket Galo da Madrugada R$2,500' from unauthorised resellers (real Camarote prices R$800–R$3,000 from official venue websites — Camarote da Praça, Camarote Boa Viagem, Camarote Estrelas); (e) 'Olinda Carnaval VIP entry R$800' (Olinda Carnaval is FREE public access — there is NO ticket); (f) 'mandatory Carnaval pousada package R$6,000 for 5 nights' that's 5× normal nightly rate; (g) on-arrival bait-and-switch from confirmed Boa Viagem to inferior unit; (h) 'cleaning deposit R$600 cash on arrival' that never returns; (i) 'frevo bloco T-shirt R$400' counterfeit (real R$150–R$350 from official bloco websites — Bloco da Madrugada, Bloco do Eu Sozinho, Bloco da Saudade); (j) 'private trio elétrico ride R$1,500/person' on Galo da Madrugada (the bloco is FREE participation — ANYONE can walk with it; only Camarote VIP balconies are paid). For travelers: (1) for Recife / Olinda Carnaval, BOOK 9–12 MONTHS AHEAD via Booking.com or established hotel chains with platform-protected payment; reputable Recife hotels: Atlante Plaza Hotel (Boa Viagem, beachfront), Mar Hotel Conventions, Best Western Premier Maceió (also Pernambuco coast), Sheraton Reserva do Paiva; reputable Olinda pousadas: Pousada do Amparo (Centro Histórico, boutique), Pousada do Bonfim, Hotel 7 Colinas; AVOID Airbnb peak-season (cancel-and-relist documented across Brazil); (2) NEVER PIX-transfer to private 'apartment' or 'villa' WhatsApp sellers — irreversible; only platform-secure payment; (3) Olinda Carnaval is FREE PUBLIC ACCESS — refuse every 'Olinda Carnaval VIP ticket R$500+' offer; (4) for Recife Galo da Madrugada Camarote VIP, buy ONLY from the Camarote's OFFICIAL website (galodamadrugada.org.br, camarotedapracarecife.com.br) at R$800–R$3,000 per night; refuse every 'private reseller R$2,500+' offer; (5) for frevo bloco T-shirts, buy ONLY from each bloco's official website at R$150–R$350; (6) for travelers, AVOID street Carnaval crowd density (2.5 million Galo da Madrugada participants is intense, pickpocketing risk is high) — pay for a Camarote (elevated VIP balcony with food / drink / restroom / security) for safe Carnaval experience; (7) cross-reference any pousada / Camarote on Google Maps + Tripadvisor BEFORE booking; (8) DEATUR Recife +55 81 3322 4830 for booking-fraud denuncia within 48 hours; (9) for budget Carnaval, base in less-stressed Boa Viagem south end (3 km south of Galo circuit) and Uber into circuits — half the Recife Antigo rate. How to avoid: Book Carnaval 9–12 months ahead via Booking.com / hotel chains Reputable Recife: Atlante Plaza, Mar Hotel, Sheraton Reserva do Paiva Reputable Olinda: Pousada do Amparo, Pousada do Bonfim, Hotel 7 Colinas Camarote ONLY from official: galodamadrugada.org.br, camarotedapracarecife.com.br Travellers: pay for Camarote (avoid 2.5M-person Galo crowd)

Scam alert in Reykjavik, Iceland — Overpriced Airport Taxi (transport, severity: high). You land at Keflavik exhausted after a long flight and head straight for the taxi rank outside arrivals. A driver approaches and quotes you what sounds like a reasonable rate, but once you arrive in Reykjavik the fare is four times what it should be — you're charged 9,000 ISK just as a starting fare. Iceland has no Uber and recent deregulation allowed more questionable operators to enter the market, so unlicensed or unethical cabs prey on tired arrivals who don't know the going rates. How to avoid: Book the official Flybus or Flybus+ shuttle in advance — far cheaper than a taxi If taking a taxi, use only Hreyfill or BSR Taxi and confirm the fixed rate (22,500 ISK for a 4-seater as of 2025) Ask for the price before getting in and check the starting meter

Scam alert in Reykjavik, Iceland — Airport Currency Exchange Trap (money, severity: moderate). You step off the plane and see a currency exchange booth right in the arrivals hall — convenient! You swap $200 for Icelandic kronas and only realize later that the rate was terrible and there was a high commission fee buried in the small print. Iceland is almost entirely cashless, so you spent money on currency you'll barely use, at a rate that cost you significantly. How to avoid: Don't exchange currency at the airport — Iceland is 95%+ cashless and your card works everywhere If you need cash, use an ATM inside the city at a bank branch (not airport kiosks) Always decline dynamic currency conversion on card payments

Scam alert in Reykjavik, Iceland — Rental Car Insurance Upsell & Hidden Damage (tourist-trap, severity: high). You pick up your rental car in Reykjavik and the agent walks you through an endless list of insurance add-ons — gravel protection, sand storm protection, ash protection, tire protection. You decline most of them to save money. When you return the car, they find a tiny scratch or chip that was there when you picked it up and charge you hundreds of euros because you declined full coverage. How to avoid: Film every centimeter of the car before driving away — including tires, undercarriage, and roof Email or WhatsApp the video to yourself as a timestamped record Understand that standard SCDW in Iceland does NOT cover gravel damage — read the fine print

Scam alert in Reykjavik, Iceland — Fake Handmade Lopapeysa Sweaters (counterfeit, severity: low). You fall in love with the classic Icelandic woolly sweaters (Lopapeysa) displayed in a charming Reykjavik shop, and the label says 'Made in Iceland.' You pay $200 feeling great about your authentic souvenir. Back home, you notice it feels cheap and a friend who knows textiles tells you it was machine-made in China using a generic Nordic pattern — not Icelandic wool at all. How to avoid: Buy from the Handknitting Association of Iceland shop on Skólavörðustígur for guaranteed authenticity Genuine Lopapeysa have slight imperfections — machine-perfect patterns are a red flag Look for the 'Handmade in Iceland' certification tag

Scam alert in Reykjavik, Iceland — Bottled Water Upsell (nightlife, severity: low). You check into your Reykjavik hotel and the front desk mentions that the tap water 'might not be suitable for drinking' and offers to put a case of mineral water in your room for a fee. You accept, not wanting to risk getting sick. In reality, Reykjavik's tap water is glacial spring water — consistently ranked among the purest in the world. One hotel owner was actually caught doing this as a deliberate money-making scheme. How to avoid: Drink the tap water freely — it is genuinely exceptional Bring a reusable water bottle and refill it everywhere Politely decline bottled water in restaurants to avoid automatic charges

Scam alert in Reykjavik, Iceland — Northern Lights Tour Non-Refund (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). You book an expensive Northern Lights tour weeks in advance, excited for the experience of a lifetime. Your tour night arrives and clouds completely obscure the sky — no auroras are visible at all. You expect a refund or rebook, but the tour operator's fine print says they only guarantee the attempt, not a sighting, and offers only a partial credit toward another tour you may not have time for. How to avoid: Only book with operators who offer a free rebooking or full refund for cloudy nights Check Veður (Icelandic Met Office) aurora forecasts yourself before booking Read cancellation policy carefully — reputable operators always offer a rebook option

Scam alert in Rhodes, Greece — Rhodes Old Town Bar Bill Extortion (nightlife, severity: high). Rhodes Old Town is a UNESCO World Heritage medieval city, and its Sokratous Street and Socratous Square are lined with bars and tavernas catering to tourists. In June 2025, Greek Herald ran 'Rhodes Old Town bars slammed for overcharging tourists' (2025-06-19), and the Daily Mail followed with 'Popular Greek tourist resort labelled the ultimate rip-off for drinks' (2025-06-06) and 'Inside the rip-off holiday haven fleecing Brit tourists' (2025-06-28). The pattern documented across these 2025 news pieces: tourists walk into Old Town bars, order 'normal' drinks, and receive bills of €40–€80 per drink. Travelers capture the community view: 'Be aware of the overcharging tactics and other scams of some unprofessional people who only look after profit.' One traveler documents a specific variant: bars serve drinks in oversized 'novelty glasses' that look like a pint but actually hold two or three pints, then charge per pint at the inflated rate. Combined with no menu visibility ('I had one of these in the old town in a bar with no prices on the menu'), the final bill regularly reaches €150+ for what felt like a normal drink round. Local Greeks also express frustration: 'Even when looking at the reviews online afterwards, everyone rated it 1-star as a rip off.' Your protection: before sitting at any Rhodes Old Town bar, verify the printed drink menu has posted prices. Walk out immediately if the bar cannot produce one. Pay per drink at the bar rather than running a tab. If served a drink in an unusual 'novelty glass,' confirm the price before drinking — 'novelty' is often the euphemism for the rip-off volume. Travel in groups for Old Town evenings; the bar staff are less aggressive with groups than with solo visitors. Daily Mail June 2025 reporting confirmed that Rhodes authorities have begun fining named bars, but enforcement is reactive rather than preventive. For legitimate Old Town dining, community-recommended options with posted prices include Nireas Restaurant, Hatzikelis, and To Meltemi — all with 4.4+ Google ratings. How to avoid: Verify the printed drink menu has posted prices before sitting — walk out if none is produced Pay per drink at the bar rather than a running tab Confirm the price of any drink served in an unusual 'novelty glass' before drinking Travel in groups for Old Town evenings — staff are less aggressive with groups Community-recommended posted-price Old Town dining: Nireas, Hatzikelis, To Meltemi (all 4.4+ ratings)

Scam alert in Rhodes, Greece — Rhodes Cruise Port & Airport Taxi Overcharge (transport, severity: moderate). Rhodes is a major Mediterranean cruise destination, and Kolona Harbour (the main cruise dock adjacent to the Old Town) sees multiple large ships most summer days. Cruise passengers step off the ship and face a fleet of taxis quoting €40 to Lindos (real metered fare €55–€70 one-way over 50 kilometres, which is a reasonable price) or €25 to Faliraki (real fare €15–€20) or €15 to Rhodes Old Town (walkable in 5 minutes). Community reports give the defensive rule: 'Make sure to agree upon the price before entering, to avoid scammers who try to overcharge tourists.' Travelers also document Rhodes-parallel taxi overcharge cases of €160+. Diagoras Airport (RHO) taxi overcharges mirror the Athens pattern: drivers claim the meter is broken, quote €40 for the 14-kilometre ride to Old Town (real fare €25–€30 metered), or take a padded route through the suburbs. Older travelers transferring to resort hotels in Ixia or Faliraki should be aware that many resort-area taxi stands operate as cartels where drivers refuse discount apps like FreeNow — meaning a €25 metered run to your Ixia hotel may require walking to the main road before a legitimate taxi will accept the fare. Your protection: from Kolona Harbour, walk to Rhodes Old Town (5 minutes) rather than taking a taxi. For the airport run, use FreeNow or Beat apps for regulated fares. The KTEL bus from Diagoras Airport to Rhodes city center is €2.40 per person and runs every 30–60 minutes — slower (30–45 minutes) but eliminates taxi exposure entirely. For Lindos day trips from Rhodes town, the KTEL bus costs €5.50 and runs every 30 minutes in peak season; the drive is 55 minutes each way. Cruise passengers pressed for time should consider the cruise line's official Lindos shore excursion (overpriced but honestly priced) rather than a roadside taxi deal. Save Tourist Police 171 for disputes; they have Rhodes offices and respond to documented overcharges. How to avoid: Walk from Kolona Harbour to Rhodes Old Town — it is 5 minutes on foot From Diagoras Airport, use KTEL bus (€2.40, 30–45 min to city) or FreeNow/Beat apps For Lindos day trips, KTEL bus is €5.50 and runs every 30 min in peak season At resort hotel driveways, walk to the main road if cartel taxis refuse app pickups Cruise passengers with tight timing should consider the cruise line's Lindos shore excursion

Scam alert in Rhodes, Greece — Lindos Acropolis Donkey Ride & ATV Rental Damage (transport, severity: moderate). Lindos is a whitewashed hilltop village topped by the Acropolis of Lindos — one of Greece's most beautiful archaeological sites. The approach from the village to the Acropolis involves a steep 10-minute walk up switchback stone paths, and donkey rides are offered at the trailhead for €5–€10 per rider. The scam variant follows the Santorini playbook: handlers quote a low price at the bottom, then demand €15–€30 mid-ascent 'because of your weight' or 'because the donkey is tired.' Cruise travelers flag the animal welfare concern: 'The other option is a donkey ride, but the donkeys are not treated' well — the same ethical framework as Santorini applies, with documented spinal injuries to overworked donkeys. For Faliraki and Rhodes city ATV rentals, the damage deposit pattern matches Heraklion: shops take €300–€500 cash deposit, 'discover' scratches on return, and charge five to ten times the real repair cost. Community reports consistently warn about ATV rentals in Faliraki's party strip where operators rotate storefront names seasonally. Car rental in Rhodes has similar issues; reputable agencies are Avis, Budget, Hertz, and Europcar at Diagoras Airport rather than Rhodes town storefronts. Your protection: for Lindos, walk the 10 minutes to the Acropolis — the path is steep but the views on the way up are part of the experience. If mobility is a real concern, consider visiting Lindos on a cruise excursion that uses golf carts for transfers within the village. Do not ride the donkeys — both for animal welfare reasons and to avoid the mid-ascent price-hike scam. For ATVs, skip rentals entirely in Faliraki; rent cars from major international brands at Diagoras Airport. Photograph every panel of any rental vehicle before departure with timestamps. Pay by credit card for chargeback leverage on fake damage claims. How to avoid: Walk the 10-minute Lindos Acropolis path — the views are part of the experience For mobility-impaired visitors, cruise excursions with golf-cart transfers are the ethical alternative Do not ride Lindos donkeys — both mid-ascent price hikes and documented welfare issues Rent cars from Avis, Budget, Hertz, Europcar at Diagoras Airport — not Rhodes town storefronts Photograph every panel of any vehicle rental before departure and pay by credit card for chargeback

Scam alert in Rhodes, Greece — Faliraki 'All-Inclusive' Bar & Tourist-Strip Overcharge (nightlife, severity: moderate). Faliraki is Rhodes's main package-holiday resort town — designated, as travelers put it, 'for tourists. Imagine that in the winter time is dead, it's a village made for tourists.' Another community summary: 'Why Faliraki? It's only a tourist trap.' The area's bars and restaurants use the classic cruise-strip pattern: 'all-inclusive' deals with small print, inflated cocktail prices once you are seated, and 'entertainment' surcharges on bills. A specific Faliraki scam: 'VIP bottle service' packages that advertise €80 per person for a bottle of spirits plus mixers and table reservation, but on checkout produce a bill with 'table fee €200,' 'service €80,' 'VIP security €40,' and an inflated spirit price. One traveler captures the scale: 'I think local restaurant I could get two entrees and two drinks for $30 or so. But the tourist traps usually will run $80 to $100 for the same amount of stuff.' Ixia and Kolymbia resort areas run similar patterns: shops near the beach charge €15 for ice cream that is €3 in Rhodes Town. Your protection: for a reliable Rhodes holiday experience, stay in Rhodes Town or in Lindos village rather than Faliraki — both have more local character and better-priced dining. If you are at a Faliraki package hotel, eat at the hotel's main restaurant (where prices are included in your package) rather than the bar strip. For independent dining, ask your hotel's front desk for locally-recommended non-tourist tavernas and confirm prices in writing. Cover charges and minimum consumptions are legally required to be posted in Greece; refuse any bar that cannot produce printed price documentation. Pay by credit card for chargeback leverage. For day trips to Lindos or Rhodes Town from Faliraki, use the KTEL bus (€4.50 per person) rather than the taxi cartel at the beach strip. How to avoid: Stay in Rhodes Town or Lindos village rather than Faliraki — better food, more local character At Faliraki package hotels, eat at the main restaurant where prices are included in your package For independent dining, ask the hotel front desk for locally-recommended tavernas with posted prices Refuse any bar that cannot produce printed cover-charge / minimum-consumption documentation Use KTEL bus (€4.50) for Faliraki → Rhodes Town or Lindos — avoid beach strip taxi cartel

Scam alert in Rhodes, Greece — Old Town Tourist-Menu Restaurant Overcharge (nightlife, severity: moderate). Inside Rhodes Old Town's medieval walls, restaurants along the main tourist spine on Sokratous Street and near the Grand Master's Palace use the tourist-menu playbook: menus posted outside with one price, menus at the table with another, welcome bread and olives billed as cover charges, and fish priced per kilogram. Travelers provide the pricing benchmark: 'I think local restaurant I could get two entrees and two drinks for $30 or so. But the tourist traps usually will run $80 to $100 for the same amount of stuff.' A 2.5–3x tourist markup is the standard. The Daily Mail's June 2025 investigation 'Inside the rip-off holiday haven fleecing Brit tourists' named specific Old Town restaurants engaging in menu substitution — tourists are shown one menu at the door and billed from a different menu at the table. Tourist Police in Rhodes have fined several venues in 2025, but the practice continues across the approximately 80 restaurants inside the Old Town walls. The older-traveler-specific concern is that cruise passengers and guided-tour groups often eat at the first convenient restaurant on their itinerary — tour guides sometimes receive commission on this, making 'recommended' restaurants a potential conflict of interest. Your protection: confirm prices match between the outside menu and the table menu before sitting. Refuse welcome bread, olives, tzatziki when they arrive — Greek law requires cover charges to be posted and prohibits unlisted additions (community reports document illegal bread charges on bills). Count the bill line by line and dispute any non-ordered items. For genuinely good Old Town dining with posted transparent prices, community recommendations include Nireas Restaurant, Hatzikelis (old Turkish fountain setting), To Meltemi, and Alexis Palace — all have 4.4+ Google ratings and 500+ reviews. For lunch during a cruise excursion, walk inland toward the Municipal Market on Socratous Square or north toward Pythagora Street where local tavernas serve residents at half the Old Town tourist prices. How to avoid: Confirm the outside menu matches the table menu before sitting — walk out otherwise Refuse welcome bread, olives, tzatziki — Greek law prohibits unlisted cover charges (€500 fines) Count the bill line by line and dispute non-ordered items Community-recommended posted-price Old Town: Nireas, Hatzikelis, To Meltemi, Alexis Palace (4.4+ ratings) For lunch during a cruise excursion, walk inland to Pythagora Street for local tavernas at half the price

Scam alert in Rhodes, Greece — Old Town 'Fake Market' Counterfeit & Bracelet Distraction (transport, severity: moderate). Rhodes Old Town has a 'fake market' zone on and around Sokratous Street where shops sell counterfeit designer goods — bags, sunglasses, watches — at €30–€150. Travelers mention this directly: 'I have heard that there should be a fake market selling copies of designer brands in Old Town Rhodes? Is that true?' EU customs law allows seizure at UK and US borders of knowingly-purchased counterfeit items, and returning travelers have had items confiscated at Heathrow and JFK with no recourse. Unknowingly-purchased items are typically only seized (not prosecuted), but you lose the item and the cash. A parallel scam targets older travelers specifically: bracelet-and-flower distraction teams operate at the Mandraki Harbour entrance, around the Grand Master's Palace, and at the main Old Town gate (Eleftherias Gate). The mechanic mirrors Athens Syntagma — one team member places a bracelet or flower, a partner 'confirms' it, and a third member blocks the escape. Greece-travel bracelet warnings apply directly: in 2025 these crews expanded from Athens/Thessaloniki to Rhodes Old Town during peak season (June–September). Your protection: do not buy counterfeit designer goods — the customs risk is real and the items are typically worthless substitutes. For genuine Rhodes souvenirs, look for handmade ceramics at Icons Art Studio or Paradise Ceramics on Sokratous Street (marked provenance), local olive oil from Kodylas or Crete-imported Sitia Co-op brands, or handmade leather goods at Apollon Leather workshops. For the bracelet/flower teams, cross your arms and step back immediately when approached; do not engage in conversation. Keep your wallet in a front zipped pocket or a crossbody bag worn in front when walking through Old Town. Report persistent crews to Tourist Police 171 — Rhodes has an active Old Town Tourist Police post at the Eleftherias Gate during summer months. How to avoid: Do not buy counterfeit designer goods — UK/US customs will seize at borders, no recourse For genuine souvenirs: Icons Art Studio or Paradise Ceramics (ceramics), Apollon Leather (leather) Cross arms and step back if anyone approaches with a bracelet or flower Keep wallet in front zipped pocket or crossbody bag worn in front in Old Town Report persistent crews to Tourist Police 171 — active post at Eleftherias Gate in summer

Scam alert in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil — Rio Galeão Airport (GIG) & Santos Dumont (SDU) Taxi Mafia & Late-Night Uber Confusion (transport, severity: high). Rio's two airports — GIG (international, 20 km north of the city) and SDU (domestic, downtown waterfront) — host one of South America's most-documented 2025 taxi-overcharge ecosystems, with late-night arrivals especially targeted. Community reports from 2024–2025 cover GIG transport for foreigners, late-night Uber safety to Copacabana, Rio newbie tips, and tourist insights. The 2025 scams: (a) 'authorized cooperative' kiosks (Transcoopass, Special Coop, Cootramo) inside arrivals quote R$280–R$450 to Copacabana / Ipanema (real Uber R$90–R$160; real metered yellow taxi R$130–R$180); (b) sign-holders at the arrivals exit posing as 'hotel transfer' agents intercepting tourists whose hotels do NOT include shuttle; (c) Uber driver cancel-and-recontract scam — driver accepts the in-app ride, cancels at the kerb, then quotes cash R$200+; (d) 'meter broken' yellow taxi demands at hotel arrival with R$250+ flat-rate cash demand; (e) GIG-to-SDU 'connecting transfer R$350' sold by touts (real Uber R$60–R$100 for the 25-km ride); (f) credit-card cloning at unofficial taxi-cooperative counters via 'manual entry' card-machines. For travelers: (1) book Uber, 99 (Brazilian rideshare), or Cabify on airport Wi-Fi AFTER luggage — typical GIG to Zona Sul (Copacabana / Ipanema / Leblon) R$90–R$160, 30–45 min depending on traffic; meet driver at the designated 'Aplicativos' (apps) pickup zone signposted near each terminal exit; (2) alternatively use the OFFICIAL Premium Auto Onibus 'BRT Transolímpica' bus or 'Frescão' (Real Auto Onibus 2018) airport-to-Zona Sul service at R$27 per person (90 min, daytime safest option); (3) IGNORE every 'authorized cooperative' kiosk inside the terminal quoting above R$200; (4) for SDU domestic arrivals, Uber is even cheaper — R$25–R$60 to Zona Sul; (5) NEVER hand a credit card to any taxi driver — pay in-app or cash only; (6) for late-night arrivals (post-22:00), Uber Comfort or Uber Black is worth the R$30–R$50 surcharge for vetted drivers; (7) save Polícia Turística Rio (DEAT) +55 21 2334 6802 (English available, Av. Afrânio de Melo Franco 159, Leblon) and US Consulate Rio +55 21 3823 2000. How to avoid: Book Uber/99/Cabify on airport Wi-Fi: GIG-Zona Sul R$90–R$160 Meet driver at 'Aplicativos' signposted pickup zone; SDU R$25–R$60 OR Premium / Frescão airport bus R$27 per person (90 min) NEVER hand credit card to any taxi driver Late-night: Uber Comfort/Black R$30–R$50 surcharge for vetted drivers

Scam alert in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil — Rio Caipirinha Bar 'R$10,000 Bill' Honeypot Scam in Lapa & Copacabana (tourist-trap, severity: high). Lapa and Copacabana bars host Rio's most-documented 2026 'caipirinha bill' honeypot scam — a friendly local invites the tourist to a specific bar, two caipirinhas arrive, and the bill comes back at R$10,000+ with bouncers blocking the door. A 2026 first-person account titled 'Esses caras tentaram golpe de R$10.000 por 2 caipirinhas' documents a near-loss of R$10,000 for two cocktails. A 2025 account titled 'I was scammed R$10000 in Rio de Janeiro and Bank of' documents the same pattern with a successful card-charge. Another 2025 Ipanema variant saw a R$27,000 loss, and 2026 community threads continue to warn of Copacabana scammers. The 2026 scam pattern: (a) friendly English-speaking local at Copacabana boardwalk or Lapa bar street invites tourist to 'best caipirinha bar nearby'; (b) walked 5–15 min to an unmarked bar (often upstairs, often a 'private room' with 'friends'); (c) 2 caipirinhas + perhaps light food arrive; (d) bill: R$4,000–R$27,000 for 'premium import cachaça', 'VIP table fee', 'live music charge', 'private hostess service'; (e) bouncers block the door until card is processed; (f) some venues threaten 'we call police' if the tourist refuses (police rarely called — extortion bluff); (g) the 'friend' who brought you in receives 30–50% commission on the inflated bill. Solo male tourists from Tinder/Bumble/Badoo dates are specifically targeted in this Rio variant — same template as Jakarta Blok M and Bangkok scams. For travelers: (1) NEVER let a stranger walk you to a 'best bar nearby' — this is the consistent opening of the scam; pick venues YOURSELF from Google 4.5+ ratings (reputable Lapa: Rio Scenarium, Carioca da Gema, Bar do Mineiro in Santa Teresa); (2) ALWAYS ask for the written menu BEFORE ordering and photograph each page; verify caipirinha is R$18–R$45 (anything above R$80 is scam-tier); (3) refuse any 'hostess' joining your table uninvited; (4) if a bill arrives with surprise charges, pay with credit card ONLY and immediately dispute via your bank — bank will reverse charges with photographed menu; (5) for solo travelers using dating apps, YOU pick the venue, never the date — and inform your hotel of your whereabouts; (6) save Polícia Turística (DEAT) Leblon +55 21 2334 6802 (English available, 24/7 hotline); (7) US Consulate Rio +55 21 3823 2000 if extorted; (8) the 2026 case study titled 'Esses caras tentaram golpe de R$10.000' is must-read community reading. How to avoid: NEVER let a stranger walk you to a 'best bar' — pick venue yourself Reputable Lapa: Rio Scenarium, Carioca da Gema, Bar do Mineiro Photograph menu BEFORE ordering; verify caipirinha R$18–R$45 Refuse hostess; pay with credit card ONLY and dispute via bank Polícia Turística DEAT +55 21 2334 6802 (24/7 English)

Scam alert in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil — Copacabana / Ipanema Beach Pickpocket & 'Arrastão' Sweep Theft Ring (pickpocket, severity: high). Rio's beaches host South America's most-documented 2025 beach-theft ecosystem — both single-target pickpocketing and the infamous 'arrastão' (sweep theft) where a coordinated 10-30-person crew sweeps a section of beach, snatching anything not anchored. Community reports from 2025 cover Rio tourist tips, newbie advice, first-person 'I got ripped off' stories, petty-theft cross-region discussions, and the broader 2025 safety baseline. The 2025 scams: (a) phone-snatch from beach towels — child or teen runs past, grabs phone, hands off to scooter accomplice on Avenida Atlântica; (b) 'arrastão' beach sweep — most documented at Copacabana Posto 2–4 and Ipanema Posto 9 on weekend afternoons / public holidays / Carnaval; coordinated group ages 14–25 sprints through a section grabbing phones, bags, sunglasses, flip-flops; (c) distraction-team: one person 'falls' or 'spills drink', partner lifts wallet/phone; (d) beach-kiosk (quiosque) drink-spike at evening hours targeting solo tourists; (e) snorkel/sarong vendor 'free henna tattoo' that becomes R$150 demand; (f) 'beach umbrella + chair rental R$100' from unauthorised vendor (real R$30–R$50 from quiosque); (g) Avenida Atlântica boardwalk evening pickpocketing at outdoor café tables. For travelers: (1) bring NOTHING to the beach you cannot afford to lose — phone, wallet, watch, jewelry stay in the hotel safe; carry only beach-tote with sunscreen, towel, R$50 cash, and a single basic card you don't mind cancelling; (2) use a quiosque (kiosk) chair-and-umbrella rental at R$30–R$50 — staff will keep an eye on your minimal belongings while you swim; (3) NEVER leave anything on the towel while you swim — 'it'll be fine for 5 min' is exactly when arrastão sweeps; (4) for evening beach walks, stick to the well-lit Avenida Atlântica side, not the sand after dusk; (5) refuse every 'free henna tattoo / sarong / massage' beach vendor; firm 'não obrigado'; (6) at outdoor café tables, keep phone in zipped bag, never on table; (7) for Carnaval / NYE / Réveillon, the arrastão risk is elevated 5–10× — leave valuables at hotel and use crossbody bag with zipper; (8) Polícia Turística (DEAT) for theft: +55 21 2334 6802; file a Boletim de Ocorrência (BO) within 24 hours for insurance claims. How to avoid: Bring NOTHING to the beach you can't afford to lose Use quiosque chair-and-umbrella R$30–R$50; staff watches belongings NEVER leave items on towel while swimming Carnaval / NYE: arrastão risk 5–10×; valuables in hotel safe DEAT Tourist Police +55 21 2334 6802; BO within 24 hours

Scam alert in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil — Christ Redeemer & Sugarloaf 'Skip-the-Line VIP' Tour Operator Fraud (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Rio's two iconic monuments — Christ the Redeemer (Cristo Redentor on Corcovado mountain) and Sugarloaf (Pão de Açúcar) cable car — are universal Rio bucket-list items, and the 2025 third-party reseller ecosystem exploits ticket-routing complexity. Community reports document the legitimate Sugarloaf booking process, a specific 2025 warning titled 'DO NOT TOUR WITH OLAFEMI TOURS' about a named operator, and broader tour-operator selection tips. Legitimate ticketing: Christ the Redeemer via the official Trem do Corcovado train (paineirascorcovado.com.br) is R$105 weekday / R$116 weekend round-trip foreigner; via Paineiras Shuttle Vans (paineirascorcovado.com.br) is R$35 + R$33 entry = R$68 round-trip. Sugarloaf cable car (bondinho.com.br) is R$140 for foreigners (round-trip both Urca Hill + Sugarloaf summit). Both sell out 1–2 weeks ahead in high season — book DIRECT. The 2025 scams: (a) 'skip-the-line Christ Redeemer VIP tour US$80–US$150 per person' resold via Viator/GetYourGuide third parties — that's 3–6× the official R$116 train ticket; the 'skip-the-line' is fictional (the train has assigned departure times, no queue to skip); (b) 'private Christ Redeemer + Sugarloaf combo US$200 per person' bundles padding 4× DIY cost; (c) hotel concierge 'recommended tour operator' kickbacks at 1.5–2× direct rate; (d) Cosme Velho station 'guide' offering to 'skip the line' for R$100 cash — no skip exists, you'll just queue with everyone; (e) Paineiras shuttle 'fast-track upgrade R$80' (no upgrade tier exists); (f) 'private cable car booking R$600' at Urca base when the cable car is shared — no private option. For travelers: (1) book Christ the Redeemer ONLINE 1–2 weeks ahead via paineirascorcovado.com.br (Trem do Corcovado R$105–R$116 OR Paineiras Shuttle R$68) — NEVER via Viator / GetYourGuide / hotel concierge marked-up packages; (2) book Sugarloaf at bondinho.com.br at R$140; (3) REFUSE every 'skip-the-line', 'VIP tour', 'fast-track upgrade' upsell — none exists; (4) for travelers with mobility concerns, the Trem do Corcovado is much easier than Paineiras Shuttle (climb avoided); the Sugarloaf cable car is fully accessible; (5) optimal timing: Christ the Redeemer at 8 AM opening (avoids cloud + crowds); Sugarloaf at sunset (~5–6 PM Sept–Mar) for the legendary view; (6) bring layers — Corcovado summit is 10°C cooler than Copacabana; (7) AVOID Olafemi Tours per 2025 community warnings; reputable English-speaking operators: Tour Brazilis, Free Walker Tours, Carioca Tropical Tours, Rio By Cab. How to avoid: Book Christ Redeemer ONLINE direct: paineirascorcovado.com.br R$105–R$116 Book Sugarloaf direct: bondinho.com.br R$140 REFUSE every 'skip-the-line' / 'VIP' / 'fast-track' upsell Optimal: Christ at 8 AM opening; Sugarloaf at sunset Reputable operators: Tour Brazilis, Free Walker Tours, Carioca Tropical, Rio By Cab

Scam alert in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil — Rio Favela Tour Unethical Operator & Fake-Charity 'Slum Safari' Scam (tourist-trap, severity: high). Favela tours — Rocinha, Vidigal, Santa Marta — are Rio's most-controversial tourism category, and 2025 community discussion is increasingly critical of the unethical 'slum safari' operator ecosystem. Community reports from 2025 discuss the ethics of slum-safari tours, favela-tour experiences, a specific warning about a named operator titled 'DO NOT TOUR WITH OLAFEMI TOURS', and perspectives from local Brazilians. The 2025 issues: (a) 'safari-style' tours run by outsider operators with no community-benefit-share, treating residents as photo subjects without consent or revenue-share — ethics widely criticised; (b) operators charging US$50–US$150 per tourist for a 3-hour 'experience' with effectively zero direct compensation to the favela community; (c) safety variance — some operators take tourists into active-conflict zones during police operations or rival-faction periods (2025 Rio police operations have caused fatalities in tourist-area favelas); (d) 'photo with kids' upcharge demands (R$100+ for unsolicited child photos); (e) Olafemi Tours specifically named by 2025 community reports for problematic operator behavior; (f) hostel tour-desk kickbacks pushing tourists toward unethical operators; (g) 'private favela house visit' upsells (R$200+) that are staged. For travelers seriously considering a favela visit: (1) the ethical case for 'favela tourism' is weak — most community organisations recommend NOT going as a tourist; the educational value can be obtained via documentaries (City of God, Wasteland) without the safety/consent issues; (2) IF you decide to visit, book ONLY community-led operators with verified resident-benefit revenue-share: Favela Inc (Rocinha resident-led), Tour Pelos Olhos da Rocinha (resident-led), Spirit Travel (community partnership); avoid Olafemi Tours per 2025 community warning; (3) NEVER book a favela tour during periods of active police operations — check Rio's official Polícia Militar updates BEFORE departure; (4) NEVER photograph residents (especially children) without explicit consent — Brazilian law and basic ethics prohibit; (5) refuse 'private house visit' upsells; (6) for cultural Rio tourism without favela-tour ethics issues, the Santa Teresa neighborhood hilltop walk gives historic Rio vibes without exploiting working-class communities; (7) US Consulate Rio +55 21 3823 2000 if any tour goes wrong; (8) safer alternative: free walking tour of Lapa + Santa Teresa via Free Walker Tours (tip-based, well-reviewed). How to avoid: Strongly consider NOT visiting — community ethics weak case for tourism If visiting, ONLY community-led: Favela Inc, Tour Pelos Olhos da Rocinha, Spirit Travel AVOID Olafemi Tours per 2025 community warning Check Polícia Militar updates BEFORE for active operations NEVER photograph residents (especially children) without consent

Scam alert in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil — Rio Carnaval & Réveillon Booking.com / Airbnb Cancel-and-Relist Fraud (tourist-trap, severity: high). Rio Carnaval (4-day event around late Feb / early Mar) and Réveillon (NYE Copacabana, 2 million attendees) drive accommodation prices 4–8× normal — and a 2025 cancel-and-relist fraud ecosystem exploits the demand. A canonical 2024 community warning titled 'Warning! scam listings on booking.com for Carnaval' documents the Booking.com fraud. Other 2025 community reports document Carnaval-period booking patterns, Ipanema stays, and general Rio newbie tips. The 2025 scam patterns: (a) Booking.com / Airbnb 'phantom listings' — high-quality photos of properties that don't exist or are already booked; tourist pays in advance, arrives, finds no property; (b) confirmed-booking cancellation 30–60 days before Carnaval / Réveillon with re-listing at 3–5× the original price; (c) WhatsApp 'private Copacabana apartment for Réveillon US$800/night' demanding 100% upfront via PIX (Brazilian instant-bank transfer, irreversible) — apartment doesn't exist; (d) Sambódromo-adjacent 'VIP balcony view' Airbnb listings at US$5,000+/night that are actually rooms 500m away with no view; (e) on-arrival bait-and-switch from a beachfront unit to a 3-block-inland unit; (f) 'cleaning deposit US$300 cash on arrival' that never returns; (g) 'Carnaval VIP Sambódromo entry US$400' resold at 2–3× official Liesa box-office rate (real Setor 9 grandstand R$200–R$600). For travelers: (1) for Carnaval and Réveillon, BOOK 6–9 MONTHS AHEAD via Booking.com or established hotel chains (Hilton, Marriott, Belmond Copacabana Palace, Fasano, Pestana) — these have legal recourse against cancellation; AVOID Airbnb peak-season for Rio (cancel-and-relist pattern documented); (2) NEVER PIX or WhatsApp-bank-transfer to private 'apartment' sellers — irreversible Brazilian payment system; only platform-secure payment; (3) for Sambódromo Carnaval tickets, buy ONLY at the official Liesa box office (liesa.globo.com) — Setor 9 grandstand R$200–R$600 fair; refuse every 'VIP balcony view' resold above 2× official rate; (4) cross-reference any property name on Google Maps + Tripadvisor BEFORE booking — fake listings have no independent footprint; (5) on arrival, photograph property condition and any defects; refuse 'cleaning deposit cash on arrival' — request via platform only; (6) for Réveillon (NYE Copacabana), the safest accommodations are major Avenida Atlântica hotels — direct beachfront, no street-walk needed; (7) DEAT Tourist Police +55 21 2334 6802 for booking-fraud denuncia within 48 hours for chargeback documentation. How to avoid: Book Carnaval / Réveillon 6–9 months ahead via hotel chains, NOT Airbnb Reputable: Hilton, Marriott, Belmond Copacabana Palace, Fasano, Pestana NEVER PIX/WhatsApp-bank-transfer to private 'apartment' sellers Sambódromo tickets ONLY from official Liesa: liesa.globo.com DEAT +55 21 2334 6802; chargeback denuncia within 48 hours

Scam alert in Rome, Italy — The Trevi Fountain Tre Campanelle Sting (fraud, severity: high). A 'finto croupier' works three metal shells on a fold-up table near Trevi, the Pantheon or Piazza di Spagna; well-dressed accomplices fake easy €50 wins while pickpocket partners work the onlookers. An April 11, 2025 ANSA report documents Carabinieri arresting a 50-year-old Romanian man and 34-year-old Romanian woman on the Trinità dei Monti steps after a tourist lost €100. A November 29, 2025 Repubblica Roma report details a six-person gang caught near Fontana di Trevi with €1,450 in euros, US dollars and British pounds. A March 29, 2026 ANSA Lazio bulletin denounced 20+ across Pincio, Trevi, Spagna, Pantheon and Piazza di Pietra; Corriere Roma estimates three organized bands in the Tridente earning ~€1,000/hour each. How to avoid: Do not stop, do not watch, do not bet — community reports confirm the game is 'always, always rigged'. Walk past with your hand on your bag zipper — accomplices pickpocket onlookers while the game holds attention. If you see the table forming near a landmark, cross to the opposite side and keep moving. Report the location to 113 (Polizia di Stato) or 112 (Carabinieri) — polizia locale now run masked-officer stings, and your tip helps.

Scam alert in Rome, Italy — Termini Station Pickpocket Rings (pickpocket, severity: high). Coordinated Latino, North African and Roma networks work Termini platforms, the underground galleria, Piazza dei Cinquecento and bus 64/40 queues. A March 2025 Repubblica Roma piece names Termini, Colosseo and Barberini as stations 'dove i turisti diventano prede.' An October 2025 Repubblica investigation found a deposito clandestino of stolen suitcases and designer goods in a Termini-area guesthouse. A February 2026 Repubblica report covered the new Polmetro base at Termini (50 agents, 5,000 cameras). Variants include 'helper' scams at ticket machines that photograph card PINs and the 'cavallo di ritorno' phone-ransom extortion (Corriere Roma, November 2022). How to avoid: Buy tickets only on Trenitalia/Italo apps or logo-marked machines — never let a 'helper' touch your card or coins. Use only the signed official taxi rank; refuse 'taxi?' solicitations inside the hall. On Frecciarossa/Italo, put luggage on the end-of-carriage rack that faces your seat. Keep phones out of back or side pockets on platforms. Download the Roma Capitale anti-borseggio app that logged 60 reports in its first six days.

Scam alert in Rome, Italy — The Metro A/B "Finto Malore" Distraction Theft (pickpocket, severity: high). A passenger fakes a sudden malore (fainting/nausea) at the metro doors while a partner lifts wallets from the tourists who lean in to help. Roma Today documents the 7:20am Metro A textbook case; a March 11, 2026 Roma Today arrest report covers three Romanian citizens (two adults plus a 14-year-old minor) caught encircling a tourist on Metro B at Colosseo. Repubblica Roma documented female pickpockets deploying pepper spray on Metro A in March 2025 and Peruvian-on-Peruvian violence at Termini in May 2025. Il Messaggero tracks a 'new generation' of borseggiatori wearing designer clothes and in-ear communications. How to avoid: Ride metro and bus 64 with bag zipped and across the chest on the side opposite the door, one hand on the zipper. Treat any 'malore' at metro doors as a pickpocket distraction first — back up one step. Never carry phone/wallet in back, hip or jacket side pockets on Roman transport. Shout 'ladro!' if groped — Roma Today documents multiple arrests after passenger reactions. Get off at the next station after a suspicious approach; check yourself on the platform.

Scam alert in Rome, Italy — The Colosseum Fake Gladiator Photo Shakedown (extortion, severity: high). Men in plastic armor and red capes drape props on tourists, pose for 'free' photos, then demand €20–€50+ per person. The racket has been a Rome political scandal for over a decade: Corriere Roma's 2010 Paolo Graldi 'Il caso Centurioni' editorial and Senator Fabrizio Cutrufo's 2011 anti-stalking proposal called for specific legislation. Il Messaggero covers them as a 'banda dei selfie' that also lifts bags in the photo density near the Arco di Costantino. A widely cited Rome community thread confirms the operators 'are part of an organized racket' documented by AGTAR (Association for Certified Tour Guides in Rome) and Il Messaggero journalists. Parallel fake-guide pattern: February 2026 Repubblica Roma documents three finti Ciceroni from Iran and Brazil fined €400 each. How to avoid: Book Colosseum, Forum and Palatine tickets in advance at coopculture.it, the Parco Archeologico app, or a verified operator — never buy from someone in costume. Say 'no, grazie' and keep walking; do not pause, do not shake hands, do not let anything be draped on you. If money is demanded after you refused, say 'chiamo la polizia' and dial 113. Wear your backpack on your front along the Fori Imperiali–Colosseo corridor.

Scam alert in Rome, Italy — The Fiumicino Fake Taxi & Fixed-Fare Scam (transport, severity: high). Rome's official fixed fare is €50 from FCO and €30 from Ciampino (CIA) to inside the Aurelian Walls — but drivers routinely overcharge. A July 2022 Corriere Roma report documented €70 in cash for the FCO-center fare with the farewell 'Benvenuto a Roma.' A July 2025 traveler report documented a driver branded 'Società Cooperativa Roma' demanding €55 for a 3.7-km FCO hop with the meter off, claiming card payments required the passenger to cover 'all commission fees.' An April 2024 Corriere Roma report named a driver forcing a 'tariffa fissa' cash-only; an August 2024 Corriere report documented a driver demanding €200 to return a forgotten laptop. The 'card reader broken' variant is documented widely in community reports. How to avoid: From FCO, take the Leonardo Express (€14, 32 min, every 15 minutes) to Termini — nothing to negotiate. If you must taxi, use only the signed official rank outside arrivals; confirm the €50 (FCO) or €30 (Ciampino) fixed fare before closing the door. Use FREE NOW or itTaxi apps — the meter runs on the app. Always demand a ricevuta with taxi number, date, time, route. Never let a driver take you to an ATM; pay cash for the posted fare and file a complaint at the Comune di Roma Ufficio Taxi.

Scam alert in Rome, Italy — The Vatican Museums "Fake Staff" Line-Jumper (fraud, severity: high). Men in uniforms, lanyards and name tags sort the Vatican Museums queue on the street and steer tourists to 'partner offices' for overpriced tickets or cash shakedowns. Community reports lay out the MO — the 'staff' look 'legit' with uniforms and name tags, police stand meters away without intervening. A parallel St. Peter's Square variant sells paid skip-the-line access to the basilica (which is actually free). February 2026 Repubblica Roma fined three finti Ciceroni €400 each at the Colosseum — the same fake-authority pattern at a parallel site. The Vatican's official policy: skip-the-line is sold only via tickets.museivaticani.va or authorized resellers. How to avoid: Buy Vatican Museums tickets only from tickets.museivaticani.va, preferably in advance with a reserved entry time. Ignore anyone on Viale Vaticano; walk to the queue at the door. If you must buy day-of, buy inside the museum building. Basilica entry is free — there is no legitimate 'skip-the-line' for it. Report sidewalk 'staff' to the Gendarmeria Vaticana at the entrance or call 112.

Scam alert in Rome, Italy — The Bracelet & Rose Aggression (Spanish Steps, Ponte Sant'Angelo, St. Peter's) (harassment, severity: high). A friendly stranger opens with 'where are you from?', praises your country, and ties a friendship bracelet (or hands a rose) 'as a gift' — then demands €20 and escalates with shoves, curses or stalking when refused. Community reports document the textbook opening and a Ponte Sant'Angelo arm-poking incident with fisticuffs. Travelers report being shoved, cursed as a 'bitch,' and having partners robbed the same day in Trastevere after a bracelet-guy approach turned physical. Il Messaggero's centro-storico dossier counted 54 borseggiatori arrested in a single Ferragosto-to-autumn window in the same tourist perimeter. How to avoid: Do not make eye contact, do not reply, do not slow your pace — 'no, grazie' once, then keep moving. Keep hands at your sides or in pockets when bracelet/rose sellers approach; a hand out to 'receive' is the cue they use. If something is placed on you, take it off and drop it — you owe nothing. Zip your bag across your chest in Spanish Steps, Piazza San Pietro and Ponte Sant'Angelo zones (all also pickpocket zones). Dial 113/112 if shoved or followed.

Scam alert in Rome, Italy — The Trevi / Pantheon / Piazza Navona Tourist-Menu Trap (overcharging, severity: moderate). Restaurants in the Trevi-Pantheon-Navona axis hit tourists with unrequested pane/acqua/antipasti, coperto over €3/head, automatic 15–22% 'servizio' on foreign cards, and branzino priced 'al etto' that arrives at 400–600g. An August 2014 Corriere Roma / Cook piece documented US tourists James and Mariann charged €42 for three gelatos and a bottle of water near Fontana di Trevi. A 2025 community report documents a $2,000 restaurant bill for two tourists near Trevi. A parallel 2025 report documents €20 for two €2.50 thermal patches near Piazza di Pasquino. How to avoid: Walk 5–7 minutes off the Trevi/Pantheon/Navona axis — Monti, Pigneto, Testaccio, southern Trastevere and Prati are locally recommended. Photograph the posted outdoor menu before sitting (Italian law requires prices); if fish/steak is only 'al etto' without portion guidance, leave. Ask at seating 'Mi conferma il coperto e se il servizio è incluso?' Refuse unrequested items — you are not legally required to pay for pane/acqua/antipasti you did not order. Sort Google Maps reviews by 'Most recent' and Italian language.

Scam alert in Rome, Italy — The Fake Five-Star Hotel & Off-Platform Rental Scam (money, severity: moderate). Scammers create falsi profili mimicking Rome's five-star hotels and vacation rentals to harvest card numbers and up-front payments for reservations that don't exist. A December 13, 2022 ANSA/Corriere Roma investigation documented 200+ American victims; the Corinthia Hotel was named in court documents and US intelligence became involved. A March 16, 2025 Corriere Roma report confirmed 20 people rinviati a giudizio for the continuing scheme. An August 2025 ANSA report documented a €2,700 casa vacanze inesistente in the same playbook at lower price points. Booking.com phishing campaigns (Corriere April 2026) add impersonation risk. Off-platform WhatsApp/email contacts and cash 'security fees' on arrival are the recurring tell. How to avoid: Book hotels only at the property's official site or major aggregators (Booking/Expedia/Marriott/IHG/Hilton apps) — never via a cold email or search-ad URL that doesn't match the hotel's domain. Confirm reservations by calling the hotel's own published number (not the one in the email) and reading your code to reception. For apartments, use Airbnb/Booking/Vrbo only — never wire money to a host. Google Street View every address. Rome's tourism tax is €7/night (€10 at 5-stars) per person and collected only by registered accommodations.

Scam alert in Rome, Italy — The POS Pirata Contactless Skimmer (card_fraud, severity: low). A wireless POS hidden in a bag reads contactless cards and phone wallets through fabric within a few centimeters. An August 1, 2025 Repubblica Roma report documented the Rome arrest of a female thief for indebito utilizzo di strumenti di pagamento. A July 25, 2025 Rainews TGR Campania investigation arrested a 36-year-old Peruvian woman in Sorrento with numerosi precedenti penali a Roma — in one Rome incident she had used a similar device to take ~€9,000 from a single tourist. A July 31, 2025 Corriere Tecnologia explainer confirms attacks operate below the €50/€100 tap thresholds that bypass PIN/face-ID. Low severity reflects the still-modest incident count; per-incident losses are unusually large. How to avoid: Carry contactless cards in an RFID-blocking wallet in Rome's crowded zones (under €15). Disable NFC on cards you don't need daily via your bank app; leave only one card contactless-active. Lower the daily tap limit in your bank app to €25–€50. Use phone wallets (Apple Pay / Google Pay) for in-store purchases — device-bound tokenization makes POS-pirata attacks much harder. Enable real-time transaction alerts and review on the spot — losses become irreversible only if unreported for hours.

Scam alert in Rosario, Argentina — ROS Fisherton Airport Taxi Overcharge vs. Uber (transport, severity: moderate). Documented scam patterns: (1) arrivals-hall 'private transfer' touts quoting $60–$120 USD one-way (1.5–3x legitimate $45); (2) unmetered street-taxi downtown: driver refuses to start meter ('taxi tarifa única' or 'meter broken'), then quotes inflated flat rate at destination; (3) 'night rate' or 'weekend rate' surcharges of $10–$20 added without disclosure; (4) 'long-route' detour where driver takes 30–50% longer route claiming traffic on a direct 2–3 km trip; (5) counterfeit peso change returned after paying with large denomination (Argentina-wide pattern, applies to Salta); (6) bus-terminal-to-downtown taxi overcharge at Terminal de Ómnibus where arriving long-distance-bus passengers are easy marks. A prudent approach for older travelers: (1) use Uber or Cabify for airport and city rides — app-priced, bypasses every meter / flat-rate scam variant; (2) for SLA airport arrival, use the official taxi counter inside arrivals with posted flat rate (~$45 USD / EUR42); pay via card if accepted, demand printed recibo; (3) refuse all arrivals-hall 'private transfer' touts quoting $60 USD+ — walk to the official counter or summon Uber from the designated rideshare zone; (4) for downtown street taxis, insist meter starts at base tariff — if driver refuses, exit and walk to next ranked cab; (5) 'taxi tarifa única' at $10–$20 USD for short 2–3 km hops is a flag — legitimate metered fares run $3–$8 USD for typical downtown trips; (6) photograph driver's license plate before entering any unfamiliar cab; (7) for Terminal de Ómnibus arrivals (long-distance buses from Jujuy, Cafayate, Buenos Aires), pre-arrange hotel shuttle or Uber rather than ranks-offered taxis; (8) pay with small bills ($500 / $1,000 / $2,000 denominations) matched to fare — never hand over a $10,000 or $20,000 peso note to a taxi. Save Salta Policía Turística (911) and Ministerio de Turismo Salta (via saltaturismo.gov.ar). How to avoid: Use Uber or Cabify for airport and city rides — app-priced at ARS15,000–25,000 ($15–$25 USD) airport, bypasses every meter/flat-rate scam variant For SLA airport arrival, use the official taxi counter inside arrivals with posted ~$45 USD flat rate — demand printed recibo and pay via card if accepted Refuse all arrivals-hall 'private transfer' touts quoting $60 USD+ — walk to the official counter or summon Uber from designated rideshare zone For downtown street taxis, insist meter starts at base tariff — if driver refuses, exit and walk to next ranked cab; 'tarifa única' at $10+ USD for 2–3 km hops is a scam flag Pay with small bills ($500 / $1,000 / $2,000 denominations) matched to fare — never hand over $10,000 or $20,000 peso note to a taxi driver

Scam alert in San Jose, Costa Rica — SJO Airport Pirate-Taxi Cartel — $40 for a 4-Minute Ride & Worse (transport, severity: high). How to avoid: Pay at the Taxi Aeropuerto orange kiosk INSIDE the SJO terminal (~$28–$40 fixed). Verify plate starts with 'T' + photograph driver's ID + plate before loading bags. If Uber: sit up front, confirm driver ENDS the trip in app before you exit the vehicle. Pre-book Interbus/Gray Line ($15–$25 pp) or hotel shuttle as safest 1 AM option. Never accept a stranger's grab for your luggage — force them to put it down.

How to avoid: Meet Uber on the SJO DEPARTURES level (upstairs) not arrivals — escapes airport-police ban. Verify in-app plate MATCHES physical plate + ask 'cuál es mi nombre?' before entering. Watch driver 'End Trip' in the app + receipt email arrive before exiting the vehicle. Screenshot quoted fare + route in app; dispute overages with Uber + credit-card chargeback. Prefer DiDi or InDrive at equivalent prices; late-night solo: orange taxi or hotel shuttle.

A March 2025 community report: the traveler bought 'FULL coverage insurance from Expedia' and paid ~$1,000 for 3 weeks; on arrival at the offsite lot was told either accept a $2,032 mandatory local insurance OR pay a $32,000 USD deposit with 20% deducted for any damage; when the traveler refused they were 'left on the side of the road with 5 suitcases.' A top reply: 'Adobe and Vamos come out on top every time, and warnings about not booking through third party sites like Expedia.' Another: 'Even had this happen with Hertz.' Another: 'Same situation with me and Expedia and Fox Rental. Would not accept the Expedia insurance.' A November 2025 community report surfaces the legal reality, confirmed by another commenter: 'The law says the only required insurance is third-party liability (SLI/TPL)… NOT REQUIRED is any collision damage coverage.' TPL in 2025/2026 runs ~$13–$20/day — anything above is optional. The scam runs two ways: (1) Expedia/Priceline/Kayak's advertised $19/day balloons at the counter with $25–$40/day mandatory insurance + $2,000 deposit hold — third-party CDWs routinely rejected; (2) Hertz/Fox/Budget/National SJO counters stack 'Super CDW' to push $29/day to $90/day. Another traveler: 'If you decline CDW, you're required to bring proof of insurance from your credit card… don't forget the deposit — $2,000 for most rental companies.' Another: 'Vamos and Adobe seem to be much more straightforward about using rental insurance from a credit card.' Another: '$700 for 10 day rental with Adobe including all insurance — they were amazing.'

For travelers 2025/2026: (1) DO NOT BOOK via Expedia, Priceline, Kayak, Hotwire, Travelocity — book DIRECT with Adobe (adobecar.com), Vamos (vamosrentacar.com), or Wildrider; online quotes include TPL and are transparent; (2) if using Hertz/Budget/National, email the CR counter for an all-in written quote before landing, and bring your credit-card's rental-coverage letter (Amex Premium, Chase Sapphire Reserve Primary, Capital One Venture X Primary) on bank letterhead — required to decline CDW legally; (3) CR requires TPL (~$13–$20/day) — accept it; above is optional unless your card doesn't cover CR (most do); (4) expect $1,500–$3,000 deposit hold clearing 7–14 days post-return; (5) PHOTOGRAPH every panel on pickup + return (video walk-around) — 'pre-existing damage' counter-scam runs often; (6) Adobe, Vamos, Alamo have ZERO counter-shakedowns reported 2024–2026; Hertz/Fox/Budget/Expedia have the worst profile; (7) file disputes at consumidor.go.cr + Amex/Visa chargeback. How to avoid: Book DIRECT with Adobe, Vamos, or Wildrider — published all-in pricing, honored at counter. If using Hertz/Budget/National: email counter for written quote including TPL before landing. Bring printed credit-card CDW coverage letter (Amex Premium, Chase Sapphire Reserve Primary). Accept mandatory TPL only (~$13–$20/day) — decline CDW/Super CDW with written proof. Video walk-around on pickup + return; dispute via consumidor.go.cr + chargeback if ambushed.

Scam alert in San Jose, Costa Rica — Coca-Cola Bus Terminal Pickpocket & Luggage-Theft at the Zona Roja Edge (pickpocket, severity: high). Every Western government advisory flags one zone of San José specifically: the Coca-Cola bus terminal and the 'zona roja' north of the Mercado Central. Canada's travel advisory (travel.gc.ca, 2025): 'Specific trouble spots include downtown San José areas near the Coca-Cola bus terminal, central market, and public parks.' Australia's Smartraveller: 'petty crime is common near the central bus terminal in the Coca Cola… most likely on weekends.' The zone is dense, unlit, and the hub for nearly every long-distance bus (Tracopa SJO→Jacó/Quepos; Alfaro SJO→Montezuma; MEPE SJO→Puerto Viejo; Empresarios Unidos SJO→Puntarenas). Pickpocket and luggage-lift crews work in 2–4-person cells — classic pattern: one person collides at the bus doorway, another lifts your daypack from the overhead rack, a third melts into the crowd. A canonical Tracopa-bus case, documented in a March 2024 community thread, describes how thieves planted as passengers wait for a rest stop, strip the bus of laptops/phones/passports from overhead bins, and vanish into a waiting car; one female passenger lost her laptop. A commenter's concise rule is 'take anything and everything with you if you want it when you return.' An October 2024 community thread collects the urban variants: 'Watch out for motorcyclists who can drive by and snatch a phone from your hand, or a necklace from your neck.' Another community thread warns: 'Plaza de la Cultura is safe during DAYLIGHT — pickpockets work the crowd.' Adjacent 'helpful stranger' scams: 'bird poop' on your shirt (sprayed by accomplice) + tissue + wallet lift; 'money on the ground' + two strangers claim it + your wallet vanishes during mediation.

For travelers 2025/2026: (1) AVOID Coca-Cola if possible — use Interbus (interbusonline.com) or Gray Line private shuttles ($49–$65 pp door-to-door, no terminal); (2) if using Tracopa/Alfaro/MEPE, arrive 15 minutes max ahead, stay inside the ticket office with bags on your lap, never accept 'help' with luggage from anyone not in company uniform; (3) SKIP Mercado Central and zona roja blocks north of Hotel Del Rey after dark; (4) on long-distance buses, never leave valuables in the overhead rack at a rest stop — daypack WITH you every time; (5) money belt for passport + 80% cash; decoy wallet in front pocket with expired card + ₡5,000; (6) phone on wrist-strap or zipped crossbody (Pacsafe); motorcycle-grab-from-stoplight is documented; (7) report at the Tourist Police Operations Center (San José hub opened 2025, English line) or OIJ 800-8000-645 within 24h. How to avoid: Skip Coca-Cola: book Interbus/Gray Line private shuttle ($49–$65 pp, door-to-door). Never leave valuables in overhead bin during bus rest stops — carry daypack every time. Money belt under clothing for passport + 80% cash; decoy wallet in front pocket. Avoid Mercado Central / zona roja after dark; daylight only, nothing valuable in pockets. Tourist Police 24/7 hub (2025) + OIJ 800-8000-645 within 24h for insurance claim.

Scam alert in San Jose, Costa Rica — Parque Central / Avenida 2 Cambista Currency-Exchange & 'Counterfeit Bill' Swap (financial-fraud, severity: moderate). Costa Rica has official casas de cambio and banks with BCCR (Banco Central de Costa Rica) rates ~₡515–₡530 per USD through 2025/2026 (~2% buy/sell spread). In Parque Central, Avenida 2 pedestrian strip, and around Plaza de la Cultura, informal cambistas (money-changers) approach tourists with whispered 'cambio, cambio?' and a fan of colones. Three scams run. First, the rate gouge — the quoted rate is 10–20% below market (₡450 per USD) and the cambista talks fast to close before the tourist pulls out xe.com. Second, the counterfeit-bill swap — the cambista takes your $100 USD, fans out ₡50,000 in real colones, palms one ₡20,000 out during the count and replaces it with a crisp counterfeit that feels plastic-smooth. A 2024 community report documents 'two dudes tried to scam me in San José' with a 'cambio del falso premio de lotería y otros timos callejeros' — the classic fake-lottery-prize + money-switch combo. Third, the snatch-and-run — the cambista 'counts,' feigns a mistake, asks for the dollars back, hands them to an accomplice instead of the tourist, and both vanish. Tico Times 'Costa Rica Expat Living: My Encounter with Money Changers' (June 2023) describes the pattern explicitly. A 2025 community traveler advises: 'pay in colones (and beware of the "this bill is counterfeit" scam)' — drivers claim the ₡20,000 you handed is fake, pocket yours, hand back a prepared counterfeit, demand replacement. Another 2024 community traveler: 'Biggest scam is exchanging your money at the airport. The conversion rate is terrible. Just go to a major bank.' BCCR ATMs and Banco Nacional / BAC / Scotiabank / BCR branches post rates within 1% of market.

For travelers in 2025/2026: (1) NEVER change money on the street — every whispered 'cambio' approach is a scam; (2) change at a bank branch with your passport, or withdraw colones from an in-branch ATM at a 1% spread; (3) pay shops, restaurants, taxis in COLONES not USD — removes the 'rounding' gouge; (4) check every ₡20,000 note: Carlos Luis Fallas watermark, a color-shifting security thread that flips green/blue when tilted, raised-print feel — counterfeits are smooth, lack the thread, don't flip colors; (5) if a cambista or driver claims your ₡20,000 is 'fake,' refuse to take it back and demand YOUR ORIGINAL visible in their hand — photograph it and call 911; the swap IS the scam; (6) use a no-FTF credit card (Capital One Venture, Chase Sapphire, Amex Platinum) for hotel + restaurants; colones cash only for taxis, tips, vendors; (7) BCCR ATM foreign-card limit ₡400,000/day (~$770); keep 3+ days of cash; (8) report at the San José Tourist Police Operations Center (2025) or OIJ 800-8000-645. How to avoid: Never change money on the street — only bank branches or in-branch ATMs. Check ₡20,000 for Carlos Luis Fallas watermark + color-shift security thread. Refuse 'your bill is counterfeit' swap — keep YOUR original note visible + photograph it. Pay shops/taxis in COLONES (not USD) — removes the rounding-up gouge. Credit card (no-FTF Capital One/Chase/Amex) for hotels/restaurants; report at OIJ 800-8000-645.

Scam alert in San Juan, United States — Old San Juan '$500 Parking Ticket' & Street-Parking Scam (nightlife, severity: moderate). Old San Juan has complex parking rules — metered street spaces require quarters or the ParkMobile app, many blocks are residential-only with two-hour tourist restrictions, and some 'parking attendants' in reflective vests are unauthorized individuals demanding $10–$20 'parking fee' for free or metered spaces (then the car gets a legitimate ticket anyway). One traveler reported a $500 ticket accumulated via a combination of expired meter + residential-zone violation + towing fee. Scam variants: (1) unauthorized 'parking attendant' demanding cash for free street space; (2) 'private parking lot' signs pointing to unmarked residential driveways that tow within 1 hour; (3) meter expired for just 10 minutes → $50–$100 ticket + same-day tow at $300+; (4) online parking-ticket 'payment portal' fake websites after seeing a ticket on your windshield. For older travelers visiting Old San Juan, the clean playbook: (1) park ONLY at official Paseo Covadonga lot ($8/day) or Doña Fela lot ($5/day) — avoid street parking entirely; (2) if a 'parking attendant' in reflective vest demands cash for a street space, refuse and find official parking; (3) download ParkMobile for any metered spaces; (4) read all signs carefully — residential-only zones tow within 1 hour; (5) if you get a ticket, pay ONLY via sanjuan.pr.gov or in person at the Municipal Court — NOT via websites linked from the ticket (fake); (6) better: Uber or taxi into Old San Juan from your hotel ($8–$15) — skip parking entirely. How to avoid: Park ONLY at Paseo Covadonga ($8/day) or Doña Fela ($5/day) official lots Refuse unauthorized 'parking attendants' demanding cash Download ParkMobile for metered spaces Pay tickets ONLY via sanjuan.pr.gov or Municipal Court in person Better: Uber or taxi into Old San Juan ($8–$15) — skip parking

Scam alert in San Juan, United States — San Juan (SJU) Airport Taxi & Rideshare Overcharge (transport, severity: moderate). SJU is 7 miles from Old San Juan and 12 miles from Condado/Isla Verde resorts. Puerto Rico has REGULATED airport taxi flat rates ('tarifa autorizada'): Old San Juan $21, Condado $19, Isla Verde $14–$17, Miramar $21 per trip (not per person; up to 5 passengers). These rates are posted at the airport taxi stand — a driver quoting higher is scamming. Uber IS legal at SJU and runs $12–$20 to most destinations — pickup at Zone E (ground transportation curb). Scam variants: (1) driver at baggage claim offering 'flat $45' to Old San Juan (regulated rate is $21); (2) driver insisting Uber 'not allowed' at SJU (it is); (3) 'luggage fee' or 'night rate' added beyond flat rate (flat rate is flat — no add-ons); (4) driver demanding cash tip beyond flat rate. For older travelers arriving at SJU, the clean playbook: (1) go to the official Autoridad de Transporte Público (ATP) tourist taxi stand — look for the white kiosk with posted flat rates; (2) pay the posted flat rate exactly — Old San Juan $21, Condado $19, Isla Verde $14–$17, Miramar $21 (plus standard $1–$3 luggage tip); (3) Uber at Zone E rideshare pickup is a legal alternative, often cheaper ($12–$20 to most destinations); (4) refuse any driver quoting higher than posted flat rate — next driver at the queue will honor posted rates; (5) print or screenshot the flat-rate chart from prtc.pr.gov before arrival; (6) do NOT tip beyond flat rate if driver adds 'luggage fee' or 'night rate' — report to ATP (787-756-1919). How to avoid: Use official ATP tourist taxi stand with posted flat rates Flat rates: Old San Juan $21, Condado $19, Isla Verde $14–$17, Miramar $21 Uber at Zone E rideshare pickup is legal ($12–$20 most destinations) Refuse drivers quoting above posted flat rate — take next queued driver Print flat-rate chart from prtc.pr.gov before arrival

Scam alert in San Juan, United States — San Juan Airbnb Off-Platform Booking & 'PR Robbery' Pattern (nightlife, severity: high). How to avoid: Book ONLY through Airbnb, VRBO, or Booking.com platform payment NEVER pay via Zelle, Venmo, Cash App, or wire transfer Consider hotels for security: Caribe Hilton, La Concha, Fairmont El San Juan, El Convento Change lockbox code on arrival if possible; photograph valuables at check-in For concerts/festivals, book 6+ months ahead — not last-minute social media

Scam alert in San Juan, United States — Condado / Isla Verde Timeshare Presentation Hustle (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Condado and Isla Verde host major timeshare-sales operations targeting cruise passengers, resort guests, and older retirees. Promoters in hotel lobbies or cruise-pier areas offer 'free San Juan tour,' '$150 dinner voucher,' or 'free catamaran sail' in exchange for a '90-minute presentation.' The presentation runs 3–5 hours with aggressive pushing of $15,000–$60,000 'vacation ownership' or 'travel club' purchases. Scam variants: (1) cruise-pier 'photo booth' promoters offering 'free Puerto Rico tour' that's a timeshare pitch; (2) Condado hotel-lobby 'concierge' promoters in plainclothes who are actually timeshare sales staff; (3) 'Vacation Club' membership at $10,000–$25,000 with opaque annual fees; (4) 'exit' companies at $5,000–$15,000 upfront to 'cancel existing timeshare' — many are themselves scams. Cross-reference with Charleston, Scottsdale, Branson timeshare patterns. For older travelers in San Juan, the defensive posture: (1) NEVER accept 'free gift' offers in cruise-pier areas, Condado hotel lobbies, or Isla Verde resorts — the time cost makes it net negative even with the gift; (2) if you do attend, bring a printed 'I will not sign anything today' rule and STICK TO IT; (3) Puerto Rico offers a 7-day right of rescission for timeshare contracts under the Timeshare Real Estate Law — cancel within 7 days by certified mail; (4) for rescission help, contact PR Department of Consumer Affairs (DACO, 787-722-7555); (5) AVOID 'exit' companies charging $5,000+ upfront — use DACO directly; (6) report timeshare high-pressure tactics to DACO and to the BBB. How to avoid: Refuse ALL 'free gift' offers from cruise-pier / hotel-lobby promoters If attending, bring 'I will not sign anything today' rule and stick to it Use PR 7-day right of rescission (DACO, 787-722-7555) Avoid 'exit' companies charging $5,000+ — use DACO directly Report to DACO and BBB
