Scam variants: (1) phone callers claiming to represent 'Cardinals ticket office' offering 'discount season tickets' (Cardinals do NOT cold-call); (2) StubHub / SeatGeek listings at 40–60% off face value that are actually transferred-revoked Ticketmaster tickets; (3) Busch Stadium perimeter scalpers selling 'skip-the-line' tickets that are actually already-scanned; (4) 'VIP stadium tour' at $150+ per person when Cardinals' own tour is $20; (5) 'Frozen Four' or 'Blues playoff' tickets at $300–$800 resale for face-value $50–$150 Cardinals games (price gouging during special events per community reports); (6) fake 'corporate box package' sold via LinkedIn or email at $500+ per person. For older travelers attending Cardinals games, the clean playbook: (1) buy Cardinals tickets ONLY at cardinals.com/tickets (primary) or verified secondary markets (Ticketmaster, official StubHub integration with Cardinals); (2) HANG UP on anyone claiming to be 'Cardinals ticket office' offering 'discount season tickets' — Cardinals do NOT cold-call per community reports; (3) for Busch Stadium tours, book direct at cardinals.com ($20 adult standard tour, $30 all-access) — skip 'VIP stadium tour' scalpers at $150+; (4) AVOID Busch perimeter scalpers selling paper tickets — modern Cardinals tickets are mobile-only, paper is a red flag; (5) for special events (Frozen Four, Blues playoffs, World Series), book 3+ months ahead — last-minute resale at $300+ over face is price gouging; (6) pay by credit card for chargeback leverage; (7) verify ticket authenticity via Ticketmaster 'Verified Fan' or Cardinals' 'MLB Ballpark' app at point of sale. How to avoid: Buy Cardinals tickets ONLY at cardinals.com/tickets or verified Ticketmaster HANG UP on 'Cardinals ticket office' cold-callers — they don't exist Book Busch Stadium tour direct at cardinals.com: $20 adult Avoid paper tickets — Cardinals are mobile-only Special events: book 3+ months ahead; pay by credit card

Scam alert in St. Louis, United States — Gateway Arch & Downtown St. Louis Tour Package Upsell (tourist-trap, severity: minor). Gateway Arch National Park is operated by the US National Park Service — legitimate pricing: Journey to the Top (tram ride to Arch observation area) $15 adult (gatewayarch.com); Documentary $7; Museum (FREE). Community reports document tourist perception of the Arch's small scale. Scam variants: (1) third-party 'Gateway Arch ticket' resellers charging $30–$60 for the $15 direct ticket; (2) hotel-concierge 'Arch VIP tour package' at $150+ per person that's identical to $15 direct; (3) 'Arch + Budweiser Brewery + City Museum combo' at $200+ per person (actual direct total: $15 + $25 Budweiser tour + $16 City Museum = $56); (4) 'downtown St. Louis walking tour' at $75+ per person for what's covered by the free St. Louis Visitor Center self-guided pamphlet; (5) 'Gateway Arch helicopter tour' offers (Arch helicopter tours exist but at $200–$300 direct, not $450+ via resellers); (6) 'Riverfront cruise' at $80+ per person when Gateway Arch Riverboats direct is $30. For older travelers visiting downtown St. Louis, the clean playbook: (1) book Gateway Arch Journey to the Top ONLY at gatewayarch.com or at the ticket kiosk: $15 adult, includes museum; (2) reserve 2–3 weeks ahead in peak season (July 4, Memorial Day, Labor Day) — tram capacity is limited and peak days sell out; (3) Budweiser Brewery Tour ($25 at budweisertours.com) is direct; (4) City Museum ($16 at citymuseum.org) is direct; (5) Gateway Arch Riverboats direct at gatewayarch.com: $30 sightseeing cruise, $60 dinner cruise; (6) AVOID third-party 'Arch ticket' resellers, hotel-concierge 'VIP package' upsells, and 'downtown walking tour' resellers; (7) for older travelers, the Arch has wheelchair-accessible entry to the Museum (FREE) and tram pods are 4-person small spaces that some find claustrophobic — consider the Arch exterior + Museum only if that's a concern. How to avoid: Book Arch Journey to the Top ONLY at gatewayarch.com: $15 adult Budweiser Tour ($25) + City Museum ($16) direct Gateway Arch Riverboats: $30 direct sightseeing cruise Avoid 'downtown walking tour' resellers — St. Louis Visitor Center has free self-guided info Reserve 2–3 weeks ahead for July 4, Memorial Day, Labor Day

Scam alert in St. Louis, United States — St. Louis Downtown Panhandling & Aggressive Solicitation (nightlife, severity: moderate). Community reports document persistent downtown St. Louis panhandling and soliciting patterns in 2025: (1) 'need gas money' sob-story panhandlers demanding $5–$20 cash; (2) 'dropped wallet' scam paired with theft accusation; (3) 'security guard' impersonators demanding 'parking fee' at Gateway Arch perimeter (no legitimate attendants); (4) 'free sample' vendors at Delmar Loop then demanding payment; (5) 'broken down car' scam with fake spouse/kid asking for 'gas money $20'; (6) 'gold chain' offers (like Memphis/Asheville) with plated-zinc at $40–$100. St. Louis downtown has areas that warrant caution — walk with awareness, especially after dark. For older travelers in downtown St. Louis, the defensive playbook: (1) say a firm 'no thank you' to all unsolicited approaches and keep walking — do NOT engage in conversation; (2) REFUSE all 'gold chain' or jewelry offers from strangers — <$5 material value; (3) if accused of 'taking a wallet,' walk toward visible St. Louis PD patrol (Gateway Arch and Market Street have patrol) — do NOT hand anything over; (4) AVOID 'broken down car with gas money' scam — call 911 if you want to help; do not give cash; (5) 'security guard' at Gateway Arch perimeter demanding 'parking fee' is a SCAM — all Arch parking is in official Arch Garage or Stadium East Garage; (6) for authentic Delmar Loop 'Loop Trolley' experience, tickets $2 at loop-trolley.com; refuse street-vendor 'tour packages'; (7) St. Louis PD non-emergency: 314-231-1212; walk in pairs after dark in Laclede's Landing and Washington Ave areas; (8) community reports also warn about specific events with repeat safety concerns. How to avoid: Firm 'no thank you' + keep walking — no engagement Refuse 'gold chain' offers — <$5 material value If accused of 'taking wallet,' walk toward visible STL PD patrol For 'broken down car' appeals, call 911 — don't give cash Arch parking: Arch Garage or Stadium East Garage only (official)

Scam alert in St. Louis, United States — St. Louis Hotel & STR Off-Platform Booking Fraud (nightlife, severity: moderate). How to avoid: Book STRs ONLY via Airbnb/VRBO/Booking.com platform payment Verified hotels: Four Seasons, Chase Park Plaza, Marriott Grand, Hilton Ballpark, Union Station Add resort + parking fees to headline hotel rate when comparing Cardinals playoffs + SEC Championship + Frozen Four: book 3+ months ahead Dispute cleaning fees above $150 on 2-night stays via platform/credit card

Scam alert in Saint-Tropez, France — Restaurant Racketeering & Minimum Spend (tourist-trap, severity: high). Saint-Tropez restaurants have developed sophisticated systems to extract maximum spending from tourists. Restaurants compile secret databases tracking how much each diner spends and tips. If you don’t spend or tip enough, you’ll be blacklisted and refused a table on your next visit. Some establishments demand €5,000 minimum spending or €1,500 per head just to secure a reservation. Despite service charges already being included, staff aggressively pressure tourists for additional ‘American-style’ tips. In one notorious incident, a waiter chased an Italian customer into the parking lot demanding he return inside to add another €500 to his already €500 tip. The mayor of Saint-Tropez has publicly condemned these practices as ‘racketeering.’ How to avoid: Research restaurant policies and reviews before booking. Ask explicitly about minimum spending requirements upfront. Remember that service charge is already included in France. Choose smaller local establishments over famous beach clubs.

Scam alert in Saint-Tropez, France — Luxury Watch Theft (robbery, severity: high). Organized crews systematically target tourists wearing watches worth €100,000 and up. The operation is disciplined: spotters identify valuable timepieces on beach terraces and at the port, then signal to thieves who either slip the watch off during a staged jostle or yank it off the wrist before escaping on mopeds with tampered plates. Three separate incidents in Saint-Tropez resulted in €400,000 worth of stolen watches in a single weekend. The thefts have grown more brazen, and some have turned violent. How to avoid: Leave valuable watches worth over €5,000 at home. If wearing expensive watches, keep them covered. Stay aware of your surroundings, especially near beach areas. Report suspicious behavior to police immediately.

Scam alert in Saint-Tropez, France — Villa Rental Fraud (online-fraud, severity: high). Scammers post attractive listings for luxury villas they do not own, using professional photos stolen from real properties and prices that sit just below the market to hook quick bookings. You wire a deposit, get back a fake Airbnb-style confirmation, and only discover the property doesn’t exist — or has already been rented to someone else — when you land. The fraudulent accounts close as soon as the money clears. How to avoid: Book through established local concierge services or established rental agencies, never direct via a stranger. Reverse-image-search every listing photo before paying a deposit. Do not wire transfer — use a credit card so you can dispute. If the price seems too good for the Riviera in July, it is.

Scam alert in Saint-Tropez, France — Hotel Room Burglary (theft, severity: high). Professional burglars target luxury hotel rooms, particularly those with terrace access. In one case, two British women lost nearly €1 million in valuables — including 11 Hermès Birkin bags, Patek Philippe watches, and Cartier jewelry — after their five-star hotel room was ransacked within hours of check-in. The thieves came in through the private terrace door and ripped the safe out of the wall. A hotel employee was questioned afterward, suggesting inside involvement. How to avoid: Don’t bring valuables worth more than €5,000. Request upper floor rooms without easy exterior access. Keep valuable items with you when possible. Consider travel insurance that covers theft.

Scam alert in Saint-Tropez, France — Gas Burglary (Villa Gassing) (burglary, severity: high). Criminals allegedly pump anesthetic gas through air conditioning vents or windows to sedate sleeping occupants before robbing them. Notable victims include F1 driver Jenson Button and TV presenter Richard Hammond. Police estimate 90% of villa raids go unreported. However, medical experts dispute whether such ‘knock-out gas’ actually exists as described. How to avoid: Choose upper floor accommodations. Lock all windows and terrace doors. Don’t sleep with windows open. Consider portable door alarms.

Scam alert in Saint-Tropez, France — Beach Club Overcharging (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Beach clubs employ questionable practices. Sun loungers cost €35-50 each, and famous clubs like Nikki Beach require €1,500 minimum spend on weekends during high season. Despite websites stating prices include service charges, staff express dissatisfaction with tip amounts. To get weekend reservations at exclusive clubs like Club 55, guests may need to ‘tip’ waiters in advance. How to avoid: Research prices and minimum spend requirements before visiting. Ask for prices upfront before ordering. Remember service charge is already included. Consider less famous beach clubs.

Scam alert in Saint-Tropez, France — Boat/Yacht Rental Hidden Fees (overcharging, severity: moderate). Boat rental companies advertise attractive daily rates, then stack hidden costs on top: fuel (Saint-Tropez diesel prices run noticeably higher than other ports), delivery and redelivery fees, mooring fees, and water-sports equipment charges. Captain fees vary wildly — the standard rate is €350, but some operators quote €500 or more without justification. Expect unexpected line items for ‘gourmet lunch’ or compulsory insurance add-ons at settlement. How to avoid: Get complete all-inclusive pricing in writing before booking. Compare total costs including fuel across companies. Ask specifically about all potential additional charges.

Scam alert in Saint-Tropez, France — Pickpocketing & Distraction Theft (pickpocket, severity: moderate). Professional pickpockets operate in crowded tourist areas during summer. Organized gangs use distraction techniques—one member causes a commotion while others target your valuables. Some teams use the ‘petition/clipboard approach.’ Scooter thieves may grab bags or phones from pedestrians. The Tuesday and Saturday markets at Place des Lices are particularly high-risk. How to avoid: Keep bags zipped and in front of you. Don’t carry bags on your street-side shoulder. Use money belts or hidden pouches. Be extra vigilant in crowded market areas.

Scam alert in Saint-Tropez, France — Taxi Overcharging (transport, severity: moderate). Unlicensed and some licensed taxi drivers target tourists with inflated fares. Common tactics include claiming the meter is broken, taking long routes, or forcing cash payment. Airport transfers from Nice to Saint-Tropez legitimately cost €240-275 (day) or €265-285 (night), but scammers may quote much higher. How to avoid: Use only official taxis from designated stands. Research standard fares before arrival. Use ride-sharing apps like Uber for tracked journeys. Pre-book airport transfers through hotels.

Scam alert in Saint-Tropez, France — Jet Ski Rental Damage Scam (fraud, severity: moderate). Some jet ski rental operators run a damage-claim scam on returning customers. After you hand back the jet ski, they point to a scratch or crack they claim you caused and demand hundreds of euros for repairs, sometimes with physical intimidation. Refuse to pay, and they threaten to involve police — where mythical ‘administrative charges’ push the demand even higher. How to avoid: Photograph and video the jet ski from every angle before you push off, with visible date and time stamps in the shots. Keep those files safe. Never surrender your passport as collateral. Read recent reviews of the operator before booking — the scam operators have reputations.

Scam alert in Saint-Tropez, France — Contactless Card Skimming (financial-fraud, severity: moderate). Thieves use digital skimming devices to steal money from contactless-enabled cards without physical contact. They carry concealed readers that capture card information when held close to your wallet or purse in crowded areas, allowing fraudulent purchases or card cloning. How to avoid: Use RFID-blocking wallets or card sleeves. Keep cards in front pockets or secure inner pockets. Regularly monitor card statements for unauthorized charges. Set up transaction alerts on your banking app.

Scam alert in Saint-Tropez, France — Fake Charity Petitions (pickpocket, severity: low). Scammers approach tourists with clipboards asking them to sign petitions for fake charities. While you’re distracted reading and signing, an accomplice targets your bag or pockets. Even if no theft occurs, you may be pressured to donate money to a non-existent cause. How to avoid: Politely refuse and keep walking. Never stop to engage with clipboard wielders. Keep your belongings secure if you do stop.

Scam alert in Stonehenge, United Kingdom — London Coach-Tour 'Stonehenge + Bath + Windsor' Combo Package Fraud (tourist-trap, severity: high). The single most-booked UK coach-tour product for older US/Canadian travelers is the London-to-Stonehenge-to-Bath-to-Windsor day-trip, sold via Viator, GetYourGuide, TripAdvisor Experiences, Golden Tours, and Evan Evans at £99–£145 per person. For older travelers with Stonehenge, Bath, or Windsor on their London day-trip shortlist: (1) pick ONE destination per day — don't try to combine three in one day; (2) for Stonehenge specifically: take the direct train from London Waterloo to Salisbury (90 min, £25-£45 off-peak), then the Stonehenge Tour Bus (£17 round-trip from Salisbury Station, 20-30 min journey, admission extra at £23 direct at english-heritage.org.uk) — total £65-£85 per person, 6 hours door-to-door, 2+ hours AT Stonehenge; (3) for Bath, direct train from London Paddington (90 min, £25-£65 off-peak); (4) for Windsor, direct train from London Waterloo (55 min, £11-£15); (5) if you MUST do a combo day-tour, use Rabbie's Tours (Edinburgh-based, higher-quality coach operators, £95-£110) or Evan Evans 'Stonehenge Only' trip — confirm your tour lists Stone Circle Inner Access (£80+) if you want to walk among the stones, otherwise you're just paying for exterior viewing; (6) refuse any 'shopping stop' over 20 min; (7) for coach-tour refunds, TripAdvisor Experiences / Viator standard policy is 24-hour cancellation — insist on this, decline 'non-refundable' bookings; (8) for older travelers with mobility concerns, a dedicated Stonehenge day with the Tour Bus is far less physically taxing than the 3-city 10-hour coach marathon. How to avoid: Pick ONE destination per day — Stonehenge via Salisbury train (90 min, £25-£45) + Tour Bus (£17) For Inner Circle Access: book at english-heritage.org.uk 2-3 months ahead (£80-£110) If you must book a combo tour, use Rabbie's Tours or Evan Evans 'Stonehenge Only' — not 3-city combos Refuse any 'shopping stop' over 20 min — insist on skipping or wait in the coach Confirm 24-hr refund window before booking — refuse 'non-refundable' deals via Viator/GetYourGuide

Scam alert in Stonehenge, United Kingdom — Stone Circle Inner Access Third-Party Reseller Markup (nightlife, severity: moderate). The Stone Circle Inner Access experience — English Heritage's ticketed early-morning or evening session that lets 30 people walk AMONG the standing stones (vs the normal audio-guide loop that stops at 10m distance) — is the premier Stonehenge experience. Official pricing is £80-£110 per person direct at english-heritage.org.uk, booked 2-3 months ahead for summer. This is part of a cross-attraction reseller inflation pattern where third-party platforms mark up tickets two to three times the official price. The specific mechanics affecting older travelers: (1) Stone Circle Access tickets release in waves — about 12 months, 6 months, and then monthly ahead of each season; summer weekends fill within hours of release; (2) third-party resellers buy up tickets in bulk using multiple accounts, then resell at 2-3x with bundled transport; (3) the bundled 'luxury private tour from London' is priced at £279-£450 per person but the actual Stone Circle Access ticket is the same £80-£110 value — you're paying £200-£350 for the car + driver + 'private guide' who is often a freelance unlicensed operator; (4) some resellers advertise 'guaranteed Stone Circle Access' for specific dates when tickets are already sold out — these deliver either refused entry at the site or a wait list; (5) the Stonehenge Visitor Centre staff confirm only official English Heritage QR codes and identity — resellers' 'voucher' tickets require name-match on the booking; (6) older travelers often pre-book from North America months ahead, then arrive to find their third-party 'voucher' doesn't work at the gate; (7) the legitimate alternative for small-group Inner Access: English Heritage members get priority booking access AND a 15% discount — membership is £78/year (£134 joint) and pays for itself if you visit 3+ English Heritage sites during a UK trip. For older travelers wanting Stone Circle Inner Access: (1) book DIRECTLY at english-heritage.org.uk — no reseller, no aggregator, no 'luxury tour company'; (2) monitor the English Heritage release calendar — tickets for April-September typically release in December-January, September-March tickets in July-August; (3) summer weekend slots sell out within hours — have the website open at release time and book immediately; (4) consider becoming an English Heritage Member (£78/year individual, £134 joint) for priority-release access and 15% discounts across 400+ UK historic sites — excellent value if you're planning UK trips for 2+ years; (5) for transport, book the direct train London Waterloo to Salisbury (90 min, £25-£45 off-peak) + Stonehenge Tour Bus (£17 round-trip, 20-30 min journey) — total £65-£85 per person for transport; (6) refuse ALL 'private luxury Stonehenge tour' offers at £279-£450 — these are transport bundles around the £80-£110 you could book directly; (7) for older travelers who want a private driver, Crown Coaches (licensed) offers Salisbury-based private driver at £180-£280 per half-day that will pick you up and return you with flexibility — still better value than aggregator 'VIP tours'; (8) at the Visitor Centre, bring the original English Heritage QR code AND ID matching the booking name — resellers' 'vouchers' are often refused entry; (9) if a reseller site fails to deliver access, dispute via UK Section 75 Consumer Credit Act (credit cards, min £100) or Visa/MC chargeback. How to avoid: Book DIRECTLY at english-heritage.org.uk — no reseller, no aggregator, no 'luxury tour' Consider English Heritage Membership (£78/year) for priority-release access + 15% discounts Monitor the release calendar — summer slots release Dec-Jan, winter slots release Jul-Aug For transport: London Waterloo → Salisbury train (£25-45) + Stonehenge Tour Bus (£17) = £65-85 total Refuse 'private luxury Stonehenge tour' at £279-£450 — you're paying £200+ markup on £80-110 access

How to avoid: Book Tour Bus at thestonehengetour.info or walk-up at Salisbury Station ticket desk — £17 round-trip Legitimate combo Tour Bus + Stonehenge admission is £35-£38 — refuse reseller quotes above For Salisbury Station taxi, use Allthesevens (+44-1722-333-777, licensed) — NO Uber in Salisbury Refuse 'priority boarding' premium offers — Tour Bus seats on first-come basis For London-Salisbury train, book at gwr.com (90 min, £25-45 off-peak, UK Senior Railcard saves 34%)

Scam alert in Stonehenge, United Kingdom — Summer & Winter Solstice Over-Pricing & 'Free Entry' Confusion (nightlife, severity: minor). English Heritage runs two major Solstice events per year at Stonehenge — the Summer Solstice (around 21 June) and Winter Solstice (around 21 December) — during which the stones are open for 'Managed Open Access' allowing thousands of visitors (~8,000 at Summer Solstice) to walk among the stones at sunrise. These events are FREE to attend — the only legitimate cost is £15-£25 for parking (pre-booked via the National Trust car park) and transport to Amesbury. The free-entry nature creates confusion that third-party operators exploit by selling 'Solstice Experience' packages at £89-£249 per person. Community reports document the free-entry nature, parking logistics, and the reseller overpricing pattern. The specific mechanics affecting older travelers: (1) Solstice attendance is FREE but parking must be pre-booked via english-heritage.org.uk (£15-£25) — this is the ONLY legitimate charge; (2) third-party operators sell 'Solstice Experience' tickets at £89-£249 claiming 'exclusive access' that doesn't exist (all Solstice access is free, first-come); (3) some tour operators bundle 'Solstice transport from London' at £149-£299 per person with the free-admission Solstice access presented as 'included' — the £150-£250 markup is for the coach transport; (4) unofficial 'Solstice camping' sites near Amesbury charge £75-£149 per night for tent pitches that are normally free or £10-£20 at local campsites; (5) Solstice Weekend is NOT the same as Solstice Day — resellers sometimes sell 'Solstice Weekend Access' for a 3-day window that has no basis in actual event logistics; (6) Winter Solstice (21 December) has a smaller crowd (typically 1,000-2,000 attendees) and easier parking but same £15-£25 parking fee structure; (7) older travelers are particularly vulnerable because Summer Solstice starts at sunrise (around 4:45 AM) and requires overnight presence — scammers exploit this by selling 'Solstice hotel + access' packages at £299-£499 that bundle any Salisbury hotel at 2-3x markup; (8) English Heritage partners with Stonehenge Alliance for sacred druid/pagan ceremony access — these are free-access events within the main Solstice timeframe. For older travelers interested in Summer or Winter Solstice at Stonehenge: (1) attendance is FREE — do not pay for 'access' or 'Solstice ticket' from any reseller; (2) book parking ONLY at english-heritage.org.uk (£15-£25) 4-6 weeks ahead of the event; (3) for Summer Solstice, the stones open at sunset before Solstice Day (20 June) through sunrise on 21 June — plan for overnight; (4) shuttle buses run from various Amesbury and Salisbury points to the Visitor Centre during the event — check the English Heritage site for the current year's transport; (5) for Salisbury hotels during Solstice, book directly (The Red Lion, Mercure White Hart, Cathedral Hotel) 3-6 months ahead — rates genuinely rise but not to the £299-£499 'Solstice package' levels resellers charge; (6) for Winter Solstice (21 December), a much quieter and less crowded experience — book parking 2-3 weeks ahead; (7) if you just want to SEE sunrise at the stones without the crowds, Stone Circle Inner Access (£80-£110, different English Heritage product) gives 30-person private access year-round; (8) refuse ALL 'Solstice VIP' or 'Druid Ceremony Access' tours that claim restrictions — these ceremonies are open to anyone attending the free Solstice event; (9) for older travelers uncomfortable with the dawn-start crowds, Winter Solstice (noon arrival, sunset at 4 PM) is more manageable than Summer Solstice. How to avoid: Solstice attendance is FREE — do not pay for 'access' or 'Solstice ticket' from any reseller Book parking ONLY at english-heritage.org.uk (£15-£25) 4-6 weeks ahead of the event For Salisbury hotels, book directly (The Red Lion, Mercure White Hart, Cathedral Hotel) 3-6 months ahead For year-round dawn-access experience, book Stone Circle Inner Access at £80-£110 (30-person private) Winter Solstice (21 Dec) is a much quieter alternative — Summer (21 June) requires 3 AM arrival

For older travelers arriving at Salisbury Railway Station: (1) exit the station, walk to the licensed Hackney Carriage rank on South Western Road — these are metered and safe; (2) refuse EVERY 'taxi to Stonehenge?' offer from anyone inside the station concourse — these are unlicensed, unregulated, and quote 2-3x legitimate fares; (3) for pre-booked taxi to Stonehenge or city center, call Allthesevens Taxis (+44-1722-333-777) — the only licensed Salisbury operator per community reports; (4) for the Stonehenge trip, STRONGLY consider the Stonehenge Tour Bus (£17 round-trip from Salisbury Station, every 30 min) instead of a taxi — it's the cheapest, most scam-proof, and community-recommended option; (5) metered Salisbury Station to Salisbury Cathedral is £6-£10; Salisbury Station to Stonehenge is £30-£45 one-way — refuse quotes above; (6) Uber, Bolt, and FreeNow do NOT operate in Salisbury — any 'Uber' pitch is a scam; (7) Salisbury is small — Salisbury Cathedral is 10 minutes walk from the Station on flat paths and is community-recommended for older travelers who are comfortable walking; (8) report unlicensed taxi-touts at Salisbury Station to Wiltshire Police non-emergency 101 and Wiltshire Council Licensing at +44-1225-713-000. How to avoid: Exit Salisbury Station, walk to licensed Hackney Carriage rank on South Western Road — metered and safe For pre-booked taxi, call Allthesevens Taxis (+44-1722-333-777, the only licensed Salisbury operator) For Stonehenge, use the Tour Bus (£17 round-trip from Salisbury Station, every 30 min) — cheapest and safest Salisbury Cathedral is 10 min walk from Station on flat paths — walk if mobility permits NO Uber/Bolt/FreeNow in Salisbury — any such pitch is a scam

Scam alert in Strasbourg, France — Petition/Deaf Charity Clipboard Scam (pickpocket, severity: high). Teams of scammers approach tourists with clipboards asking if they speak English, then request signatures for a fake ‘deaf charity’ petition. While you’re distracted reading or signing, accomplices pickpocket your bags or pockets. After signing, they demand a donation, pointing to text claiming you agreed to donate. The petition is always in English (a red flag in France) and they use exaggerated sign language to appear hearing-impaired. How to avoid: Never stop for clipboard petitioners. Say ‘Non’ firmly and keep walking. Never sign anything on the street. Keep hands on your belongings when approached.

Scam alert in Strasbourg, France — Friendship Bracelet/String Scam (aggressive-selling, severity: moderate). A vendor grabs your hand and begins wrapping colorful string around your wrist before you can refuse. Within seconds, they’ve tied a difficult-to-remove bracelet and demand €10-20 for the ‘gift.’ They become aggressive if you refuse to pay, and may follow you while creating a scene. Sometimes an accomplice uses the distraction to pickpocket you. How to avoid: Keep hands in pockets when walking through tourist areas. Say ‘Non’ firmly and keep walking. Pull your hand away immediately if they try to grab it. Carry small scissors to cut yourself free if necessary.

Scam alert in Strasbourg, France — Gold Ring Scam (street-scam, severity: moderate). A stranger bends down near you and ‘finds’ a gold ring, then asks if you dropped it. When you say no, they examine it and claim it’s marked ’18K gold’ and must be valuable. They offer to sell it for a fraction of its ‘worth’ or ask for a finder’s fee. The ring is worthless brass. While engaging you, an accomplice may be pickpocketing you. How to avoid: Simply say ‘non’ and walk away. Don’t engage in conversation. Be aware of accomplices nearby. Keep hands on belongings.

Scam alert in Strasbourg, France — Tram/Public Transport Pickpocketing (pickpocket, severity: high). Pickpockets work the crowded Strasbourg trams, particularly Lines B and C that serve the tourist corridors. They move during rush hours and at boarding and exiting, when the crush gives them cover. Teams use distraction techniques: one person blocks your path or stages a bump while an accomplice lifts from your bag or pocket, then exits just as the doors close. How to avoid: Keep bags in front with hands on them. Don’t keep valuables in back pockets. Be extra vigilant when boarding and exiting. If bumped, immediately check belongings.

Scam alert in Strasbourg, France — Counterfeit Attraction Tickets (fraud, severity: moderate). The tickets are fake, already used, or for non-existent tours. The seller disappears before you discover the scam. Some pose as official guides offering ‘special access.’ How to avoid: Buy tickets only from official ticket offices. Book tours through established companies. Be suspicious of ‘special deals’ from strangers. Research official prices beforehand.

Scam alert in Strasbourg, France — Christmas Market Pickpocketing (pickpocket, severity: high). Strasbourg’s famous Christmas markets attract over 2 million visitors annually, creating ideal conditions for pickpockets. The dense crowds, distracting lights, and hands occupied with food and drinks make tourists easy targets. Professional teams work the markets, using distraction techniques or simply taking advantage of the chaos. Valuable items disappear from bags, pockets, and even hands. How to avoid: Wear cross-body bags in front. Keep zippers secured and hands on bags. Leave valuables at hotel. Be extra vigilant in crowded market lanes. Visit during less crowded morning hours.

Scam alert in Strasbourg, France — Taxi Meter Manipulation (transport, severity: low). Some taxi drivers target tourists unfamiliar with local fares. Consider using Uber or official taxi apps. Get receipt for any disputes.

Scam alert in Strasbourg, France — Fake Police/Document Check Scam (impersonation, severity: high). Criminals pose as plainclothes police, flash fake badges, and say they need to check your wallet for counterfeit currency or verify your ID for ‘border security.’ While inspecting your wallet or documents, they palm cash. Strasbourg’s proximity to the German border lets them invent authority for ‘cross-border checks’ — but real French police do not inspect tourists’ wallets on the street. How to avoid: Ask to see official ID clearly and note badge number. Insist on going to nearest police station before showing documents. Never hand over your wallet to anyone on the street. Scam alert in Strasbourg, France — Restaurant Menu Overcharging (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Restaurants near the Cathedral and in Petite France run a familiar playbook. Walk a few streets from major monuments for better value.

Scam alert in Strasbourg, France — ATM Skimming (financial-fraud, severity: high). Criminals attach skimming devices to ATMs that capture card data and PINs. Private ATMs like Euronet charge excessive fees and poor exchange rates. Some offer Dynamic Currency Conversion at terrible rates while making it seem like a benefit. Card trap devices may also be used — your card gets stuck and a ‘helpful’ stranger watches you enter your PIN. How to avoid: Use ATMs inside bank branches only. Cover keypad when entering PIN. Wiggle card slot before inserting. Decline dynamic currency conversion. If card gets stuck, don’t leave — call bank immediately.

Scam alert in Strasbourg, France — Bump and Grab/Distraction Theft (pickpocket, severity: high). A well-dressed person ‘accidentally’ bumps into you, spills something on you, or drops items near your feet. While apologizing profusely and helping clean you up or as you helpfully bend down to assist, an accomplice steals from your bag or pockets. Another variation: someone points out a ‘stain’ on your back to distract you. How to avoid: If spilled on, immediately check belongings and move away. Don’t let strangers touch your clothing. Be suspicious of any unusual contact. Keep bags secured in front of you.

Scam alert in Strasbourg, France — Street Vendor Overcharging (overcharging, severity: low). Unlicensed vendors sell cheap souvenirs, ‘artwork,’ or photos at massively inflated prices. Never hand your camera/phone to unsolicited helpers. Know that most legitimate vendors have fixed prices displayed.

How to avoid: Book Shanghai-Suzhou high-speed rail yourself via Trip.com / 12306.cn (¥40) Use Suzhou Metro (Line 2) for intra-city trips (¥3–¥6) DiDi for app-regulated short taxis At Suzhou Station, walk past touts to official rank; 'da biao' expect ¥15–¥30 SKIP hotel-concierge 'Shanghai-to-Suzhou' packages — self-guided ¥250–¥350 per person

Scam alert in Tamarindo, Costa Rica — 'Guachimán' Yellow-Vest Watchmen Parking Extortion on the Tamarindo Strip (impersonation, severity: moderate). A May 2024 community thread (305 upvotes) is the canonical account of the guachimán (Tico slang for 'watchman') racket running every busy hour along Tamarindo's single main strip. One traveler wrote: 'IF YOU TRY TO PARK ANYWHERE IN TOWN AS A GRINGO — you will be harassed by scammers in yellow vests demanding you pay them to watch your car and keep it safe. Others will box you in with multiple vehicles and then demand you pay them to get out.' The same traveler noted the harassment vanished when a native Spanish-speaking Latina was in the car. An April 2025 community post documents the punitive side: a traveler refused, returned to a car windshield 'smeared with something that looks like poop.' Commenters note: 'Most lots will have someone who watches cars, throw them a couple hundred Colones and you're good'; another cuts to it: 'They'll either make sure something doesn't happen or make sure something does.' One local explains: 'Guachimán = Watch man. It's a horrible disease… some are honest, some are plain scammers.' An October 2025 community post documents the golf-cart twist — a traveler didn't tip, returned to find his cart 'gone,' until rental company Easy Ride confirmed another drunk tourist had grabbed the wrong cart on a shared key. Travelers share the trick 'pay IF the car is safe — half the time they aren't there when we return' and note the same operators at Manuel Antonio on every tourist beach.

For travelers in 2025/2026, the defensive playbook: (1) keep a roll of ₡500 and ₡1,000 coins in the cup holder — ₡1,000–₡2,000 (~$2–$4) is the standard accepted tip and avoids escalation; (2) if the crew blocks the road or demands $10+ USD, that's the extortion version — don't hand over cash, roll the window most of the way up and creep forward (they always move, same as the Manuel Antonio Route 618 crews); (3) park ONLY in staffed paid lots — Plaza Tamarindo underground ($5/day), Cala Luna behind Diria, or the gravel lots near Langosta bridge — avoid unpaved shoulder pullouts; (4) never leave ANYTHING visible in the car because the 'watching' racket pairs with smash-and-grabs; (5) in golf carts remember keys are often shared across rentals — photograph your cart's ID number before walking off; (6) report extortion to the Tamarindo Fuerza Pública (town entrance, near the Monkey Bar turn) or dial 911 / tourist line 2511-9260. How to avoid: Keep ₡500/₡1,000 coins in the cup holder — tip ₡1,000–₡2,000 (~$2–$4) before walking off. Park in paid staffed lots (Plaza Tamarindo $5, Cala Luna) — not unpaved shoulder pullouts. Never leave bags, phones, sunglasses, or electronics visible — guachis pair with smash-and-grabs. If extorted for $10+, roll windows mostly up and creep forward; don't argue roadside. Report extortion to Tamarindo Fuerza Pública (entrance to town) or dial 911 / 2511-9260.

Scam alert in Tamarindo, Costa Rica — Beach-Hustler 'Surf Instructor' Lesson & $200 Board-Damage Ambush (financial-fraud, severity: moderate). Tamarindo has ~40 legitimate surf schools (Iguana Surf, Kelly's Surf Shop, Witch's Rock Surf Camp) — and alongside them a beach-front ecosystem of freelancing 'instructors' the local cooperative openly calls a scam. Tico Times on X (Feb 2024) reported 'Tamarindo surf instructors organization reports 50+ unauthorized foreign surf teachers operating illegally — urging action to address unfair undercutting.' The classic sting has two variants. Variant A: approach on the beach, $40–$60 for a 'private' lesson, pay up front, instructor disappears or pushes you onto a damaged board and vanishes. Variant B is the canonical TripAdvisor case 'Beware predatory surf instructor William — San Jose, Costa Rica': an instructor 'William' gave one traveler a board that was too small, steered them onto rocks at Langosta, then produced pre-existing scratches 'noticed' on the fins and pointed to the contract — $200 'damage fee.' The traveler wrote: 'We've noticed some scratches everywhere on the board before renting it but they said it was just the coat, no need to put it on paper.' A parallel TripAdvisor thread 'SCAM ALERT — POLICE INVOLVED — Walter Surf Shop' (Jan 2020, still live 2025): 'Don't use this place. We were scammed and HELD UP before demanded to pay MONEY. We had to get the Police involved and luckily we are still alive.' February 2025 community surfing and Costa Rica travel threads confirm the pattern into 2026. Going rate for a legit 2-hour lesson in 2025/2026 is $54–$85 pp (Viator via Iguana, Kelly's, or Witch's Rock includes board + rash guard + insurance); beach-hustlers quote $30–$50 with no paperwork, no photos, no insurance, and a surprise $200 'board damage' invoice.

For travelers in 2025/2026 trying Tamarindo's beginner-friendly river-mouth waves: (1) book ONLY through ICT-certified operators — Iguana Surf (iguanasurf.net, $84 group / $120 private), Kelly's Surf Shop (TripAdvisor 4.4, 120+ reviews), or Witch's Rock Surf Camp at Langosta — verify licenses at visitcostarica.com; (2) ask to see the instructor's ICT carnet and INS insurance policy before handing over cash; (3) before the first paddle PHOTOGRAPH every side of the board (top, bottom, both rails, nose, tail, fins) and text the photos to yourself with a timestamp — kills the 'damage fee' move; (4) refuse any verbal 'scratches are just coating, no paperwork needed' pitch — no paperwork means no insurance; (5) pay by credit card (Visa/Mastercard dispute > cash); (6) beach-hustlers almost always approach with a single board, no branded shirt, no shop-front — walk into an Iguana or Kelly's shop instead; (7) escalations: Tamarindo Fuerza Pública (2653-0283) or 24/7 tourist line 2511-9260. How to avoid: Book via ICT-licensed schools — Iguana Surf, Kelly's Surf Shop, Witch's Rock Surf Camp ($54–$85 pp). Ask to see ICT carnet + INS insurance BEFORE paying; verify at visitcostarica.com. Photograph all sides of the board + text photos to yourself with timestamp before paddling. Pay by credit card (Visa/Mastercard) — cash has no recourse after a $200 'damage' invoice. Escalations: Tamarindo Fuerza Pública 2653-0283; tourist police 24/7 line 2511-9260.

Scam alert in Tamarindo, Costa Rica — Rental-Home & Airbnb Home Invasion — The Los Jobos Tamarindo Pattern (accommodation, severity: high). The US Embassy San José explicitly called this out in its November 25, 2025 Security Alert: 'Break-ins and armed robberies at vacation rentals have increased, particularly targeting foreign tourists.' The anchor case: Christopher Deir, a 40-year-old Canadian life coach from Toronto, was fatally shot during a home invasion at his rental house in the Los Jobos area of Tamarindo on July 11, 2025. OIJ reported that an intruder broke in; Deir's partner's screams drew him into the hallway where he was shot. A July 2025 community thread (41 upvotes) anchors the discussion, with one commenter (29 upvotes) reposting the OIJ account verbatim. An October 2025 community thread (369 upvotes) documents a parallel Tilarán case — one family was held at gunpoint 30 minutes at a Guanacaste Airbnb; robbers 'kept asking for the cocaine,' suggesting targeted scouted jobs. One traveler (37 upvotes) described 'a gang of thugs who have been terrorizing the area for months.' An August 2025 community 'Attempted Robbery on Honeymoon' post: a 5–6-flashlight invasion at a Playa Negra VRBO; the couple's husband had locked the second-floor gate; Vrbo demanded they 'work it out with the property owner' who told them to 'watch their backs.' An April 2025 community post (40 upvotes) — Playa Grande — a burglar took 3 laptops and $800 on day 2. Another traveler (48 upvotes) noted: 'Costa Rica Tourism Police are actively investigating theft operations targeting tourists in Airbnb rentals, especially in coastal and popular tourist areas.' Mechanics: Airbnb/VRBO calendars leak arrival times; isolated villas are scouted; 4–6-man gangs breach a second-floor window 9 PM–2 AM.

For travelers in 2025/2026: (1) SKIP isolated beachfront villas — book inside a 24-hour guarded gated community (Hacienda Pinilla, Reserva Conchal, Langosta Beach Club) or a hotel with armed guards (Diria Beach Resort, Tamarindo Diria, Witch's Rock Surf Camp); (2) verify security BEFORE booking — message the host: 24/7 armed guard? Panic button? Patrol logs? 'Yes to all three' in writing is the minimum bar; (3) don't advertise arrival time on social media or let the Airbnb calendar show 'first night'; (4) on arrival confirm every door, window, and second-floor gate — pile furniture at weak points as the honeymoon traveler did; (5) program 911 + OIJ 800-8000-645 + US Embassy San José 2519-2000 into speed dial; (6) if invaded: hide, call 911, don't confront — OIJ data confirms resistance correlates with shooting; (7) file at Tamarindo Fuerza Pública + OIJ within 24h for Vrbo/Airbnb refund and insurance claims. How to avoid: Stay inside 24/7 guarded gated communities (Hacienda Pinilla, Reserva Conchal) or guarded hotels. Message host IN WRITING: 24/7 guard? Panic button? Patrol logs? 'Yes' to all three or skip. Don't post arrival dates to social media; ask host to calendar-block two days either side. Program 911, OIJ 800-8000-645, US Embassy San José 2519-2000 into speed dial on arrival. If invaded: hide, call 911, do NOT resist; file at Tamarindo Fuerza Pública within 24h.

Scam alert in Tamarindo, Costa Rica — Rental-Car Relay-Theft & Main-Strip Smash-and-Grab outside Witch's Rock / Volcano Brewing (accommodation, severity: high). A January 2025 community post (187 upvotes) is the anchor case and the first widely-surfaced account of RFID relay theft in Costa Rica. One traveler and his wife — final lunch at Volcano Brewing/Witch's Rock Surf Camp in Tamarindo before their flight — parked 150 ft from their table on the main street, locked. Twenty minutes later their camera bag was emptied of $14,000 in pro camera gear + laptop + headphones — all neatly closed up again, bags untouched. Staff and police told them: RELAY THEFT. A thief with a signal-amplifier walks within 10 m of your table to capture the car's key-fob signal and relays it to an accomplice at the car who opens the keyless-entry locks without tripping the alarm. A Tile tracker in the camera bag was also stolen — these crews know exactly what they're looking for. One traveler (259 upvotes) wrote: 'Never leave anything in your car, ever.' Another: 'En el carro nunca.' A third cautioned: 'plenty of warnings… whether it's a touristy area or not.' The lower-tech smash-and-grab pattern runs alongside: a June 2025 community post documented a son's Beats stolen; one commenter: 'thefts of belongings in cars is probably one of the more common crimes… thieves wait and watch'; another: 'Tico Times reported 2 girls went into a gas station and came back to their car and everything was gone — just takes a minute or two while the owner is distracted.' Multiple 2024 and 2025 community traveler threads — including the widely-shared May 2024 'Tamarindo Watchmen' post (305 upvotes) — corroborate: the 'watchman' crew and the smash-and-grab crew often share the same ecosystem.

For travelers in 2025/2026: (1) EVERYTHING of value goes in the hotel/villa safe — not the trunk, not 'hidden'; never leave cameras, laptops, passports, AirTag/Tile, wallets, or designer sunglasses in a rental car; (2) buy a Faraday key-fob pouch ($10 Amazon) BEFORE the trip — blocks the key-fob relay signal; put the fob inside when you sit down at Volcano Brewing; (3) use the key's physical-button unlock, NOT proximity — disables relay attack; (4) prefer paid/staffed lots (Plaza Tamarindo underground $5, Cala Luna, Calle Central Main Lot) over unpaved main-strip shoulder; (5) take a daypack into every restaurant, beach, and surf break — dry-bag-in-the-water rule applies; (6) if hit: file OIJ 800-8000-645 + Tamarindo Fuerza Pública within 24h — required for travel insurance (Amex Platinum, Chase Sapphire Reserve, Capital One Venture X all cover rental-car theft with a filed report). How to avoid: NEVER leave valuables in the car — hotel safe only; treat every parking spot as compromised. Use a Faraday key-fob pouch ($10) + physical-button unlock instead of proximity unlock. Park in staffed paid lots (Plaza Tamarindo, Cala Luna, Diria) not main-strip shoulder pullouts. Waterproof dry-bag in the water with passport/phone/cash every surf; daypack into restaurants. If hit: file OIJ 800-8000-645 + Fuerza Pública within 24h for Amex/Chase/CapOne insurance.

Scam alert in Tamarindo, Costa Rica — LIR Shuttle / Pirate-Taxi Tamarindo Gouge — $80–$150 for a $55 Ride (transport, severity: moderate). The legit 2025/2026 shuttle economy Tamarindo ↔ LIR (Guanacaste / Daniel Oduber) is well-established: Tamarindo Daily Airport Shuttles and Interbus run shared shuttles ~$29–$45 pp pre-booked; private transfer LIR ↔ Tamarindo is $120–$135 1–4 pax (Tamarindo Shuttle, RideCR, Easy Ride); drive is 1–1.5 hours. Three scams run parallel. First, LIR arrivals-hall pirate taxis — non-orange unauthorized cars that crowd arrivals and quote $100–$150 for what should be $45 shared / $120 private; ride ends at a 'broken meter' argument and cash-only demand. One January 2024 community traveler wrote: 'in Liberia Costa Rica… $9 ride and the guy dropped us off and didn't complete the ride on the app. I got a charge over $30.' Second, hostel/beach-bar 'friend with a van' — in a July 2025 community thread, local respondents warn of 'old beat-up pirate taxis missing official logo and tags' and note 'at worst they could rob you, or take a long route.' Third, the Tamarindo main-street red-taxi 'broken meter' trick — driver quotes ₡15,000–₡25,000 ($29–$48) for a ₡5,000 (~$10) in-town hop; one commenter advises: 'if a red taxi is using the meter and says it's broken, he's trying to scam you. Get out and try another.' Uber IS available in Tamarindo — one commenter notes: 'Uber works great in the Tamarindo area' — but is gray-legal and drivers ask you to sit up front. An October 2025 community post (124 upvotes) documents a Puerto Viejo Uber robbing a passenger of $130. DiDi is a cheaper Guanacaste alternative per community reports.

For travelers in 2025/2026: (1) pre-book LIR ↔ Tamarindo via Interbus.com, Gray Line, Tamarindo Transfers, or Easy Ride — $29–$45 pp shared, $120–$135 private; save the confirmation email + driver name + vehicle plate BEFORE landing; (2) at LIR arrivals walk past 'taxi taxi' curb freelancers to your named-sign driver only; legit airport taxis are orange; (3) in town use Uber or DiDi (₡2,000–₡5,000 per hop) or RideCR pro service; (4) red taxis: say 'maría por favor' before moving; 'broken' = get out; MOPT LIR→Tamarindo range $85–$95 (above = scam); (5) NEVER accept a 'friend with a van' pushed by the hostel — staff take commissions not safety audits; (6) solo women late: Uber or hotel shuttle, not a street taxi; file complaints at ctp.go.cr/inconformidades or call 911 / tourist line 2511-9260. How to avoid: Pre-book via Interbus, Gray Line, Tamarindo Transfers, Easy Ride — $29–$45 shared / $120–$135 private. At LIR arrivals walk past 'taxi taxi' freelancers to your named-sign driver only. In town use Uber or DiDi (₡2,000–₡5,000 per hop) or RideCR pro service. Red taxis: say 'maría por favor' before moving; broken meter = get out; MOPT LIR→Tamarindo $85–$95. File complaints at ctp.go.cr/inconformidades or dial 911 / tourist police 2511-9260.

Scam alert in Tamarindo, Costa Rica — Tamarindo Banco Nacional / BAC ATM Skimming + Counterfeit-Bill Swap (financial-fraud, severity: moderate). A 2024 archived community thread documents the Tamarindo-specific skimming hit: 'This happened to me as well a couple of weeks ago at the Banco Nacional in Tamarindo… Better to use the BAC ATM machines.' A parallel 2024 'Lost business visa in Tamarindo, Guanacaste Province ATM' thread anchors card-eating and retention fraud at the same ATM cluster. An April 2025 community post warns older expats to 'use BAC or BCR only, never Banco Nacional' and pull colones to avoid the DCC (dynamic-currency-conversion) upcharge. Three scams run: (1) card-skimming overlays on standalone strip-side ATMs — card data + PIN captured, cloned within days; (2) 'ATM ate my card' — device-level retention brackets prevent return, helpful 'stranger' observes your PIN re-entry; (3) the restaurant-adjacent counterfeit-bill swap, where change includes a torn or copied ₡10,000 or ₡20,000 note. A 2025 community traveler (10 upvotes) advises: 'pay in colones (and beware of the "this bill is counterfeit" scam)' — driver swaps your real ₡20,000 for a pre-palmed counterfeit. Tamarindo beach-restaurant variant: tourist hands real USD $100; waiter returns saying bill is 'torn or marked' and demands a replacement. CR banks and shops DO legally refuse damaged US notes — but the quick-switch uses that real rule to swap your good bill for a genuinely torn one.

For travelers in 2025/2026: (1) withdraw cash only INSIDE a bank branch during business hours — Scotiabank, BAC Credomatic, BCR, or Banco Nacional lobby — not from standalone curb units; branches have guards and tamper-checked machines; (2) withdraw COLONES not USD — the USD option at ATMs runs DCC ~5–9% worse; max legal foreign withdrawal is ₡400,000/day (~$770); (3) pull ₡10,000 and ₡20,000 notes for daily spend — removes counterfeit-USD-swap exposure; (4) inspect every colón note handed back — legit ₡20,000 has a Carlos Luis Fallas Sibaja watermark and color-shifting thread; counterfeits feel plastic-smooth; (5) use a no-FTF credit card (Capital One Venture, Chase Sapphire, Amex Platinum) for restaurants and hotels, colones cash only for vendors and tips; (6) if you bring USD, bring only pristine post-2013 bills (CR banks reject torn/marked/pre-2013 notes by law); (7) if skimmed: freeze the card within 30 minutes, file at Tamarindo Fuerza Pública + OIJ 800-8000-645, save the ATM receipt as chargeback evidence. How to avoid: Use ATMs INSIDE bank branches during business hours (Scotiabank, BAC, BCR) — avoid curb units. Always withdraw colones not USD — decline DCC; saves 5–9% on every pull. Inspect every ₡20,000 note for Carlos Luis Fallas watermark + color-shift thread. Bring only pristine post-2013 USD bills; carry a credit card (Capital One, Chase, Amex) for restaurants. If skimmed: call bank within 30 min, file at Tamarindo Fuerza Pública + OIJ 800-8000-645.

Scam alert in Tamarindo, Costa Rica — Tamarindo Nightlife Drink-Spiking & 'Sexpat' Prostitution-Ring Extortion at the Casino (drug-crime, severity: high). An August 2023 community post anchors the pattern. Across 2024-2025 community threads, the pattern shows up in multiple traveler voices. One commenter (10 upvotes) noted: 'Sexpat grifters all over Guanacaste these days. The whole region has shifted considerably and isn't what it once was. There are plenty of drug gangs and prostitution rings that have moved into the area as well.' Another (7 upvotes): 'Avoid tamarindo at all… tamarindo and jaco are gentrified and that's the main reason prostitutes are all over the place.' An August 2023 community post (26 upvotes) documents the 'bartender takes you home' variant: a flirty female bartender says she lives 'an hour drive outside town,' needs somewhere to stay after her shift. For travelers in 2025/2026: (1) never accept a drink from a stranger already at the bar — buy your own and watch it poured; use Nightcap / SipChip test strips ($12 Amazon) if uncertain; (2) if you meet someone who needs 'somewhere to stay,' decline and book them an Uber home — as one traveler put it, 'if you aren't into it send her home in an Uber'; (3) if pressed for $500 next morning, refuse, pack, leave; call 911 not pay — pimp threats are usually bluffs; (4) Costa Rican hotels require cédula (ID) for every overnight guest (per community reports) — a partner who won't show cédula is a red flag; (5) at the casino, cash the bare minimum chips you're willing to lose; never walk to the ATM drunk — use the in-hotel ATM at Diria under camera; (6) the unlit beach path between Monkey Bar and Langosta is a documented mugging corridor — take an Uber or walk the main road; (7) emergency: 911, US Embassy 2519-2000, Tamarindo Fuerza Pública — file drink-spiking WITHIN 6 HOURS (toxicology window). How to avoid: Buy and watch your own drinks; carry Nightcap/SipChip test strips if uncertain. Anyone asking to stay the night — Uber them home; decline and still enjoy the date earlier next day. Demand cédula at any hotel check-in; a refusal = leave; Costa Rican law requires it. If extorted for $500: refuse, pack, call 911 + US Embassy 2519-2000 — don't pay. Drink-spiking: file at Fuerza Pública within 6h for toxicology + OIJ + travel-insurance claim.

Scam alert in Taormina, Italy — The Catania Fontanarossa Airport Taxi Overcharge to Taormina (transport, severity: high). Unlicensed and discretionary-pricing drivers quote €150–€250 for the 55km Catania Fontanarossa to Taormina run against a regulated €90–€100 zone fare. A TripAdvisor Sicily forum topic 'Watch out for official taxi scams from Catania Airport' documents a driver who dropped from €250 to €185 and then €135 when the hotel concierge intervened. Pre-book a licensed NCC with a quoted fixed fare (€85–€110 with receipt). Demand a receipt with taxi number, time, route, and total.

Scam alert in Taormina, Italy — The Teatro Antico "Skip-the-Line" Ticket Markup (overcharging, severity: high). The Teatro Antico di Taormina official price is €14 intero / €7 ridotto at the Sicilia Region archaeological gate (parchiarcheologici.regione.sicilia.it). Third-party resellers on Corso Umberto bundle the same entry at €24–€26 as 'skip the line' or 'guided' — sicilia.info, City Sightseeing, Tiqets and Musement all list €24+ packages. A May 20, 2025 Gazzetta del Sud cronaca ('Taormina, i turisti pagano il biglietto al Teatro Antico ma dentro trovano impalcature e teli') documented tourists with pre-paid tour tickets arriving to find scaffolding and tarps inside, with no refund offered. If scaffolding is visible from outside, ask what percentage of the theater is under restoration before paying. Only 'skip-the-line' through refundable platforms (GetYourGuide, Tiqets, Headout). Always pay by card for chargeback recourse.

Scam alert in Taormina, Italy — The Isola Bella Fake-Ticket & "Beach Massage" Hustle (fraud, severity: high). Isola Bella is a WWF-managed nature reserve charging €5 intero / €2.50 ridotto (per the April 2024 98zero.com reopening notice) — or €6/€3 in some seasons via traveltaormina.com, with €1 Messina-province-resident rate. A Facebook 'Vacanze in Sicilia' post documents a tourist being scammed out of €1,000 by a fake 'resident' ticket reseller. A TripAdvisor 'Beware the massage scam' review documents Asian women working together to impose unquoted €40–€80 'massage' fees on beach-goers after offering a 'free' sample — the same MO runs at Mondello (Palermo) and other Sicilian beaches. How to avoid: Pay only at the Isola Bella causeway booth (WWF/Comune) — €5 intero / €2.50 ridotto, printed ticket with date and barcode. Refuse any roaming massage, 'sample', or bracelet with a firm 'no grazie' — physical contact is the charge cue. Use the funivia (€3/€6) rather than the stairs if mobility is a concern, and buy funivia tickets only at the funivia booth. Carry only €40–€60 cash to the beach.

Scam alert in Taormina, Italy — Mount Etna Unlicensed Guide & Summit-Access Scam (fraud, severity: high).
